metadata.title: IR band map for CO₂ hydrogenation
metadata.description: Approximate band positions for surface and gas-phase species in CO₂ hydrogenation. Exact positions depend on support, coverage, and reaction conditions. The asterisk (*) denotes a surface-bound species.

co2_hydrogenation_rwgs_ch4.label: IR: CO₂ to CO/CH₄
co2_hydrogenation_rwgs_ch4.note: Everything the RWGS and CO₂ methanation story touches.

co_methanation.label: IR: CO methanation
co_methanation.note: Everything the CO₂ methanation story touches.

adsorbed.label: IR: Adsorbed & surface species
adsorbed.note: Everything that only exists because there is a solid under it.

fluids.label: Raman: Gases + Fluids
fluids.note: The free molecules only: reactants and products as gas or fluid, dissolved ones included, no surface species. Their adsorbed bands are left out too.

co2_oxides.label: Raman: CO₂ with Al₂O₃ and SiO₂
co2_oxides.note: CO₂ beside the lattice lines of the two oxides most often in the beam with it, as a support, a bed or a window; every other family is left out.

raman_oxides.label: Raman: Oxides
raman_oxides.note: The lattice lines of the oxides themselves, the specimen rather than anything on it: alumina, silica, indium oxide and titania.

carbonate.label: Carbonate
carbonate.note: Monodentate and bidentate coordination are `topology` on the band, not separate species.

formic_acid.label: Formic acid
formic_acid.note: Formate that has kept its proton: HCOOH adsorbed without dissociating. The C=O stretch near 1700 to 1730 cm⁻¹ is what separates it from formate, which has no localised carbonyl at all, so an absorption in that window is the test for whether the acid dissociated on contact.

carbonic_acid.label: Carbonic acid
carbonic_acid.note: Carbonic acid held on a hydroxylated silica surface. Free H₂CO₃ is famously unstable, but multiple hydrogen bonds to surface silanols stabilise it enough to be seen: it sits in equilibrium with adsorbed CO₂ and water rather than existing on its own.

methylenebisoxy.label: Methylenebisoxy
methylenebisoxy.note: Formate one hydrogenation step further on, with both oxygens still held by the surface; also written dioxymethylene. It sits between HCOO* and H₂CO* on the methanol path, and because it cannot be dosed, the sources that name it rest on a calculated frequency plus a band that rises and falls out of step with the formate it comes from.

acyl.label: Acyl
acyl.note: Generic acyl group; the R is left open because the sources do not fix it.

hydroxyl.label: Surface OH
hydroxyl.note: A hydroxyl on an oxide surface. Deliberately not split into isolated and hydrogen-bonded: that split needs evidence a source actually gives, and where a paper does resolve several hydroxyls it resolves them by the cation they sit on, which the claim records as its site.

o_vacancy.label: Oxygen vacancy
o_vacancy.note: A missing lattice oxygen in a reducible oxide, and the electrons left behind with it. Not a molecule and it has no normal modes; it is here because the electron trapped in it absorbs infrared light, which puts a band on the chart that belongs to no adsorbate.

gallia.label: Gallia framework
gallia.note: The Ga-O network of a gallium oxide support itself, not anything adsorbed on it. Here for the same reason as the silica framework and the oxygen vacancy: its own vibrations put bands on the chart that no adsorbate made.

titania.label: Titania framework
titania.note: The Ti-O network of titanium dioxide itself, not anything adsorbed on it: its lattice phonons and the second-order bands of the crystal. Which polymorph a band belongs to, anatase or rutile, is said by the surface the claim names, not here.

alumina.label: Alumina framework
alumina.note: The Al-O network of an aluminium oxide itself, not anything adsorbed on it: its lattice phonons, and the defect lines of the crystal. Which polymorph a band belongs to is said by the surface the claim names (α-Al₂O₃, sapphire), not here.

silica.label: Silica framework
silica.note: The Si-O-Si network of a silica or silicate support itself, not anything adsorbed on it. Here for the same reason as the oxygen vacancy: its overtones put bands on the chart that no adsorbate made.

indium_oxide.label: Indium oxide framework
indium_oxide.note: The In-O network of indium oxide itself, not anything adsorbed on it: its lattice phonons. Which polymorph a band belongs to is said by the surface the claim names (c-In₂O₃), not here.

hydride.label: Hydride
hydride.note: Metal hydride from heterolytic H₂ dissociation. Written metal-generic; the band names the element.

h2.label: H₂
h2.note: The highest-frequency and simplest vibration in the atlas. Infrared-forbidden, being homonuclear, so every band on it is Raman.

n2.label: N₂
n2.note: Infrared-forbidden, being homonuclear, so every band on it is Raman. Present as the diluent and internal standard of a flame or a reactor feed rather than as a reactant.

o2.label: O₂
o2.note: No bands in the atlas: here for the vibration-modes page.

f2.label: F₂
f2.note: No bands in the atlas: here for the vibration-modes page.

cl2.label: Cl₂
cl2.note: No bands in the atlas: here for the vibration-modes page.

br2.label: Br₂
br2.note: No bands in the atlas: here for the vibration-modes page.

i2.label: I₂
i2.note: No bands in the atlas: here for the vibration-modes page.

nh3.label: NH₃
nh3.note: No bands in the atlas: here for the vibration-modes page, as the counterpart to the diatomics where every mode is active in both techniques.

ag_0.label: Ag⁰
ag_0.note: Metallic silver. Binds atomic hydrogen weakly and formate strongly enough, which is the combination that gives it the lowest barrier to formate of the three coinage metals.

ag_111.label: Ag⁰(111)
ag_111.note: Metallic silver exposing its (111) plane, the close-packed face of an fcc metal: a hexagonal layer in which each surface atom keeps nine of its twelve neighbours, the smoothest and lowest-energy face. It offers atop, bridge and two kinds of threefold hollow, fcc and hcp, which differ only in whether an atom of the second layer lies beneath. It is the slab a calculation reaches for when it models a silver electrode. A refinement of Ag⁰ by its facet: a search for Ag⁰ finds it.

au_0.label: Au⁰
au_0.note: Metallic gold. Binds formate too weakly to accumulate it, the opposite failure to copper, which binds hydrogen too strongly.

cu_0.label: Cu⁰
cu_0.note: Metallic copper. Carries ν(CO) roughly 40–80 cm⁻¹ below the Cu⁺ carbonyl.

cu_110.label: Cu⁰(110)
cu_110.note: Metallic copper exposing its (110) plane, the most open of the three low-index faces of an fcc metal: close-packed rows of atoms separated by troughs, each surface atom keeping seven of its twelve neighbours. CO sits atop the rows. A refinement of Cu⁰ by its facet, so a search for Cu⁰ finds it.

pd_100.label: Pd⁰(100)
pd_100.note: Metallic palladium exposing its (100) plane: a square net of surface atoms, each keeping eight of its twelve neighbours, with atop, twofold bridge and fourfold hollow sites. CO prefers the bridge on this face, which is why its band lies in the bridged range across most of the coverage. A refinement of Pd⁰ by its facet, so a search for Pd⁰ finds it.

pt_100.label: Pt⁰(100)
pt_100.note: Metallic platinum exposing its (100) plane: a square net of surface atoms, each keeping eight of its twelve neighbours, with atop, bridge and fourfold hollow sites. Clean, the top layer reconstructs into a denser quasi-hexagonal one; adsorbed CO lifts that back to the square (1×1) net, on which CO sits atop and bridged. A refinement of Pt⁰ by its facet, so a search for Pt⁰ finds it.

si_0.label: Si⁰
si_0.note: Elemental silicon, the internal-reflection prism a film electrode is deposited on.

ag_1p.label: Ag⁺
ag_1p.note: Oxidised silver, carrying a carbonyl well above the gas-phase CO value because there is little back-donation to lower it. Its position moves when the silver is alloyed, which is what makes it a probe of alloying rather than only of oxidation state.

al_3p.label: Al³⁺
al_3p.note: An aluminium cation of alumina or of a zeolite framework. Coordinatively unsaturated, it is the Lewis acid site of γ-Al₂O₃.

au_1p.label: Au⁺
au_1p.note: Oxidised gold. Distinguished from metallic Au⁰ by a carbonyl above 2120 cm⁻¹; the attribution is contested, since restructured metallic gold gives bands low enough to confuse the picture from the other side.

ce_3p.label: Ce³⁺
ce_3p.note: A reduced cerium cation, left beside an oxygen vacancy when ceria gives up lattice oxygen; the cerium side of a reduced metal-ceria perimeter.

ce_4p.label: Ce⁴⁺
ce_4p.note: The cerium cation of stoichiometric CeO₂.

cu_1p.label: Cu⁺
cu_1p.note: The carbonyl marker that separates a partly oxidised copper surface from Cu⁰.

cu_2p.label: Cu²⁺
cu_2p.note: Fully oxidised copper, carrying a carbonyl some 25 cm⁻¹ above the Cu⁺ one. Rare in this dataset, because a working methanol catalyst is reduced: where a source reports it on one, it is claiming a minority site that survived the reduction, and the claim is worth reading against the Cu⁺ attribution it sits next to.

fe_2p.label: Fe²⁺
fe_2p.note: The ferrous cation of magnetite, Fe₃O₄.

fe_3p.label: Fe³⁺
fe_3p.note: The ferric cation of haematite and of magnetite.

ga_3p.label: Ga³⁺
ga_3p.note: A gallium cation of Ga₂O₃ or of a Ga-doped oxide. The Ga-H papers write Ga-H and state no charge; they are filed here because the hydride forms by heterolytic H₂ splitting on a Ga³⁺-O²⁻ pair, which is the author’s reading rather than the papers’.

mo_4p.label: Mo⁴⁺
mo_4p.note: A reduced molybdenum cation of MoOₓ, as in MoO₂.

mo_5p.label: Mo⁵⁺
mo_5p.note: A partly reduced molybdenum cation of MoOₓ, beside an oxygen vacancy.

mo_6p.label: Mo⁶⁺
mo_6p.note: The fully oxidised molybdenum cation of MoO₃ and of the unreduced MoOₓ layer.

mo_dp.label: Moᵟ⁺
mo_dp.note: Molybdenum reduced below Mo⁴⁺ with no integer charge assigned, written δ+ the way the MoOₓ literature writes it. The one cation here without an oxidation state, because δ is the statement: partly reduced, not a stated charge.

la_3p.label: La³⁺
la_3p.note: A lanthanum cation dispersed in alumina as a stabiliser, not a phase of its own.

ni_2p.label: Ni²⁺
ni_2p.note: The nickel cation of NiO and of the NiAl₂O₄ spinel.

si_4p.label: Si⁴⁺
si_4p.note: The silicon of a silica or silicate network, written as the cation it formally is. Too shielded to bind most adsorbates itself; the silanol beside it does.

o_2m.label: O²⁻
o_2m.note: A lattice oxide anion, the O of every oxide component. The basic half of a cation-anion pair; heterolytic H₂ splitting and carbonate formation both start on it.

h_bronsted.label: H⁺
h_bronsted.note: A proton-donating surface hydroxyl, as opposed to the Lewis-acidic cations above.

sioh.label: Si–OH
sioh.note: A silanol, the hydroxyl that terminates a silica surface. Recorded so the Ag⁰-SiO₂ perimeter can name a site on the silica side rather than the whole oxide.

ga_oct.label: Ga³⁺(o)
ga_oct.note: Octahedrally coordinated gallium, the Ga³⁺(o) of β-Ga₂O₃, its charge inherited from Ga³⁺. Coordinatively unsaturated at the surface, which is why it, and not the saturated tetrahedral site, is where H₂ dissociates in the calculations.

ga_tet.label: Ga³⁺(t)
ga_tet.note: Tetrahedrally coordinated gallium, the Ga³⁺(t) of β-Ga₂O₃, its charge inherited from Ga³⁺. Its hydride and hydroxyl sit about 25 and 150 cm⁻¹ above those of the octahedral site, which is how the two are told apart.

o_vac.label: Vₒ
o_vac.note: A bare oxygen vacancy. Listed on its own so ensembles can point at it.

o_vac_1p.label: Vₒ⁺
o_vac_1p.note: An oxygen vacancy that has given up one of its two electrons, the donor centre whose photoionization to the conduction band is the broad electronic absorption under an operando Cu/ZnO spectrum. Its concentration, not just its existence, is what the band measures.

zn_ovac_hf.label: Zn–Vₒ–Hf
zn_ovac_hf.note: An oxygen vacancy flanked by Zn and Hf: the two cations and the vacancy act as one site.

ag_sio2_interface.label: Ag⁰-SiO₂ perimeter
ag_sio2_interface.note: The rim where a silver nanoparticle meets the silica, named as the active site for methyl formate: the formate sits on the metal and the carbonic acid and adsorbed methanol on the silica beside it, so the esterification happens where the two meet rather than on either alone.

pt0_ceo2_interface.label: Pt⁰-CeO₂ perimeter
pt0_ceo2_interface.note: The perimeter where Pt particles meet ceria: Pt⁰ on one side, the ceria lattice on the other, Ce⁴⁺ and O²⁻, and under reduction Ce³⁺ beside oxygen vacancies (2 Ce⁴⁺ + O²⁻ → 2 Ce³⁺ + Vₒ + ½ O₂, eased by hydrogen spilling over from the metal). Vico van Berkel and Urakawa write of a highly reduced ceria surface and of oxygen vacancies; Ce³⁺ is the author's reading of that phrase, the standard one.

fe3o4.label: Fe₃O₄
fe3o4.note: Magnetite with no termination stated. The two facet variants below point at it, and all three are the same compound: only the cut differs.

fe3o4_001.label: Fe₃O₄(001)
fe3o4_001.note: Magnetite cut on the (001) plane. Magnetite is an inverse spinel, Fe³⁺ on the tetrahedral sites and Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ on the octahedral ones, and this face is commonly described as ending in a layer of octahedral iron and oxygen, reconstructed (√2×√2)R45° by an ordered array of cation vacancies just beneath it. A refinement of Fe₃O₄ by its facet: the cut is a termination, not a composition, so a search for Fe₃O₄ finds it and a search for the (001) cut finds only it.

fe3o4_111.label: Fe₃O₄(111)
fe3o4_111.note: Magnetite cut on the (111) plane, parallel to the close-packed oxygen layers of the spinel. The termination depends on preparation and is still debated; the one most often reported is a quarter monolayer of tetrahedral iron above a close-packed oxygen layer. It is kept apart from Fe₃O₄(001) because the two cuts expose different Fe spacings and carry different formate geometries: a structural difference, not a compositional one. A refinement of Fe₃O₄ by its facet, so a search for Fe₃O₄ finds it.

ga2o3.label: Ga₂O₃
ga2o3.note: Gallia, as a component of a promoted catalyst and as a specimen in its own right. Made of Ga³⁺ and O²⁻. The β polymorph carries tetrahedral and octahedral gallium, which is why hydride and hydroxyl bands on it come in pairs; those two are refinements of Ga³⁺, named on a claim only where the paper resolves the coordination.

hfo2.label: HfO₂
hfo2.note: Hafnia, ZrO₂'s chemical twin. Monoclinic when precipitated and calcined on its own; the Zn-doped solid solutions are cubic and are the znhfox specimen, not this.

kbr.label: KBr
kbr.note: Potassium bromide, the infrared-transparent salt a powder is diluted in for DRIFTS or pressed into for a pellet. Named only as a diluent on a claim, never as a part of a catalyst.

moo3.label: MoO₃
moo3.note: Molybdenum trioxide, all Mo⁶⁺: the crystalline phase XRD shows on an unreduced MoO₃/TiO₂, and the parent of the reduced MoOₓ.

moox.label: MoOₓ
moox.note: Molybdenum oxide reduced below MoO₃, a refinement of MoO₃ by its stoichiometry as ZnO₁₋ₓ is of ZnO: the reduced, oxygen-deficient state is the point, and its vacancies are what CO₂ re-oxidises. Not a mixture of MoO₃ and MoO₂ phases: on Pt/MoOₓ/TiO₂ the MoO₃ reflections fade on reduction and no crystalline Mo oxide is left (Toyao). The reduced cations Mo⁵⁺, Mo⁴⁺ and Moᵟ⁺ are the general MoOₓ literature's; Toyao's XANES shows only that Mo is reduced below Mo⁶⁺.

nial2o4.label: NiAl₂O₄
nial2o4.note: Nickel aluminate spinel, formed where Ni reacts with an alumina support on calcination; harder to reduce than NiO.

nio.label: NiO
nio.note: Nickel oxide, the phase a calcined Ni catalyst carries before it is reduced to the metal.

sio2_fumed.label: fumed SiO₂
sio2_fumed.note: Amorphous fumed silica (Cab-O-Sil, Aerosil), the high-area powder used as a catalyst support.

sio2_glass.label: SiO₂ glass
sio2_glass.note: Vitreous silica, v-SiO₂: a dense glass, here sintered from fumed silica or melted, rather than a high-area powder.

sio2_cristobalite.label: β-cristobalite
sio2_cristobalite.note: The high-temperature cristobalite polymorph of silica, which a silica glass starts to crystallise into when sintered near 1450 °C.

sio2_quartz.label: α-quartz
sio2_quartz.note: The common crystalline polymorph of silica, which turns into the closely related β-quartz above about 900 K.

sno2.label: SnO₂
sno2.note: Tin dioxide, the classic oxide cathode for CO₂ reduction to formate. Under strongly cathodic potentials it is not stable: a Pourbaix analysis at pH 6.8 puts metallic Sn as the stable phase near −1.1 V vs. RHE, so the entry names what was put in the cell, not what the surface is during reduction.

tio2_anatase.label: anatase TiO₂
tio2_anatase.note: Anatase, the tetragonal TiO₂ polymorph (I4₁/amd) that low-temperature syntheses and most catalyst supports give. It converts irreversibly to rutile on heating, in fine powders from about 600 to 750 °C rather than the 900 °C and more of single crystals.

tio2_rutile.label: rutile TiO₂
tio2_rutile.note: Rutile, the tetragonal TiO₂ polymorph (P4₂/mnm) that is stable at every temperature and the one anatase turns into on heating.

zno_1mx.label: ZnO₁₋ₓ
zno_1mx.note: Zinc oxide that has lost lattice oxygen under reduction, a refinement of ZnO by its stoichiometry: it is still ZnO, with oxygen vacancies added to its parts. A search for ZnO finds it.

al2o3_alpha.label: α-Al₂O₃
al2o3_alpha.note: Corundum, the low-area thermodynamically stable alumina, used as a reference oxide or as an inert diluent.

in2o3.label: In₂O₃
in2o3.note: Indium oxide, the reducible oxide whose oxygen vacancies are the methanol-synthesis sites on In₂O₃ catalysts.

in2o3_c.label: c-In₂O₃
in2o3_c.note: Cubic bixbyite In₂O₃ (PDF 06-0416), the stable polymorph and the one precipitation and calcination give.

sapphire.label: Sapphire
sapphire.note: α-Al₂O₃ grown as one crystal: a window, a rod or a substrate rather than a powder. A refinement of α-Al₂O₃ by form, because a single crystal's Raman lines are sharp and their relative intensities depend on how the crystal is turned to the laser, which a powder averages away. Which axis faced the laser, where a paper gives it, goes in the claim's note: it moves no line.

al2o3_gamma.label: γ-Al₂O₃
al2o3_gamma.note: Gamma alumina, the high-area transition alumina used as a support; its strongest Lewis sites are coordinatively unsaturated Al³⁺.

ag_au.label: Ag/Au on Si
ag_au.note: Ag/Au deposited on a silicon prism: the layers, whatever shape they were made in. The film electrode is its refinement by form.

ag_au_film.label: Ag/Au on Si, film electrode
ag_au_film.note: A SEIRAS working electrode: a chemically deposited Au film of about 60 nm on a Si prism, with Ag electrodeposited over it. The silver is what faces the electrolyte, so it is the only site listed; the gold is an underlayer that carries the surface enhancement, and the silicon is the prism the beam comes through, which is optics rather than catalyst and is left out of the elements.

ag_sio2.label: Ag/SiO₂
ag_sio2.note: Silver nanoparticles under 11 nm at 1 wt % on a 155 m² g⁻¹ silica, by wetness impregnation. Silica is chosen as a neutral support so the metal is what differs; it makes no methyl formate without the metal present.

au_si.label: Au on Si
au_si.note: Au deposited on a silicon prism: the layers, whatever shape they were made in. The film electrode is its refinement by form.

au_film.label: Au on Si, film electrode
au_film.note: A chemically deposited Au film of about 60 nm on a Si prism, the underlayer the Ag, Cu and SnO₂ SEIRAS electrodes are built on, measured bare as a control. The silicon prism is optics, not catalyst.

au_ag_silicalite.label: Au-Ag/silicalite-1
au_ag_silicalite.note: Gold and silver nanoparticles embedded in silicalite-1, the all-silica MFI zeotype. Recorded with sio2 as its component rather than with zsm5: silicalite-1 has no aluminium and therefore none of the exchange sites that make ZSM-5 what it is.

au_sio2.label: Au/SiO₂
au_sio2.note: Gold nanoparticles under 11 nm at 1 wt % on silica, prepared alongside the Cu and Ag counterparts so the three coinage metals can be compared on one support.

co_al2o3.label: Co/Al₂O₃
co_al2o3.note: 14% Co on γ-alumina (85 m² g⁻¹, calcined at 500 °C), prepared after Shi et al. with citric acid, as Paredes-Nunez et al. describe it.

co_siralox.label: Co/Siralox
co_siralox.note: Cobalt on Siralox, a commercial silica-alumina of 5% SiO₂ and 95% Al₂O₃. Kept apart from co_al2o3: the support differs, and so does the carbonyl position reported on it. SiO₂ is not listed as a component: at 5% it dopes the alumina rather than forming a phase of its own, so the part is the Si⁴⁺ site. The paper names no alumina phase, so the support is plain Al₂O₃.

cu_gazrox.label: Cu-GaZrOₓ
cu_gazrox.note: Coprecipitated Cu-Ga-Zr mixed oxide, around 20 wt% Cu. Sources publish it as a series with different Ga and Zr loadings, written Cu-GaZrOₓ-Z where Z is Zr/(Zr+Cu+Ga) as a molar percentage; the family is recorded here and the individual member named in the note, since the distinction the spectra turn on is against the Cu-free GaZrOₓ rather than between members.

cuga_sio2.label: Cu-Ga₂O₃/SiO₂
cuga_sio2.note: Ga₂O₃-promoted Cu on silica, published as a loading series written CuGa(x) where x is the Ga/(Cu+Ga) molar ratio. The family is recorded here and the member named in the note, because the distinction the spectra turn on is against the Ga-free cu_sio2 rather than between members: the Cu⁺ carbonyl is absent without Ga and its area grows with the loading.

cu_zsm5.label: Cu-ZSM-5
cu_zsm5.note: Copper-exchanged ZSM-5, reduced in CO before adsorption to raise the share of Cu⁺. Built on H-ZSM-5: Zdravkova et al. calcine NH₄-ZSM-5 (Si/Al 25) and exchange copper into it, and at about 1 wt% Cu most framework charges are still balanced by protons, whose bridging hydroxyls the spectra show. Their aluminol band at 3664 cm⁻¹ points to some extra-framework alumina as well, not listed as a part while no claim turns on it.

cu_au.label: Cu/Au on Si
cu_au.note: Cu/Au deposited on a silicon prism: the layers, whatever shape they were made in. The film electrode is its refinement by form.

cu_au_film.label: Cu/Au on Si, film electrode
cu_au_film.note: A SEIRAS working electrode: a chemically deposited Au film of about 60 nm on a Si prism, with Cu electrodeposited over it, roughly 150 monolayers. The copper is what faces the electrolyte, so it is the only site listed; the gold underlayer carries the enhancement and should not be exposed, which a CO band above 2100 cm⁻¹ (CO on Au) would reveal. The silicon prism is optics, not catalyst.

cu_sio2.label: Cu/SiO₂
cu_sio2.note: Copper on silica with no promoter. Silica is close to inert here, so this is the reference against which a promoter's effect is read, and it is listed with Cu⁰ alone: the sources that pair it with a promoted counterpart find no Cu⁺ carbonyl on it at all.

cu_zro2.label: Cu/ZrO₂
cu_zro2.note: Copper on monoclinic zirconia by incipient wetness, 6 wt% Cu, calcined at 450 °C and reduced in situ at 350 °C. The zirconia carries about 93 % of the surface area, which is why almost every band on it is a zirconia band and why the copper-bound formate had to be dug out of a difference spectrum.

cuga_sio2_somc.label: CuGa/SiO₂
cuga_sio2_somc.note: Cu nanoparticles on silica decorated with isolated Ga³⁺ sites, made by surface organometallic chemistry: 3.88 wt% Cu, 1.61 wt% Ga, Ga/Cu 0.40. A different material from cuga_sio2, which carries a Ga₂O₃ phase: here the gallium is single cations, fully re-oxidised under reaction, with no oxide phase.

cuin_sio2.label: CuIn/SiO₂
cuin_sio2.note: Cu nanoparticles on silica decorated with isolated In³⁺ sites, made by surface organometallic chemistry: 3.81 wt% Cu, 1.82 wt% In, In/Cu 0.26. About a third of the In alloys with Cu after reduction and re-oxidises to In³⁺ under reaction; no In₂O₃ phase.

cuzn_sio2.label: CuZn/SiO₂
cuzn_sio2.note: Cu nanoparticles on silica decorated with isolated Zn²⁺ sites, made by surface organometallic chemistry: 4.16 wt% Cu, 1.62 wt% Zn, Zn/Cu 0.40. There is no ZnO phase, which is the point of the material: the Zn is single cations at the Cu interface, partly alloyed after reduction and partly re-oxidised under reaction, so it is listed as Zn²⁺ and not as ZnO.

gazrox.label: GaZrOₓ
gazrox.note: The Cu-free counterpart of the Cu-GaZrOₓ series, 48 wt% Ga and 25 wt% Zr. Run to separate what the oxide does from what Cu does.

la_al2o3.label: La-Al₂O₃
la_al2o3.note: γ-alumina (SASOL) impregnated with lanthanum and calcined, 6 wt% La in the Rajput series: La³⁺ dispersed in the alumina as a stabiliser, not a phase of its own.

ni_ce_fe_la_al2o3.label: Ni-Ce-Fe/La-Al₂O₃
ni_ce_fe_la_al2o3.note: 40Ni₀.₇₅(Ce₀.₇₅Fe₀.₂₅)₀.₂₅/6La-Al₂O₃ as measured by DRIFTS: fresh, purged in N₂ at 300 °C and not reduced before the CO₂/CH₄ feed at 600 °C. Its XRD shows NiO, NiAl₂O₄ and CeO₂, and Fe₂O₃ as a dispersed, nearly amorphous oxide, so those are its components.

pd_al2o3.label: Pd/Al₂O₃
pd_al2o3.note: Palladium on alumina, the monometallic reference against which the Sn- and Zn-modified counterparts are read: it is the one that still has Pd-Pd pairs, so it is the one that still shows bridged CO. The review names no alumina phase, so the support is plain Al₂O₃.

pt_ceo2.label: Pt/CeO₂
pt_ceo2.note: 3 wt% Pt on ceria by incipient wetness impregnation with Pt(NH₃)₄(NO₃)₂, calcined at 500 °C and reduced in H₂ at 300 °C, as Vico van Berkel and Urakawa use it for the reverse water–gas shift. The Pt-ceria perimeter is a part of its own, being where that paper places its carbonyls.

pt_moox_tio2.label: Pt/MoOₓ/TiO₂
pt_moox_tio2.note: Platinum on a molybdenum-oxide-covered titania, made by sequential impregnation and reduced in H₂ at 300 °C. Both metals are needed: neither Pt on bare TiO₂ nor MoOₓ/TiO₂ alone gives the methanol yield, which is what the specimen entry is here to keep together.

ru_na2o_al2o3.label: Ru/"Na₂O"/Al₂O₃
ru_na2o_al2o3.note: The sodium-promoted counterpart of Ru/Al₂O₃ on the same γ-Al₂O₃ (SBA-150); the quotes are the authors’ own, since the "Na₂O" is in fact Na⁺ in surface aluminate species.

ru_al2o3.label: Ru/Al₂O₃
ru_al2o3.note: 5 wt% Ru on high-surface-area γ-Al₂O₃ (SBA-150, BASF), pre-reduced in H₂ at 320 °C: the conventional methanation catalyst Proaño et al. compare their dual-function material against.

sno2_au.label: SnO₂/Au on Si
sno2_au.note: SnO₂/Au deposited on a silicon prism: the layers, whatever shape they were made in. The film electrode is its refinement by form.

sno2_au_film.label: SnO₂/Au on Si, film electrode
sno2_au_film.note: A SEIRAS working electrode: commercial SnO₂ nanoparticles (50 to 70 nm) cast onto a chemically deposited Au film on a Si prism. The oxide faces the electrolyte; the gold underneath carries the enhancement. Whether the SnO₂ stays oxide or reduces to Sn under reaction is not settled by the spectra, so no site is listed.

znhfox.label: ZnHfOₓ
znhfox.note: Co-precipitated Zn–Hf mixed oxide, published as a series written xZnHfOₓ with x the Zn/(Zn+Hf) molar percentage. Up to about 35 mol% it is Zn-doped cubic HfO₂ in solid solution; above 40 mol% bulk ZnO segregates and carries HfOₓ clusters on its surface. One key for the family, with the member named in the note, because the IR bands of both regimes agree within a few wavenumbers and that agreement is the claim the spectra turn on. ZnO is not listed as a part: the low-Zn members contain none.

zsm5.label: ZSM-5
zsm5.note: The MFI aluminosilicate framework, MₙAlₙSi₉₆₋ₙO₁₉₂ with n below 27: corner-sharing SiO₄ and AlO₄⁻ tetrahedra in one crystalline phase, not Al₂O₃ + SiO₂, which is only the way its composition is sometimes written. Each framework Al carries a negative charge balanced by an extra-framework cation M, and which cation that is is a refinement of its own (H-ZSM-5, Na-ZSM-5, …), named on the claim where the paper names it. The Si/Al ratio goes in the claim's note while no band turns on it.

h_zsm5.label: H-ZSM-5
h_zsm5.note: The proton form, usually made by calcining NH₄-ZSM-5: the charge of each framework Al is balanced by a proton on a bridging Si-(OH)-Al hydroxyl, near 3610 cm⁻¹, the Brønsted acid site. A refinement of ZSM-5 by its counter-cation, so a search for ZSM-5 finds it.

li_zsm5.label: Li-ZSM-5
li_zsm5.note: ZSM-5 exchanged with Li⁺, the smallest and most polarising of the alkali cations. A refinement of ZSM-5 by its counter-cation, so a search for ZSM-5 finds it.

na_zsm5.label: Na-ZSM-5
na_zsm5.note: ZSM-5 with Na⁺ as the extra-framework cation, the as-synthesised form. A refinement of ZSM-5 by its counter-cation, so a search for ZSM-5 finds it.

k_zsm5.label: K-ZSM-5
k_zsm5.note: ZSM-5 exchanged with K⁺. A refinement of ZSM-5 by its counter-cation, so a search for ZSM-5 finds it.

rb_zsm5.label: Rb-ZSM-5
rb_zsm5.note: ZSM-5 exchanged with Rb⁺. A refinement of ZSM-5 by its counter-cation, so a search for ZSM-5 finds it.

cs_zsm5.label: Cs-ZSM-5
cs_zsm5.note: ZSM-5 exchanged with Cs⁺, the largest and least polarising of the alkali cations. A refinement of ZSM-5 by its counter-cation, so a search for ZSM-5 finds it.

infrared.label: IR (unspecified)
infrared.tip: An infrared measurement whose sampling geometry the source does not name.
infrared.note: The placeholder of the infrared family: the source says only IR or FTIR, and FTIR names the interferometer rather than the sampling geometry. The value and the family umbrella are one chip, as for raman. Use it when the paper genuinely does not say, and replace it once it does.

drifts.label: DRIFTS
drifts.tip: Infrared light scattered back from a powder bed (diffuse reflectance).
drifts.note: Diffuse reflectance off a powder bed. The workhorse for supported catalysts.

transmission.label: Transmission
transmission.tip: Infrared light passed straight through a thin wafer or a gas cell.

atr.label: ATR
atr.tip: Infrared light totally reflected inside a crystal, probing the sample pressed against it.
atr.note: Attenuated total reflectance against an internal-reflection crystal. Common for liquid-phase and wet surfaces.

seiras.label: ATR-SEIRAS
seiras.tip: ATR through a thin metal-film electrode that enhances the absorption near the metal.
seiras.note: Surface-enhanced infrared absorption, almost always in the ATR (Kretschmann) geometry: a nanostructured metal film, tens of nm thick, is deposited on an internal-reflection prism and serves as the electrode, with the electrolyte on its far side. The beam reaches the film through the prism, so the bulk electrolyte barely absorbs, and the film’s islands enhance the field within a few nm of the metal by one to two orders of magnitude. Two consequences make it an experiment of its own rather than plain ATR. The surface selection rule applies, as for IRRAS: only dipole components normal to the metal are enhanced, so an absent band can mean a mode lying flat. And the spectra are almost always differences against a reference potential, so a band can point down, meaning a species consumed (interfacial CO₂) rather than formed. The film is the electrode, so its own metal (and any underlayer, often Au) is the surface the claim is about.

irras.label: IRRAS
irras.tip: Infrared light reflected at grazing incidence off a flat, usually metal, surface.
irras.note: Grazing-incidence reflection off a flat, usually single-crystal sample, in vacuum. The surface selection rule applies: only dipole components along the surface normal absorb, so a mode missing from the spectrum may be lying flat rather than absent.

pm_irras.label: PM-IRRAS
pm_irras.tip: Grazing-incidence reflection with the polarisation switched to cancel the gas background.
pm_irras.note: IRRAS with the polarisation modulated between s and p, which cancels the isotropic gas and window background. It is what makes reflection work outside vacuum.

emission.label: Emission
emission.tip: Infrared light emitted by the hot sample itself.
emission.note: The hot sample is the source: no beam is passed through it. Used where a bed is too opaque or too hot for the other geometries.

mioirs.label: MIOIRS
mioirs.tip: An infrared spectrum of a deliberately mixed isotopic feed, which detunes the coupling between neighbouring adsorbates.
mioirs.note: Mixed Isotope Operando Infrared Spectroscopy: the sample is fed a deliberately mixed isotopic stream, a little ¹³CO in ¹²CO, so that neighbouring adsorbates no longer vibrate at the same frequency and the dipole coupling between them is detuned. The odd value of the infrared family, since it names what is fed to the cell rather than how the beam reaches the sample, but a decoupled adlayer is a different measurement whatever geometry recorded it, which is why it is a value and not a tag. Proposed by Monai in 2024; nothing in the atlas carries it yet.

raman.label: Raman (unspecified)
raman.tip: Raman scattering whose kind the source does not name.
raman.note: Inelastic scattering of a laser rather than absorption: a Raman shift, the same vibrational energy seen through the polarizability. The placeholder of its family, the way infrared is for the infrared: it says the source named Raman and nothing finer. Use srs where the paper says spontaneous.

srs.label: Spontaneous Raman
srs.tip: Laser light scattered inelastically by the sample on its own (spontaneous Raman).
srs.note: Spontaneous Raman scattering, named explicitly. The specific value under raman, the way DRIFTS and transmission sit under the infrared: the scattering happens by itself from one laser, rather than being driven by a second beam as in the coherent techniques (CARS, stimulated Raman). Use it only where the source says spontaneous; plain raman stays the value for a paper that does not.

computational.label: Computational
computational.tip: A frequency calculated rather than measured.
computational.note: Not a geometry at all: a frequency from a calculation. Arguably a separate origin axis.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ asymmetric stretch (νₐₛ) — R-branch envelope maximum at ~2360 cm⁻¹, paired with the P-branch at ~2335. The Q-branch between them is symmetry-forbidden — see co2_asym_q. Saturates at high pCO₂.

references.note: νₐₛ band origin (00011←00001) at 2349 cm⁻¹ (Table 2); 2360 here is the R-branch envelope maximum, not a single measured line.
Gas-phase CO₂ R-branch observed at 2373 cm⁻¹ during DRM at 600°C (Table 3); reactant concentration marker.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ asymmetric stretch (νₐₛ) — Q-branch at the 2349 cm⁻¹ band origin. Forbidden by symmetry for this Σᵤ⁺←Σg⁺ parallel transition, so no rotational line actually appears here; marks the gap between the R- and P-branch envelopes.
Gas CO₂ asymmetric stretch (νₐₛ) — P-branch envelope maximum at ~2335 cm⁻¹, paired with the R-branch at ~2360. Same forbidden-Q gap as the R-branch entry — see co2_asym_q. Saturates at high pCO₂.

references.note: νₐₛ band origin (00011←00001) at 2349 cm⁻¹ (Table 2); 2335 here is the P-branch envelope maximum, not a single measured line.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ bending fundamental (δ) — R-branch (ΔJ = +1) at ~700 cm⁻¹. Higher-frequency rotational envelope; pair-mate of the P-branch at ~660. Q-branch is allowed (Σ→Π transition) and appears as a sharp spike at ~667 between P and R envelopes.

references.note: Reports the δ band origin (01101←00001) at 667 cm⁻¹ (Table 2); ~700 here is the R-branch envelope maximum.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ bending fundamental (δ) — Q-branch (ΔJ = 0) at ~667 cm⁻¹. Sharp, intense spike between P and R envelopes; allowed because this mode is a Σ→Π (perpendicular) transition. Saturates very quickly at modest pCO₂.

references.note: Q-branch coincides with the reported δ band origin (01101←00001) at 667 cm⁻¹ (Table 2) — the fundamental bending mode.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ bending fundamental (δ) — P-branch (ΔJ = −1) at ~660 cm⁻¹. Lower-frequency rotational envelope; pair-mate of the R-branch at ~700. Atmospheric CO₂ in the beam path contributes to this region; routinely seen even with good purging.

references.note: Reports the δ band origin (01101←00001) at 667 cm⁻¹ (Table 2); ~660 here is the P-branch envelope maximum.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ combination (νₛ + νₐₛ) — Q-branch at the ~3715 cm⁻¹ band origin. Forbidden by symmetry for this Σᵤ⁺←Σg⁺ parallel transition, so no rotational line appears here; it marks the gap between the P- and R-branch envelopes rather than a feature to look for. Carried so the upper Fermi component has the same three branches as the νₐₛ fundamental it is built on, and so the gap is drawn where the origin is. Deliberately unreferenced: a paper quoting 3715 is quoting the origin, and that number belongs to the band, not to a line in it.

Gas CO₂ combination band at ~3730 cm⁻¹; (νₛ + νₐₛ) R-branch — upper Fermi-resonance component, R-side. Useful for high-pressure quantification when the νₐₛ fundamental saturates. Genuinely Fermi-coupled to the 2δ+νₐₛ doublet below (~3600 cm⁻¹), not just two coincidentally nearby combination bands — see co2_sym for why the resonance between νₛ and 2δ carries through into both bands' own +νₐₛ combination levels.

references.note: Table 2 gives the band origin of the ν₁+ν₃ combination at ~3715 cm⁻¹. For a Σ to Σ transition that origin is the gap between the two branches rather than a position in either, and the paper tabulates no maximum for the R branch, so no wavenumber is taken from it here. DRIFTS of pure KBr under 10 bar CO₂ at 278 K.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ combination band at ~3699 cm⁻¹; (νₛ + νₐₛ) P-branch — upper Fermi-resonance component, P-side. P/R-branch separation ~30 cm⁻¹; pair-mate of the R-branch at ~3730. See co2_sym for why this combination doublet is genuinely Fermi-coupled to the 2δ+νₐₛ one below, not just nearby.

references.note: Table 2 gives the band origin of the ν₁+ν₃ combination at ~3715 cm⁻¹. For a Σ to Σ transition that origin is the gap between the two branches rather than a position in either, and the paper tabulates no maximum for the P branch, so no wavenumber is taken from it here. DRIFTS of pure KBr under 10 bar CO₂ at 278 K.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ combination (2δ + νₐₛ) — Q-branch at the ~3613 cm⁻¹ band origin. Forbidden by symmetry for this Σᵤ⁺←Σg⁺ parallel transition, so no rotational line appears here; it marks the gap between the P- and R-branch envelopes. The lower half of the Fermi pair above 3500 cm⁻¹, and carried for the same reason as its partner's Q: the origin is where the branches are counted from. Deliberately unreferenced, the origin being a property of the band rather than an observed line.

Gas CO₂ combination band at ~3627 cm⁻¹; (2δ + νₐₛ) R-branch — lower Fermi-resonance component, R-side. Separation between Fermi pair (3730 vs 3627) ~107 cm⁻¹ is fixed. See co2_bend_overtone for why this combination doublet is genuinely Fermi-coupled to the νₛ+νₐₛ one above, not just nearby.

references.note: Table 2 gives the band origin of the 2ν₂+ν₃ combination at ~3613 cm⁻¹. For a Σ to Σ transition that origin is the gap between the two branches rather than a position in either, and the paper tabulates no maximum for the R branch, so no wavenumber is taken from it here. DRIFTS of pure KBr under 10 bar CO₂ at 278 K.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ combination band at ~3597 cm⁻¹; (2δ + νₐₛ) P-branch — lower Fermi-resonance component, P-side. P/R-branch separation ~30 cm⁻¹; pair-mate of the R-branch at ~3627. See co2_bend_overtone for why this combination doublet is genuinely Fermi-coupled to the νₛ+νₐₛ one above, not just nearby.

references.note: Table 2 gives the band origin of the 2ν₂+ν₃ combination at ~3613 cm⁻¹. For a Σ to Σ transition that origin is the gap between the two branches rather than a position in either, and the paper tabulates no maximum for the P branch, so no wavenumber is taken from it here. DRIFTS of pure KBr under 10 bar CO₂ at 278 K.

bands.description: A hot band: two quanta of the symmetric stretch reached from a molecule that already holds one quantum of the bend, so the lower state is the bend and not the ground state. Nothing absorbs here at ambient conditions; the band needs a pressurised cell and grows as that cell is heated, because heating is what populates the level it starts from. Medium and narrow, it sits in the middle of the linear metal-carbonyl window and has been published three times as CO on Cu⁺. The temperature is what separates the two readings: a carbonyl population falls as the cell heats, and this rises.

based_on.label: less one quantum of the bend: a hot band, from an already bending molecule

references.note: Table 3 of a DRIFTS spectrum of pure KBr under 10 bar of CO₂ at 278 K, 4 cm⁻¹ and 64 scans, intensities normalised to the 2077 cm⁻¹ band. Fehr's band E: 2130 cm⁻¹, medium and narrow, the Q branch of the 20001←01101 transition of ¹²C¹⁶O₂, marked as rising with temperature and one of the bands Gausemel et al. had already described. Table 1 lists Bailey et al. and Table 4 both Fisher and Bell and Martin et al., all three reading this position as CO on Cu⁺.

bands.description: The hot companion of the 2077 cm⁻¹ combination: the same symmetric stretch with the bend, but reached from a molecule that already holds one bending quantum rather than from the ground state, which puts it about 17 cm⁻¹ higher. Medium and narrow, and among the steepest with temperature of any gas CO₂ band in this window, since heat is what populates the level it starts from and pressure is what makes it visible at all. It lands where CO on stepped or high-index copper is looked for, and has been published three times as exactly that.

based_on.label: less one quantum of the bend: a hot band, from an already bending molecule

references.note: Table 3 of a DRIFTS spectrum of pure KBr under 10 bar of CO₂ at 278 K, 4 cm⁻¹ and 64 scans, intensities normalised to the 2077 cm⁻¹ band. Fehr's band I: 2094 cm⁻¹, medium and narrow, the Q branch of the 12201←01101 transition of ¹²C¹⁶O₂, one of the few in the range marked as rising strongly with temperature. Table 1 lists Bailey et al. reading it as CO on Cu(755); Table 4 adds Fisher and Bell as CO on Cu(110) and Martin et al. as CO on high-index faces such as Cu(755).

bands.description: Gas CO₂ combination of the infrared-forbidden symmetric stretch with the bend: the combined level is dipole-allowed although the stretch alone is not. Very strong and narrow, the most prominent gas band between 2200 and 1900 cm⁻¹, sitting squarely in the linear metal-carbonyl window, and the most misassigned band in this atlas: eight published studies read this one position as adsorbed CO. Its intensity tracks CO₂ pressure rather than anything on the surface, which is the discriminator. Heat and pressurise the cell and the same molecule adds hot and difference bands, absent at ambient conditions, at 2130 and 2094 cm⁻¹ among the carbonyls and 1079, 1050, 973 and 948 cm⁻¹ among the methoxy bands.

references.note: Table 3, band J: very strong and narrow, the Q branch of the 11101←00001 transition of ¹²C¹⁶O₂ and the most intense combination band in the range, which every other intensity in the paper is normalised to. Table 1 lists three earlier papers and Table 4 five more that assigned this position to adsorbed CO. The two hot bands at 2130 and 2094 cm⁻¹ have entries of their own. Weaker gas bands are left undrawn: 2112 cm⁻¹, either this transition’s R branch or the P branch of the 2130 cm⁻¹ hot band, which the source cannot separate; and 1933 and 1920 cm⁻¹, the 11102←00001 pair published as CO on a CuZn alloy. All of them need CO₂ pressure to show at all.

Table S5 and Fig. S17 (operando DRIFTS, Cu/SiO₂ and CuGa(0.20), 220 to 280 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 6 bar, 25 mL min⁻¹): listed as gas-phase CO₂ and cited to Fehr et al., the source of the claim on this band above. Worth recording as a second reading of the same position: it sits between the two gas CO branches at 2177 and 2112 cm⁻¹ in the same spectra, exactly where a CO band on a copper catalyst would be looked for, and this paper does not read it as one.

bands.description: The P branch of the same combination band whose Q branch sits 20 cm⁻¹ above. Equally intense but broad rather than narrow, so it reads as a shoulder or a hump rather than the peak its partner makes, and it is the less often reported of the two for that reason. It has still been published four times as adsorbed CO, once specifically as CO at a copper-zinc interface. Rotational structure resolves it at 0.5 cm⁻¹; at the 4 cm⁻¹ usual in catalysis it is one smooth band.

references.note: Table 3 of a DRIFTS spectrum of pure KBr under 10 bar of CO₂ at 278 K, 4 cm⁻¹ and 64 scans, intensities normalised to the 2077 cm⁻¹ band. Very strong and broad, the P branch of the 11101←00001 transition whose Q branch is the 2077 cm⁻¹ normalisation band. Table 4 lists four papers that assigned this position to adsorbed CO, against eight for the Q branch.

bands.description: The R branch of a difference band: the asymmetric stretch reached from a molecule already holding two quanta of bend rather than from the ground state. Only a fraction of a percent of molecules sit in that level at room temperature, but a pressurised cell shows it clearly and it climbs steeply with both pressure and temperature. It lands on the methoxy C-O stretch, the worst place for a CO₂ artefact in a methanol experiment: it rises with temperature, which is what a methanol signal is expected to do.

based_on.label: less two quanta of the bend: a difference band, from an already vibrating molecule

references.note: Table 3 of a DRIFTS spectrum of pure KBr under 10 bar of CO₂ at 278 K, 4 cm⁻¹ and 64 scans, intensities normalised to the 2077 cm⁻¹ band. Fehr's band P: about 1079 cm⁻¹, strong and broad, transition 00011←10002 of ¹²C¹⁶O₂, marked as rising strongly with temperature. Table 4 lists it as having been published as methoxy on ZnO.

bands.description: The Q branch of the same difference band, which does not appear. Both states are Σ, so ΔJ = 0 is forbidden and nothing is observed between the P and R maxima; this entry marks where the band origin sits, near 1064 cm⁻¹. Carried for context, since the gap between the two branches is what identifies the pair as one band rather than two species.

based_on.label: less two quanta of the bend: a difference band, from an already vibrating molecule

bands.description: The P branch of a difference band: the asymmetric stretch reached from a molecule already holding two quanta of bend rather than from the ground state. Only a fraction of a percent of molecules sit in that level at room temperature, but a pressurised cell shows it clearly and it climbs steeply with both pressure and temperature. It lands on gas-phase methanol, the worst place for a CO₂ artefact in a methanol experiment: it rises with temperature, which is what a methanol signal is expected to do.

based_on.label: less two quanta of the bend: a difference band, from an already vibrating molecule

references.note: Table 3 of a DRIFTS spectrum of pure KBr under 10 bar of CO₂ at 278 K, 4 cm⁻¹ and 64 scans, intensities normalised to the 2077 cm⁻¹ band. Fehr's band Q: about 1050 cm⁻¹, strong and broad, transition 00011←10002 of ¹²C¹⁶O₂, marked as rising strongly with temperature. Taken here as the P branch rather than a Q: the transition is Σ to Σ, which forbids ΔJ = 0, and 1079 and 1050 straddle the 1064 cm⁻¹ origin symmetrically. Table 4 lists it as having been published as gaseous methanol or a methoxy species.

bands.description: The R branch of a difference band, reached from a molecule already holding one quantum of the symmetric stretch rather than from the ground state. Strong and broad in a pressurised cell. It has been published as methoxy bound to copper. The test is the temperature: it climbs steeply as the cell is heated, because heating populates the level it starts from, and a surface methoxy population does not behave that way.

based_on.label: less one quantum of the symmetric stretch: a difference band, from an already vibrating molecule

references.note: Table 3 of a DRIFTS spectrum of pure KBr under 10 bar of CO₂ at 278 K, 4 cm⁻¹ and 64 scans, intensities normalised to the 2077 cm⁻¹ band. Fehr's band R: the R branch at about 973 cm⁻¹, strong and broad, transition 00011←10001 of ¹²C¹⁶O₂, marked as rising strongly with temperature. Table 4 lists it as having been published as methoxy on Cu.

bands.description: The Q branch of the same difference band, which does not appear. Both states are Σ, so ΔJ = 0 is forbidden and nothing is observed between the P and R maxima; this entry marks where the band origin sits, near 960 cm⁻¹. Carried for context, since the gap between the two branches is what identifies the pair as one band rather than two species.

bands.description: The P branch of a difference band, reached from a molecule already holding one quantum of the symmetric stretch rather than from the ground state. Strong and broad in a pressurised cell. It has been published as methoxy on Cu⁰. The test is the temperature: it climbs steeply as the cell is heated, because heating populates the level it starts from, and a surface methoxy population does not behave that way.

based_on.label: less one quantum of the symmetric stretch: a difference band, from an already vibrating molecule

references.note: Table 3 of a DRIFTS spectrum of pure KBr under 10 bar of CO₂ at 278 K, 4 cm⁻¹ and 64 scans, intensities normalised to the 2077 cm⁻¹ band. Fehr's band S: the P branch at about 948 cm⁻¹, strong and broad, transition 00011←10001 of ¹²C¹⁶O₂, marked as rising strongly with temperature. Table 4 lists it as having been published as methoxy on Cu⁰.

bands.description: Symmetric stretch of CO₂ held linearly on a surface cation through one oxygen, without becoming carbonate. In the free molecule this mode is infrared-forbidden and seen only in Raman; binding breaks the symmetry just enough to give it a weak infrared band. The asymmetric stretch near 2340 cm⁻¹ is far stronger and the usual marker of adsorbed CO₂, but it sits under the gas-phase band. This one falls among the carbonate and formate symmetric stretches, where it is easily read as one of them.

references.note: Fig. S56f and the accompanying SI text (ZnO reference, 20 vol% CO₂ in N₂, 320 °C, 20 bar): assigned to linearly adsorbed CO₂, CO₂*, citing earlier work. The paper names the species and not the mode; the symmetric stretch is the only CO₂ fundamental near this position. It lies between the bidentate and polydentate carbonate bands of the same spectrum.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ symmetric stretch, strictly IR-forbidden (Σg⁺, no dipole change) and seen only in Raman. It is carried here as the explicit parent of the νₛ+νₐₛ combination band and as the Fermi partner of the bending overtone: the cubic anharmonic term that mixes those two also mixes their +νₐₛ combination levels, which is why the pair of combination doublets higher up is marked as a Fermi pair as well.

references.note: Fig. 2 right (in situ Raman, 1 wt % Cu/SiO₂ at 230 °C, 200 and 400 bar; Renishaw InVia, 532 nm Nd:YAG, 60 mW, 600 s accumulation through a micro-view-cell, SI p. S34). Marked on the figure with a filled circle as a band of the reactant mixture rather than a surface species, the stronger, upper member of the CO₂ Fermi dyad, which is what a Raman spectrum of CO₂ shows in this window. No position is printed for the marker, so none is recorded.

Table 3 and Fig. 3: formally infrared-inactive, yet observed in DRIFTS of pure KBr once the CO₂ pressure passes roughly 10 bar, together with its Fermi partner at 1285 cm⁻¹ and with an intensity ratio near 1.0 at 30 bar. The pair is the Fermi resonance itself made visible: the deperturbed ν₁ lies at 1337 cm⁻¹ and is pushed up to 1388, while 2ν₂ falls from 1334 to 1285 cm⁻¹. Both grow with pressure and, unlike every combination band in the same spectrum, weaken as the temperature rises.

Fig. 2, gaseous CO₂: Neat CO₂ flowed at 100 mL min⁻¹ (at 291 K) through a Si/glass microreactor, 785 nm excitation, 10 s spectra. At 298 K, 1386.9 cm⁻¹ at 5 MPa and 1386.5 at 6 MPa, below the gas–liquid transition the paper places at 6–7 MPa; at 307 K, 1388.5 at 5 MPa to 1387.7 at 7 MPa, below the transition at 7–8 MPa; at 323 K, 1388.7 at 5 MPa to 1388.4 at 7 MPa, below the critical pressure of 7.4 MPa. The band falls as the gas densifies, and the higher the temperature the higher it sits. Positions read off Fig. 2 to about ±0.1 cm⁻¹: the paper tabulates none and quotes only "ca. 1284 and 1387 cm⁻¹" for the Fermi dyad. Which component is ν₁ and which 2ν₂ follows the atlas.

Fig. 2, liquid CO₂: Neat CO₂ flowed at 100 mL min⁻¹ (at 291 K) through a Si/glass microreactor, 785 nm excitation, 10 s spectra. At 298 K, above the gas–liquid transition at 6–7 MPa, the band drops abruptly and then holds at 1386.2 cm⁻¹ from 7 to 9 MPa and 1386.1 from 10 to 14 MPa, flat because a liquid barely compresses. The relative intensity, read by the authors as density, steps at the same pressure. Positions read off Fig. 2 to about ±0.1 cm⁻¹: the paper tabulates none and quotes only "ca. 1284 and 1387 cm⁻¹" for the Fermi dyad. Which component is ν₁ and which 2ν₂ follows the atlas.

Fig. 2, supercritical CO₂: Neat CO₂ flowed at 100 mL min⁻¹ (at 291 K) through a Si/glass microreactor, 785 nm excitation, 10 s spectra. At 307 K, just above the critical temperature (304 K), the band steps down across the transition at 7–8 MPa and then falls from 1387.0 cm⁻¹ at 8 MPa to 1386.2 at 14 MPa; at 323 K, well above it, it falls smoothly with no step, from 1388.2 at 8 MPa to 1386.5 at 14 MPa, the continuous gas–supercritical transition the paper describes. Values above 7.4 MPa are filed here. Positions read off Fig. 2 to about ±0.1 cm⁻¹: the paper tabulates none and quotes only "ca. 1284 and 1387 cm⁻¹" for the Fermi dyad. Which component is ν₁ and which 2ν₂ follows the atlas.

Fig. 2: Cyclohexene and H₂, 5 % each in CO₂, 10 MPa total, before the Pd/Al₂O₃ bed (Fig. 2, inverted triangles). At 305 K the dyad sits at or below the value of neat liquid CO₂ at 298 K, which the authors read as phase segregation between CO₂ and the reactants: the CO₂ behaves as a liquid. The mixture points overlap at 10 MPa, so no position is recorded.

Fig. 2: Cyclohexene and H₂, 5 % each in CO₂, 10 MPa total, before the Pd/Al₂O₃ bed (Fig. 2, inverted triangles). Warming from 305 to 318 K moves the dyad up to close to neat CO₂ at 307 K, which the authors read as the CO₂ acting as a supercritical solvent at 318 K, and the cyclohexene conversion rises with it (27 to 33 % by Raman). The mixture points overlap at 10 MPa, so no position is recorded.

bands.description: Gas CO₂ bending overtone, the l=0 component of two bending quanta. Like νₛ it is IR-forbidden and seen only in Raman. It is in genuine Fermi resonance with νₛ: the cubic anharmonic coupling pushes both away from their uncoupled positions to the observed 1285/1388 cm⁻¹ split, and the same coupling carries up into the two combination doublets near 3700 and 3600 cm⁻¹.

references.note: Fig. 2 right (in situ Raman, 1 wt % Cu/SiO₂ at 230 °C, 200 and 400 bar; Renishaw InVia, 532 nm Nd:YAG, 60 mW, 600 s accumulation through a micro-view-cell, SI p. S34). Marked on the figure with a filled circle as a band of the reactant mixture rather than a surface species, the lower member of the CO₂ Fermi dyad, which is what a Raman spectrum of CO₂ shows in this window. No position is printed for the marker, so none is recorded.

Table 3 and Fig. 3: the lower Fermi component, formally infrared-inactive but seen in DRIFTS above roughly 10 bar of CO₂ alongside the 1388 cm⁻¹ partner. Its unperturbed position is 1334 cm⁻¹, and the resonance pushes it down to 1285. Both bands weaken with rising temperature, which is what separates them from the combination bands nearby.

Fig. 2, gaseous CO₂: Neat CO₂ flowed at 100 mL min⁻¹ (at 291 K) through a Si/glass microreactor, 785 nm excitation, 10 s spectra. At 298 K, 1283.7 cm⁻¹ at 5 MPa and 1282.7 at 6 MPa, below the gas–liquid transition at 6–7 MPa; at 307 K, 1285.4 at 5 MPa to 1284.5 at 7 MPa; at 323 K, 1285.5 at 5 MPa to 1284.7 at 7 MPa, below the critical pressure of 7.4 MPa. The same measurement as the upper band. Positions read off Fig. 2 to about ±0.1 cm⁻¹: the paper tabulates none and quotes only "ca. 1284 and 1387 cm⁻¹" for the Fermi dyad. Which component is ν₁ and which 2ν₂ follows the atlas.

Positions read off Fig. 2 to about ±0.1 cm⁻¹: the paper tabulates none and quotes only "ca. 1284 and 1387 cm⁻¹" for the Fermi dyad. Which component is ν₁ and which 2ν₂ follows the atlas.

At 307 K the band drops abruptly across the transition at 7–8 MPa, from 1284.5 cm⁻¹ at 7 MPa to 1282.8 at 8 MPa, then falls to 1282.0 at 14 MPa; at 323 K it falls smoothly from 1284.3 at 8 MPa to 1282.7 at 14 MPa. Values above 7.4 MPa are filed here. Positions read off Fig. 2 to about ±0.1 cm⁻¹: the paper tabulates none and quotes only "ca. 1284 and 1387 cm⁻¹" for the Fermi dyad.
