bands.description: Gas-phase CO stretch (ν) — R-branch (ΔJ = +1) at ~2170 cm⁻¹. Higher-frequency rotational envelope; pair-mate of the P-branch at ~2115. Q-branch forbidden for diatomic CO (Σ→Σ transition), leaving a characteristic gap at ~2143 cm⁻¹ between R and P branches — see co_stretch_q.

references.note: Fig. 5a and Section 3.3 (Spectra-Tech DRIFTS cell, 14% Co/Al₂O₃ at 220 °C, 30% CO + 60% H₂ + 10% Ar, ambient pressure). The paper uses this branch to measure the cell: over a mirror at 80 °C it is 2.97 times weaker than in a 10 cm transmission gas cell, which puts the beam's path through gas above the bed at 3.37 cm of a 3.50 cm total, leaving about 1.3 mm through the bed voids (Fig. 4). Fig. 6 shows the envelope widening as its height falls between 50 and 400 °C over SiC. The gas temperature cannot be fitted to one value, because the beam crosses gas from the 80 °C windows to the hot bed.

Table S5 and Fig. S17 (operando DRIFTS, Cu/SiO₂ and CuGa(0.20), 220 to 280 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 6 bar, 25 mL min⁻¹): the R branch of the CO the reaction is making, paired with the P branch at 2112 cm⁻¹. Both grow with temperature in the same proportion on the promoted and unpromoted catalysts, which matches the kinetics: Ga raises the methanol rate by about an order of magnitude and leaves the CO rate alone.

bands.description: Gas-phase CO stretch (ν) — Q-branch at the ~2143 cm⁻¹ band origin. Forbidden by symmetry for this Σ→Σ transition, so no rotational line actually appears here; marks the gap between the R- and P-branch envelopes.

references.note: Fig. 5a and Sect. 3.3 (Spectra-Tech DRIFTS cell, 14% Co/Al₂O₃ at 220 °C, 30% CO + 60% H₂ + 10% Ar, ambient pressure): the paper records this transition as the pair at 2114 and 2176 cm⁻¹ and works throughout with the gap between them. Nothing is observed at this position and nothing could be, the Q branch of a Σ→Σ transition being forbidden. The claim is carried for completeness, so the band origin holds the same sources as the two branches flanking it, and it records that the source read the feature as one P/R envelope with a hole at its centre rather than as two unrelated bands.

Table S5 and Fig. S17 (operando DRIFTS, Cu/SiO₂ and CuGa(0.20), 220 to 280 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 6 bar, 25 mL min⁻¹): product CO is reported there as the pair 2112 and 2177 cm⁻¹, a 65 cm⁻¹ separation whose midpoint is this band origin. No line is observed here, and none can be: the Q branch is symmetry-forbidden for this Σ→Σ transition. Recorded for completeness beside the branches it separates, so the forbidden centre carries the same sources as the P and R entries instead of standing unreferenced.

bands.description: Gas-phase CO stretch (ν) — P-branch (ΔJ = −1) at ~2115 cm⁻¹. Lower-frequency rotational envelope; pair-mate of the R-branch at ~2170. P/R splitting ~55 cm⁻¹ at room temperature; envelope broadens and shifts intensity to higher-J lines as temperature increases (Maxwell–Boltzmann redistribution). Same forbidden-Q gap as the R-branch entry — see co_stretch_q.

references.note: Fig. 5a and Section 3.3 (14% Co/Al₂O₃ at 220 °C, 30% CO + 60% H₂ + 10% Ar, ambient pressure): the P branch, on the high side of linear CO on cobalt. Subtracting a CO(g) spectrum taken over SiC at 50 °C fails at every scaling tried (Fig. 5b to 5e): too little leaves the branches positive, too much makes them negative and still leaves a spurious positive band near 2220 cm⁻¹, because the rotational envelope changes shape with temperature. A SiC reference at 220 °C in the same feed subtracts cleanly (Fig. 7b); the feed matters too, since H₂ conducts heat differently from CO and Ar.

Table S5 and Fig. S17 (operando DRIFTS, Cu/SiO₂ and CuGa(0.20), 220 to 280 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 6 bar, 25 mL min⁻¹): the P branch of product CO, with its R branch at 2177 cm⁻¹, a 65 cm⁻¹ separation. On this catalyst it overlaps the window where linear Cu⁰-CO is reported at high coverage, 2120 cm⁻¹ in the same paper's CO-dosing experiments, so the gas envelope has to be accounted for before any adsorbed carbonyl is read out of a spectrum taken under reaction.

bands.description: CO hydrogen-bonded through its carbon to a surface hydroxyl, not to a metal. The OH pulls weakly on the CO, raising its stretch above the gas-phase 2143 cm⁻¹ by an amount that grows with the acidity of the hydroxyl, near 2157 cm⁻¹ on silanols and 2170 to 2180 on the bridging Si-(OH)-Al of zeolites, while the OH stretch itself drops by tens to hundreds of wavenumbers. It forms only at low temperature, which is why it serves as the standard probe of Brønsted acidity.

references.note: Sect. 3.1.3 (Cu-ZSM-5, Si/Al 25 and 1.01 wt% Cu, reduced in 5 kPa CO at 473 K and evacuated; self-supporting pellet, transmission, CO dosed at 100 K and kept in the gas phase): CO on the bridging zeolite hydroxyls at 2175 cm⁻¹, appearing alongside the tricarbonyls and physisorbed CO once gas-phase CO is present. The paper names the band without arguing it, the assignment being standard for H-ZSM-5. Its background spectra show those bridging hydroxyls at 3612 cm⁻¹, 3616 at 100 K.

bands.description: CO held only by dispersion and weak electrostatic forces, in pores or on a cold surface, a near-liquid layer just below the gas-phase 2143 cm⁻¹. It appears only at low temperature under CO pressure and leaves on evacuation, so it marks that the real sites are saturated rather than a site of its own. It lands on the Q region of gas-phase CO and on CO at water-coordinated or oxide-like Cu⁺, so position alone does not identify it.

references.note: Sect. 3.1.3 (Cu-ZSM-5, Si/Al 25 and 1.01 wt% Cu, reduced in 5 kPa CO at 473 K and evacuated; self-supporting pellet, transmission, CO dosed at 100 K and kept in the gas phase): physically adsorbed CO at 2138 cm⁻¹, alongside the tricarbonyls and CO on the bridging hydroxyls, under gas-phase CO at 100 K. Not placed on any site, as physisorbed CO has none.

bands.description: Gas methane asymmetric C-H stretch (νₐₛ, ν₃, T₂ mode): the sharp Q branch at the ~3019 cm⁻¹ band origin, the feature gas methane is usually recognised by. Active in both IR and Raman. Its rotational P and R branches spread either side (ch4g_asym_p, ch4g_asym_r), and the P side overlaps νₛ near 2917 cm⁻¹ in Raman.

references.note: Fig. 1a and Fig. 3a, methanation step (320 °C, 20% H₂/N₂): the C-H stretch of gas-phase CH₄, appearing together with the formate bands at 1520 and 1320 cm⁻¹. It is the paper's product marker, and it is absent over the support without Ru, which is the evidence that Ru is what dissociates H₂.
Table 3: νₛ(–CH₃) at 3016 cm⁻¹; gas-phase CH₄ C-H stretch during DRM at 600°C over Ni-Ce-Fe/La-Al₂O₃.

Table No. 71, methane, Td: selected value 3019 cm⁻¹, uncertainty code A (0 to 1 cm⁻¹), the triply degenerate f₂ stretch. This is the one methane fundamental measured cleanly in both: infrared 3018.9 cm⁻¹ and Raman 3019.5 cm⁻¹. It is the band a catalysis spectrum actually sees, since ν₁ and ν₂ have no infrared intensity of their own.

Sect. 4.2 and Fig. 3: the anisotropic part of the pentad Raman spectrum is dominated by the fundamental ν₃ (F₂), whose rotational structure depends strongly on temperature (room temperature to 700 K in Fig. 3); spontaneous Raman of ¹²CH₄ in a heated gas cell at low density (about one amagat, below 1 atm to avoid line mixing), 4 W argon-ion laser, room temperature to 900 K. The fit needed only the zeroth-order ν₃ polarisability operator. The text gives no position for the band. Laser line assumed, not reported: the paper names only a 4 W argon-ion laser, and 515 nm is its strongest green line.

bands.description: Gas methane asymmetric C-H stretch (ν₃, T₂): the P branch, the rotational lines below the 3019 cm⁻¹ Q branch (ch4g_asym). Active in IR and Raman. It overlaps νₛ near 2917 cm⁻¹ and the δₛ+δₐₛ combination near 2830 cm⁻¹, so a band here is not by itself νₛ. In Raman the wings also hold the O and S branches (ΔJ = −2, +2), which a spherical top allows alongside P and R; the atlas files the low side under P and the high side under R.

references.note: Sect. 4.2, Fig. 3 and Fig. 13 (totally depolarised, room temperature): ν₃ dominates the anisotropic pentad spectrum, and its low-wavenumber rotational wing is this side of the sharp Q branch. The paper names neither the branches nor their positions, so no number is recorded; the wing gains lines as the temperature rises (Fig. 3, up to 700 K). Spontaneous Raman, gas cell at about one amagat, 4 W argon-ion laser. Laser line assumed, not reported: the paper names only a 4 W argon-ion laser, and 515 nm is its strongest green line.

bands.description: Gas methane asymmetric C-H stretch (ν₃, T₂): the R branch, the rotational lines above the 3019 cm⁻¹ Q branch (ch4g_asym). Active in IR and Raman. In Raman the wings also hold the O and S branches (ΔJ = −2, +2), which a spherical top allows alongside P and R; the atlas files the low side under P and the high side under R.

references.note: Sect. 4.2, Fig. 3 and Fig. 13 (totally depolarised, room temperature): the high-wavenumber rotational wing of ν₃, the stronger of the two sides in Fig. 13. The paper names neither the branches nor their positions, so no number is recorded. Spontaneous Raman, gas cell at about one amagat, 4 W argon-ion laser, room temperature to 900 K. Laser line assumed, not reported: the paper names only a 4 W argon-ion laser, and 515 nm is its strongest green line.

bands.description: Gas methane asymmetric bending (δₐₛ, T₂ mode) at ~1306 cm⁻¹.

references.note: Table 3: ν(CH₄, Gaseous) at 1306 cm⁻¹; present across all catalysts under DRM at 600°C; gas-phase CH₄ concentration marker.

Table No. 71, methane, Td: selected value 1306 cm⁻¹ for the f₂ deformation, infrared 1306.2 cm⁻¹ and no Raman entry. Its uncertainty code is C, 3 to 6 cm⁻¹, against A for the other three fundamentals — the least precisely fixed of methane’s four, which is worth knowing before reading a few wavenumbers of shift as chemistry.

bands.description: Gas methane symmetric bending (δₛ, E mode) at ~1534 cm⁻¹. IR-forbidden by symmetry: E in Td has no T₂ component, so the mode carries no dipole derivative of its own. It is still seen in the infrared, near 1533 cm⁻¹, by borrowing intensity through Coriolis coupling to the δₐₛ bend below it — a reminder that a forbidden mode is one with no dipole derivative, not one that is never observed. In Raman it is the band that dominates the dyad. This entry is the Q branch; in Raman its P and R wings (ch4g_bend_sym_p, ch4g_bend_sym_r) spread either side.

references.note: Table No. 71, methane, Td: selected value 1534 cm⁻¹, uncertainty code A (0 to 1 cm⁻¹). The infrared column reads "ia, 1533" with a footnote saying the band is observed in the infrared through Coriolis interaction with ν₄, and the Raman column gives 1533.6 cm⁻¹. So the compilation records both that the mode is formally inactive and that it is nonetheless seen: the two are not in conflict.

Sect. 4.1 and Fig. 2: the Raman spectrum of the dyad (about 1300–1850 cm⁻¹) is totally anisotropic and dominated by ν₂ (E), a strong central Q branch with rotational lines on both sides; spontaneous Raman of ¹²CH₄ in a heated gas cell at low density (about one amagat, below 1 atm to avoid line mixing), 4 W argon-ion laser, room temperature to 900 K. No number is recorded: the text’s only one, “near 1530 cm⁻¹”, is printed against ν₄, which the same paragraph calls very weak in Raman and leaves out of the fit. That it belongs to ν₂ is the author’s reading, not the paper’s. Laser line assumed, not reported: the paper names only a 4 W argon-ion laser, and 515 nm is its strongest green line.

bands.description: Gas methane symmetric bend (δₛ, ν₂, E): the P branch, the rotational lines below the ~1533 cm⁻¹ Q branch (ch4g_bend_sym). Raman-active and IR-forbidden like the Q branch. Its low end runs towards δₐₛ near 1306 cm⁻¹, which is very weak in Raman. In Raman the wings also hold the O and S branches (ΔJ = −2, +2), which a spherical top allows alongside P and R; the atlas files the low side under P and the high side under R.

references.note: Sect. 4.1, Fig. 2 and Fig. 13: the dyad Raman spectrum is totally anisotropic and dominated by ν₂, with rotational lines on both sides of its strong Q branch; this is the low-wavenumber side. The paper names neither the branches nor their positions, so no number is recorded. Spontaneous Raman, gas cell at about one amagat, 4 W argon-ion laser. Laser line assumed, not reported: the paper names only a 4 W argon-ion laser, and 515 nm is its strongest green line.

bands.description: Gas methane symmetric bend (δₛ, ν₂, E): the R branch, the rotational lines above the ~1533 cm⁻¹ Q branch (ch4g_bend_sym). Raman-active and IR-forbidden like the Q branch. In Raman the wings also hold the O and S branches (ΔJ = −2, +2), which a spherical top allows alongside P and R; the atlas files the low side under P and the high side under R.

references.note: Sect. 4.1, Fig. 2 and Fig. 13: the high-wavenumber side of the ν₂ dyad spectrum, where Fig. 2 shows the longer, better separated series of rotational lines. The paper names neither the branches nor their positions, so no number is recorded. Spontaneous Raman, gas cell at about one amagat, 4 W argon-ion laser. Laser line assumed, not reported: the paper names only a 4 W argon-ion laser, and 515 nm is its strongest green line.

bands.description: Gas methane symmetric C-H stretch (νₛ, A₁ mode) at ~2917 cm⁻¹. IR-forbidden by symmetry (A₁ in Td has no T₂/dipole component); observed only in Raman spectroscopy.

references.note: Table No. 71, methane, Td: selected value 2917 cm⁻¹ with uncertainty code A, the compilation's best grade at 0 to 1 cm⁻¹. The infrared column is marked ia, inactive, and the number comes from the Raman column at 2917.0 cm⁻¹, so this is a Raman position rather than an infrared one, and the technique is recorded as raman. The compilation itself selects rather than measures.

Recommended experimental value 0.362 eV (≈2920 cm⁻¹) for ν₁, A₁ symmetric stretch, Raman-active/IR-inactive; calculated value 0.390 eV (≈3146 cm⁻¹) given alongside it in the same table. Two caveats. The paper is a close-coupling calculation of electron-impact vibrational excitation and reports no infrared spectrum of its own: the mode energies are inputs it adopts from the literature, so it is a secondary source for this position. And no copy is on file and the article is paywalled, so this row could not be checked against the paper on the pass that added the compilation value above. Recorded as the free molecule in a gas, the state the compiled value refers to.

Sect. 4.2, Fig. 3 and conclusions: the strong isotropic ν₁ (A₁) band near 2916 cm⁻¹, a Q branch that is unresolved at the 0.3 cm⁻¹ apparatus width; spontaneous Raman of ¹²CH₄ in a heated gas cell at low density (about one amagat, below 1 atm to avoid line mixing), 4 W argon-ion laser, room temperature to 900 K. The stimulated Raman spectrum at 0.08 bar and 300 K (Fig. 8) resolves that Q branch into lines between about 2916.5 and 2918 cm⁻¹, read off the figure. From 400 K on, hot bands ν₁+nνᵢ−nνᵢ fill 2900–2920 cm⁻¹ (ν₁+ν₄−ν₄ at 2913 cm⁻¹, Fig. 10), which is what makes the band a thermometer. ν₁ is in Fermi resonance with 2ν₂ and 2ν₄ and in Dennison resonance with ν₂+ν₄. Laser line assumed, not reported: the paper names only a 4 W argon-ion laser, and 515 nm is its strongest green line.

bands.description: Gas methane combination band ν₃+ν₄ (δₐₛ+νₐₛ) near 4300 cm⁻¹, the strongest band of the octad in the near-infrared and in Raman. F₂×F₂ gives A₁, E and F₂ components, so it is active in both. Close neighbours in the same polyad blur it: ν₁+ν₄ on the low side, ν₁+ν₂ on the high side, and ν₂+ν₃ further up near 4540 cm⁻¹, which is where δₛ+νₐₛ belongs, not here. Useful for quantification when νₐₛ saturates; often outside a standard DRIFTS window. This entry is the Q branch, the sharp centre; its P and R wings are ch4g_combo_p and ch4g_combo_r.

references.note: Sect. 4.3, Figs. 11–13 and Table 5: the octad Raman spectrum (Table 1: about 3500–4700 cm⁻¹), extremely weak, recorded over 1 h with the 300 gr/mm grating at room temperature, in the same gas cell (about one amagat, 4 W argon-ion laser). Its fit needed six first-order polarisability operators: ν₁+ν₂ (E), ν₁+ν₄ (F₂), ν₂+ν₃ (F₂) and the A₁, E and F₂ components of ν₃+ν₄, the E one the largest. The paper ties no peak to a band, so reading the main feature near 4300 cm⁻¹ as ν₃+ν₄ is the author’s inference, and no number is recorded. Its neighbours ν₁+ν₄ and ν₁+ν₂ fill the wings. Laser line assumed, not reported: the paper names only a 4 W argon-ion laser, and 515 nm is its strongest green line.

bands.description: Gas methane combination band ν₃+ν₄ (δₐₛ+νₐₛ): the P branch, the rotational lines below the ~4310 cm⁻¹ Q branch (ch4g_combo). Active in IR and Raman. It overlaps ν₁+ν₄ of the same polyad, so a feature here is not necessarily ν₃+ν₄. In Raman the wings also hold O and S branches (ΔJ = −2, +2); the atlas files the low side under P and the high side under R.

references.note: Sect. 4.3 and Figs. 11–13: the low-wavenumber side of the octad feature near 4300 cm⁻¹, at room temperature in the same gas cell (about one amagat, 4 W argon-ion laser, 300 gr/mm grating). The paper names neither the branches nor their positions and ties no peak to a band, so reading this wing as ν₃+ν₄ is the author’s inference, and no number is recorded. Laser line assumed, not reported: the paper names only a 4 W argon-ion laser, and 515 nm is its strongest green line.

bands.description: Gas methane combination band ν₃+ν₄ (δₐₛ+νₐₛ): the R branch, the rotational lines above the ~4310 cm⁻¹ Q branch (ch4g_combo). Active in IR and Raman. It overlaps ν₁+ν₂ of the same polyad, so a feature here is not necessarily ν₃+ν₄. In Raman the wings also hold O and S branches (ΔJ = −2, +2); the atlas files the low side under P and the high side under R.

references.note: Sect. 4.3 and Figs. 11–13: the high-wavenumber side of the octad feature near 4300 cm⁻¹, at room temperature in the same gas cell (about one amagat, 4 W argon-ion laser, 300 gr/mm grating). The paper names neither the branches nor their positions and ties no peak to a band, so reading this wing as ν₃+ν₄ is the author’s inference, and no number is recorded. Laser line assumed, not reported: the paper names only a 4 W argon-ion laser, and 515 nm is its strongest green line.

bands.description: CO bonded end-on to a single metal atom, the commonest coordination and usually the strongest, sharpest band in a CO-probe spectrum. Its position follows metal to CO π-backdonation: more backdonation into the 2π* orbital weakens the C-O bond and pushes the band down, while electron-poor or oxidised sites push it up, so metal identity, oxidation state, coordination and coverage all move it. ¹³CO substitution shifts it by tens of cm⁻¹, the standard check that a band really is a CO stretch. Coverage moves it as far as the site does, partly by stiffening the bond and partly by coupling neighbouring oscillators, so the observed bands are collective modes of the adlayer rather than one band per kind of CO.

references.note: Fig. 1a and Section 3.1 (5%Ru/Al₂O₃, 320 °C, 15% CO₂/N₂): CO bound to Ru, read as linear CO on Ru⁰ alongside CO co-adsorbed with other ligands. Under H₂ it moves to 2035 cm⁻¹, which the paper reads as the Ru-CO bond of the forming formate rather than as a second species. On the DFM the same region is only a weak feature between 1990 and 2000 cm⁻¹.

Fig. 3a (KRS-5 transmission cell, −160 °C, 0.15 mbar CO, static vacuum, after in-situ reduction in H₂ at 300 °C and evacuation to 10⁻⁴ mbar): the deconvolution of the unpromoted Cu/SiO₂ gives three linear Cu⁰-CO components at 2098, 2065 and 2030 cm⁻¹, the last two read as very unsaturated centres. Low coverage and static vacuum put these about 20 cm⁻¹ below the 2120 cm⁻¹ the same group measures under flowing CO; the Cu⁰ to Cu⁺ separation stays near 27 cm⁻¹ either way.

Figs. S3a and S3b (DRIFTS, 5% CO/He flowing at 20 mL min⁻¹, 1 bar, 15 min, high coverage): linear Cu⁰-CO at 2120 cm⁻¹ on the unpromoted Cu/SiO₂ at 30 °C. At 220 °C no adsorbed CO is left on it (Fig. S3b), the baseline against which the Ga-promoted samples hold CO. Desorption is followed in Figs. S5 and S6.

Fig. 5a and Section 3.3 (14% Co/Al₂O₃ reduced in situ at 450 °C for 1 h in 60% H₂/Ar, then 220 °C, 30% CO + 60% H₂ + 10% Ar at ambient pressure, steady state, background SiC under Ar at the same temperature): a large band of linear, on-top CO on metallic cobalt, with ill-resolved bridged and multibonded CO below it. The CO(g) branches sit on its high side and only subtract cleanly against SiC at the same temperature and feed (Fig. 7b), which then leaves the same flat baseline as removing CO altogether (Fig. 7c).

Fig. 4c and Section 3.2 (14% Co/Siralox reduced at 450 °C, then 80 °C, 30% CO + 60% H₂ + 10% Ar, background the same sample under Ar): the paper describes a cobalt carbonyl signal spanning 2100 to 1700 cm⁻¹ and gives only its maximum, without separating linear from bridged CO. It is recorded here because the maximum is where linear CO sits. The spectrum was taken to measure the gas path through the bed, for which the CO(g) R branch was used because it does not overlap this signal.

Fig. 4a (spatially resolved SSITKA-DRIFTS, 3 wt% Pt/CeO₂ reduced in 10% H₂ at 300 °C; 200 °C, 1 bar, H₂/CO₂ = 4 in He): linear ¹²CO on Pt at 2053 cm⁻¹, red-shifted from the usual 2070–2080 cm⁻¹ of CO on Pt. The paper reads the shift as stronger back-donation from Pt, because the highly reduced ceria surface hinders electron transfer from Pt to the support, and takes it to place the carbonyls at the Pt-ceria interface. After the ¹³CO₂ switch the carbonyl exchanges at the pace of CO(g) at every bed position (Fig. 5) and is most abundant at the inlet (Fig. 6), the paper's case for it as an RWGS intermediate rather than readsorbed product. The ¹³C counterpart is its own band, ν(¹³CO) linear (μ₁).

On-top (linear, μ₁) CO on Pd nanoparticles typically observed at 2080–2090 cm⁻¹ (Introduction, citing prior SFG work), distinct from this same paper's own focus on bridge-site coverage dependence (see co_bridge_mu2). The cited work spans ultrahigh vacuum to atmospheric pressure; vacuum follows the paper’s own calculations and is this collection’s choice.

Fig. 7a (He+CO₂ against H₂+He, 20 bar): MCR-resolved component spectra of CuZn/SiO₂, 230 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 10 NmL min⁻¹, after H₂ at 300 °C. Linear CO* on metallic Cu at 2113 cm⁻¹, made in situ when the H₂ comes back rather than dosed: its rise mirrors the decay of the Cu-bound formate, which the authors read as formate decomposing to CO, the RWGS route. Invisible at steady state on every catalyst, being hydrogenated as fast as it forms; only the alternating feed shows it.

Fig. 2A (3 % Au/SiO₂ pre-reduced in H₂, 1 % CO in He at 50 °C, 2 to 120 min; unpublished results reported in this review): a band at 2113 cm⁻¹ turns into one at 2076 through an isosbestic point, so one kind of site is converting quantitatively into another rather than two species growing side by side. The review's own conclusion for gold is three ranges: terraces near 2130 but unoccupied above 70 K, unreconstructed edges and corners 2115 to 2095, and the kinks and roughened edges of a CO-restructured surface 2080 to 2060 (p. 61). Silica cannot make oxygen vacancies, so the low band here is not negatively charged gold.

Section 2.1 and Fig. 2 of a perspective: 2077 cm⁻¹ is the singleton frequency chosen as the input of a coupled-oscillator calculation, "to resemble" atop CO on the Pt(100) facet (ref. 16), not a spectrum the perspective measured or quotes as one. From it the model gives the in-phase mode of coupled arrays: 9 cm⁻¹ above the singleton for a line of five, more for larger patches. Recorded as a calculation on a model surface, in vacuum as such a model is.

Section 2.3.2, p. 96 of a monograph summarising infrared work on oxide surfaces rather than reporting one measurement, which is why no position, surface or sampling geometry is recorded here. Where the metal has d electrons to donate into CO's 2π*, a genuine carbonyl forms and ν(CO) falls below the gas-phase value: linear CO between 2100 and 1900 cm⁻¹, bridged below 1900, three-coordinated below 1800. The book's point is that one probe molecule reports two opposite things depending on the site, because a σ-only bond to a cation pushes the same band the other way instead. A summary rather than one measurement; the experiments it draws on adsorb CO on samples held under the probe gas, so gas is this collection’s reading.

Figs. S16 and S17: Ag film electrode in CO-saturated 0.1 M Cs₂CO₃ (so the SI caption; the main text says CsHCO₃), one spectrum every 50 mV from +0.7 to −1.1 V vs. RHE, against a reference taken at open circuit in Ar-saturated 0.1 M CsHCO₃. Nothing adsorbs at positive potentials; linear CO appears near 0 V and redshifts from 2010 to 1950 cm⁻¹ with a Stark tuning slope of 57.7 cm⁻¹ V⁻¹, strongest near −0.35 V, then gives way to bridged CO. The two numbers are the ends of the sweep, not two species.

Fig. 2b, c: Ag film in CO₂-saturated 0.1 M CsHCO₃, pulsed electrolysis at E(c) = −1.1 V with E(a) = −0.2 V (Fig. 2b) or +0.7 V (Fig. 2c) vs. RHE, 10 s each, 85 % iR compensation. Linear CO is labelled at 1960 cm⁻¹ under the −0.2 V pulses and at 1928 to 1935 under the +0.7 V ones. It interconverts with bridged CO on every switch and fades within the +0.7 V pulse as the CO is stripped oxidatively. Static electrolysis at −1.1 V shows bridged CO only. The positions are figure labels and depend on the potential; compare the CO-dosed sweep in the same paper.

Fig. S31: Cu film electrode in CO₂-saturated 0.1 M CsHCO₃, one spectrum every 50 mV from −0.2 to −1.1 V vs. RHE, against open circuit in Ar-saturated CsHCO₃. Linear CO from CO₂ reduction appears near −0.4 V and sits between 2049 and 2077 cm⁻¹. Nothing shows near 2125 cm⁻¹, where CO on the bare Au underlayer lies (Fig. S32), so the authors take the Au as covered. Under pulses (Fig. 4, E(c) = −1.1 V, E(a) = −0.8 or +0.6 V) its decay at E(c) is fitted as first order: about 0.005 rising to 0.02 s⁻¹ over 100 s with +0.6 V pulses, 0.011 falling to 0.004 s⁻¹ with −0.8 V ones. The authors read that depletion rate, not the coverage, as what sets C₂₊ selectivity.

Fig. 2d, with coordinates in Supplementary Data 1 (not read): spin-polarised DFT, RPBE with D3 dispersion in VASP, a three-layer 3 × 3 Ag(111) slab, frequencies by finite differences in ASE (±0.005 Å). The applied potential is left out of the frequency calculation, which the authors do for simplicity, so this is a zero-field value set against Stark-shifted measurements. Linear CO calculated at 2005 cm⁻¹, against 2010 to 1928 measured. The slab carries 15 Å of vacuum and the frequency calculation no solvent.

Fig. S32: the bare Au film on the Si prism, the underlayer of the Ag and Cu electrodes, in CO-saturated 0.1 M CsHCO₃ at +0.4 V vs. RHE, against a reference taken before CO was let in. Linear CO on gold at 2125 cm⁻¹ is the control: neither the Ag nor the Cu overlayer shows a band there, which is the authors’ evidence that the gold is covered.

Supplementary Note 5, Figs. S36 and S39: CO reduction on the Cu film in CO-saturated 0.05 M Cs₂CO₃ (pH 10.6). In a sweep the linear CO band is strongest near −0.5 V and depletes below −0.8 V vs. RHE, unlike under CO₂. Under pulses with E(a) = −0.5 or +0.6 V it builds up during −0.5 V and is stripped during +0.6 V; its decay is fitted as 0.0051 falling to 0.0040 per s with −0.5 V pulses and 0.0026 rising to 0.0041 with +0.6 V ones. The text puts E(c) at −0.7 V, the caption of Fig. S39 at −1.1 V. No position is given, so none is recorded.

Fig. S18 (He+CO₂ against H₂+He, 20 bar): MCR-resolved spectra of the unpromoted Cu/SiO₂, 230 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 10 NmL min⁻¹, after H₂ at 300 °C. Linear CO* on Cu at 2115 cm⁻¹, rising as the Cu-bound formate decays.

Fig. S19 (He+CO₂ against H₂+He, 20 bar): MCR-resolved spectra of CuIn/SiO₂, 230 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 10 NmL min⁻¹, after H₂ at 300 °C. Linear CO* on Cu at 2108 cm⁻¹, the lowest of the three catalysts that show it. None forms on CuGa/SiO₂ (Fig. S20), which the authors take as the reason for its selectivity: spillover of formate to Ga³⁺ outruns its decomposition on Cu.

Section 2.2 and Fig. 3B of a perspective, reviewing RAIRS of atop CO on Cu(110) (Woodruff, Pritchard and co-workers, 1982): the band moves only from 2088 to 2094 cm⁻¹ across the whole coverage range, because a chemical redshift near −44 cm⁻¹ almost cancels a coupling blueshift near +50, as isotope dilution showed. A single crystal, not a supported catalyst. Single-crystal RAIRS is a vacuum measurement; the perspective does not state the pressure, so vacuum is this collection’s assumption.

Fig. 3a (KRS-5 transmission cell, −160 °C, 0.15 mbar CO, static vacuum, after in-situ reduction in H₂ at 300 °C and evacuation to 10⁻⁴ mbar), the Ga-promoted CuGa(x) series: the same linear Cu⁰-CO components as on Cu/SiO₂, the 2065 and 2030 cm⁻¹ pair losing intensity as Ga is loaded, which the authors attribute to Ga₂O₃ diffusing to the edge of the Cu particles, beside a new Cu⁺-CO band at 2125 cm⁻¹. No separate positions are printed for the Ga samples.

Figs. S3a and S3b (DRIFTS, 5% CO/He flowing at 20 mL min⁻¹, 1 bar, 15 min, high coverage): linear Cu⁰-CO at 2120 cm⁻¹ on the CuGa(x) series at 30 °C, beside Cu⁺-CO at 2147, and still present at 220 °C on CuGa(0.15) and CuGa(0.20) alone; at Ga/(Cu+Ga) ≤ 0.10 it is gone at that temperature, as on Cu/SiO₂. That it survives on the Ga-rich samples is the paper’s evidence that the promoter strengthens CO binding.

bands.description: Atop CO carrying ¹³C, the same stretch as the ¹²CO band roughly 45 to 50 cm⁻¹ lower. It exists mainly as the landing zone for the standard isotope check: substitute ¹³CO and see whether a candidate band moves by the predicted amount. It matters in its own right in ¹³CO₂ transient work, where the shifted position is where the surface CO pool is tracked.

references.note: Fig. 4a (3 wt% Pt/CeO₂ reduced in 10% H₂ at 300 °C; 200 °C, 1 bar, H₂/CO₂ = 4 in He, after the switch to ¹³CO₂/H₂/Ar): the linear carbonyl at 2005 cm⁻¹, 48 cm⁻¹ below its ¹²CO position of 2053, which the paper reads as exchange to ¹³C carbonyls. It sits close to the 2007 cm⁻¹ the harmonic ratio predicts, this collection's check rather than the paper's. Placed, like its ¹²C form, at the Pt-ceria interface.

Section 3 of a perspective, on the isotope-dilution method rather than on one spectrum, which is why no position is recorded here; the technique is the one the perspective proposes, MIOIRS. The ¹³CO and ¹²CO singletons lie about 50 cm⁻¹ apart, enough to cut the coupling between a molecule and its neighbours by roughly an order of magnitude once one is diluted in the other; ¹³C¹⁸O against ¹²C¹⁶O gives 100 cm⁻¹ and cuts it further. Diluting at a fixed coverage separates the chemical and coupling halves of a coverage shift, and recovers bands that intensity transfer had hidden, such as CO on copper terraces. The perspective proposes running it under reaction conditions and names that MIOIRS. No measurement of its own; gas is recorded because the method is proposed for catalysts under reaction, this collection’s reading.

bands.description: Bridging CO coordinated between two metal atoms. Lower frequency than linear CO due to increased metal→CO π-backdonation from the extra metal center, and typically broader/weaker than the linear band, often appearing as a shoulder below it rather than a fully separate peak. Usually emerges or grows in only at higher CO coverage, since it needs two adjacent free metal sites to form.

references.note: Fig. 1a and Section 3.1 (5%Ru/Al₂O₃, 320 °C, 15% CO₂/N₂): the lower of the two CO-Ru bands, recorded here on position. The paper names it only as one of several vibrational modes of CO-Ru bonds and does not separate bridged from multibonded CO.

Fig. 5a and Section 3.3 (14% Co/Al₂O₃ at 220 °C, 30% CO + 60% H₂ + 10% Ar, ambient pressure, steady state): ill-resolved bands below 2000 cm⁻¹ that the paper associates with bridged and multibonded CO, citing its own earlier work, without giving a position or separating the two. Not resolved from the tail of the linear band.

DFT-calculated (scaled) frequency of bridge-bound CO at the edges of Pd nanoparticles, growing from ~1886 cm⁻¹ for an isolated bridge CO up to ~1989 cm⁻¹ once the edge bridge sites are fully occupied by coadsorbed CO (Table 1) — matching the experimentally observed 1980–1990 cm⁻¹ band and implying particles ≥3 nm to host the necessary 10–12-CO edge ensemble. Calculated on Pd nanoparticle models in vacuum.

Fig. 3a (KRS-5 transmission cell, −160 °C, 0.15 mbar CO, static vacuum, after in-situ reduction in H₂ at 300 °C and evacuation to 10⁻⁴ mbar): bridge-bound (Cu⁰)₂-CO at 1890 cm⁻¹, the fourth and weakest component of the deconvolution of the unpromoted Cu/SiO₂, some 140 cm⁻¹ below the linear band. Not reported for the Ga-promoted samples. It needs the low temperature to be seen at all; nothing at this position survives into the flowing-CO experiments at 30 and 220 °C.

Fig. 6A, p. 63 (2 % Pd/Al₂O₃, 1 % CO in He at 300 K, adapted from Jbir et al.; the review says IR and not which sampling geometry): two bridged carbonyls at 1987 and 1954 cm⁻¹ beside atop CO at about 2090. On a Pd-Sn sample of equal Pd and Sn loading only the atop species survives, at about 2075, and Zn does the same (Fig. 7A). That disappearance is the review's evidence for an intermetallic compound: bridged CO needs two adjacent palladium atoms, so its absence says the pairs are gone. Adsorption heats separate the two cleanly, about 90 kJ mol⁻¹ for the atop CO against more than 165 for the bridged.

Section 2.2 and Fig. 3A of a perspective, reviewing RAIRS of CO on the Pd(100) single crystal (ref. 46, 1982): a single band moving from 1895 to 1997 cm⁻¹ as the coverage goes from about zero to 0.8, almost 100 cm⁻¹ in all, of which roughly 60 is a chemical shift and the rest dipole coupling. The perspective labels the band atop CO; the positions are the bridged range for palladium, and it is recorded on the bridged band here for that reason. The integrated area levels off near half a monolayer, so area stops tracking coverage well before saturation. Single-crystal RAIRS is a vacuum measurement; the perspective does not state the pressure, so vacuum is this collection’s assumption.

Section 2.3.2, p. 96 of a monograph, not one measurement: bridged carbonyls lie below 1900 cm⁻¹ and three-coordinated ones below 1800. The book adds a constraint the position alone does not give: a carbonyl on a cation can only be linear, because in an M–O–M arrangement the cations are too far apart for one CO molecule to bond to two of them at once. A bridged band is therefore evidence of an ensemble of reduced metal atoms rather than of a cation, whatever else is on the surface. Where a cation has two free coordination places it forms a dicarbonyl instead. A summary rather than one measurement; the experiments it draws on adsorb CO on samples held under the probe gas, so gas is this collection’s reading.

Figs. S16 and S17: Ag film electrode in CO-saturated 0.1 M Cs₂CO₃ (SI caption; the main text says CsHCO₃), swept from +0.7 to −1.1 V vs. RHE. Below about −0.35 V bridged CO takes over from linear CO, between 1848 and 1774 cm⁻¹, with a Stark tuning slope of 85.8 cm⁻¹ V⁻¹, steeper than the 57.7 of linear CO; its integrated intensity peaks near −0.7 V. The two numbers are the ends of the sweep. They lie low for a bridge because the potential is strongly cathodic.

Fig. 2a, e, f: Ag film in CO₂-saturated 0.1 M CsHCO₃. Under static electrolysis at −1.1 V vs. RHE bridged CO is the only CO species, at 1760 cm⁻¹, its intensity levelling off after about 8 s. Deconvolved: 1757 under static conditions (Fig. 2e, 188.3 s) and 1765 under +0.7 V pulses (Fig. 2f, 526.7 s); the pulsed spectra of Fig. 2b label it across 1857 to 1760. It trades intensity with linear CO at every potential switch. The bridge attribution rests on the CO-dosed sweep and on a calculation on Ag(111).

Fig. 2d, with coordinates in Supplementary Data 1 (not read): spin-polarised DFT, RPBE with D3 dispersion in VASP, a three-layer 3 × 3 Ag(111) slab, frequencies by finite differences in ASE (±0.005 Å). The applied potential is left out of the frequency calculation, which the authors do for simplicity, so this is a zero-field value set against Stark-shifted measurements. Bridged CO calculated at 1867 cm⁻¹, against 1848 to 1757 measured. The slab carries 15 Å of vacuum and the frequency calculation no solvent.

Fig. S31: Cu film electrode in CO₂-saturated 0.1 M CsHCO₃, one spectrum every 50 mV from −0.2 to −1.1 V vs. RHE. Bridged CO is labelled at 1800 cm⁻¹, weak and broad beside the *CHO band that spans 1700 to 1800; the main text calls the region "likely CO(B) or *CHO" and settles on *CHO from the pulsed data, so this row is the figure’s label rather than an argued attribution.

bands.description: Three-fold hollow CO coordinated to three metal atoms at once. Stronger multi-center π-backdonation shifts ν(CO) well below both bridge and linear adsorption. Generally needs a close-packed facet to offer this coordination geometry at all, and tends to appear or strengthen with increasing coverage as simpler one- and two-fold sites fill up first.

references.note: DFT-calculated (scaled) frequencies of 3-fold hollow CO on Pd(111)-type facets/nanoparticles range from ~1802–1815 cm⁻¹ at low coverage up to ~1902 cm⁻¹ at the high-coverage (2×2)-3CO structure (0.75 ML), tracking the same coverage-dependent blue shift seen for bridge-bound CO. Calculated on Pd nanoparticle models in vacuum.

Figs. 8A and 9A, p. 65 (14 % Co/Al₂O₃, operando DRIFTS at 220 °C, 30 % CO + 60 % H₂ in Ar, atmospheric pressure, 22 h on stream): a broad band near 1850 cm⁻¹ the review calls Hollow-CO and describes as bridged or multi-coordinated without separating the two, sitting under two linear components between 2100 and 1950. Small amounts of tin, Sn:Co from 1:120 to 1:30, titrate it selectively, and the methane and propene rates track the Hollow-CO fraction. Its decomposition rate is about twice the rate of methane formation, which the review takes as evidence that it is on the main path to hydrocarbons while the linear CO is not.

Section 2.3.2, p. 96 of a monograph, not one measurement: three-coordinated bridged carbonyls lie below 1800 cm⁻¹, the lowest of the three coordination ranges the book sets out, because the more metal atoms share the CO the more they donate into its 2π* and the weaker the C–O bond becomes. A summary rather than one measurement; the experiments it draws on adsorb CO on samples held under the probe gas, so gas is this collection’s reading.

Fig. 2e, f: deconvolved spectra of the Ag film during CO₂ reduction, E(c) = −1.1 V vs. RHE, at 188.3 s and 526.7 s. A broad shoulder from about 1650 to 1730 cm⁻¹ under −0.2 V pulses is read as formate and hollow-site CO overlapping, and the CO part is fitted at 1704 and 1719. The main text hedges it ("likely"); the CO-dosed sweep labels the same species. Their calculation puts hollow CO far higher, which they put down to the large overpotential and the missing Stark slope. That "hollow" on Ag(111) means this three-fold band is this collection’s assumption; Fig. S20c draws the CO in a hollow.

Fig. 2d, with coordinates in Supplementary Data 1 (not read): spin-polarised DFT, RPBE with D3 dispersion in VASP, a three-layer 3 × 3 Ag(111) slab, frequencies by finite differences in ASE (±0.005 Å). The applied potential is left out of the frequency calculation, which the authors do for simplicity, so this is a zero-field value set against Stark-shifted measurements. Hollow CO calculated at 1882 cm⁻¹, above the bridge value, against 1720 to 1704 measured; the authors attribute the gap to large overpotentials and the missing Stark slope. The slab carries 15 Å of vacuum and the frequency calculation no solvent.

Fig. S16a: Ag film electrode in CO-saturated 0.1 M Cs₂CO₃ (SI caption; the main text says CsHCO₃), swept from +0.7 to −1.1 V vs. RHE against open circuit in Ar-saturated CsHCO₃. Hollow-site CO is labelled from 1720 to 1710 cm⁻¹ at the cathodic end, below bridged CO; the main text does not discuss it for this experiment. The two numbers are the ends of the label, not two species.

bands.description: Four-fold hollow CO coordinated to four metal atoms at once — a comparatively rare coordination geometry, since it needs a specific square arrangement of surface atoms to form. Exhibits the lowest ν(CO) frequencies among metal-CO adsorption modes, since backdonation from four neighbors at once weakens the C-O bond more than any other coordination geometry.

Linear CO adsorbed on a Lewis-acidic cation site rather than a reduced metal atom. Markedly less metal→CO π-backdonation than on a metallic surface, blue-shifting ν(CO) above the free-gas value (2143 cm⁻¹) rather than below it — the opposite direction from every metallic-surface CO band in this dataset. Position correlates with the cation's formal charge and Lewis acidity, making this band a widely used spectroscopic probe of acid-site strength and oxidation state; the same ¹³CO isotope-shift check used for metallic sites applies here too.

references.note: Table 1, the measured HF band on LiZSM-5 (Si/Al = 14), from self-supporting wafers activated at 723 K in vacuo and dosed with about 1 Torr of CO at liquid-nitrogen temperature. Above the 2143 cm⁻¹ of free CO, and the shift falls as the cation grows, which is what marks the interaction as electrostatic rather than backdonating.

Table 1, the measured HF band on NaZSM-5 (Si/Al = 14), from self-supporting wafers activated at 723 K in vacuo and dosed with about 1 Torr of CO at liquid-nitrogen temperature. Above the 2143 cm⁻¹ of free CO, and the shift falls as the cation grows, which is what marks the interaction as electrostatic rather than backdonating.

Table 1, the measured HF band on KZSM-5 (Si/Al = 14), from self-supporting wafers activated at 723 K in vacuo and dosed with about 1 Torr of CO at liquid-nitrogen temperature. Above the 2143 cm⁻¹ of free CO, and the shift falls as the cation grows, which is what marks the interaction as electrostatic rather than backdonating.

Table 1, the measured HF band on RbZSM-5 (Si/Al = 14), from self-supporting wafers activated at 723 K in vacuo and dosed with about 1 Torr of CO at liquid-nitrogen temperature. Above the 2143 cm⁻¹ of free CO, and the shift falls as the cation grows, which is what marks the interaction as electrostatic rather than backdonating.

Table 1, the measured HF band on CsZSM-5 (Si/Al = 14), from self-supporting wafers activated at 723 K in vacuo and dosed with about 1 Torr of CO at liquid-nitrogen temperature. Above the 2143 cm⁻¹ of free CO, and the shift falls as the cation grows, which is what marks the interaction as electrostatic rather than backdonating.

Table 1, the measured HF band on HZSM-5 (Si/Al = 14), from self-supporting wafers activated at 723 K in vacuo and dosed with about 1 Torr of CO at liquid-nitrogen temperature. Above the 2143 cm⁻¹ of free CO, and the shift falls as the cation grows, which is what marks the interaction as electrostatic rather than backdonating.

Table 2, B3-LYP on a single naked Li⁺ cation: ν(CO) of the C-bonded adduct at 2317 cm⁻¹, against 2218 cm⁻¹ computed for free CO at the same level. The naked-cation shift is far larger than the measured one because the zeolite framework is left out; embedding the cation in an Al(OH)₃H⁻ cluster cuts it to about a third. An isolated cation-CO complex, so the model is in vacuum.

Table 2, B3-LYP on a single naked Na⁺ cation: ν(CO) of the C-bonded adduct at 2296 cm⁻¹, against 2218 cm⁻¹ computed for free CO at the same level. The naked-cation shift is far larger than the measured one because the zeolite framework is left out; embedding the cation in an Al(OH)₃H⁻ cluster cuts it to about a third. An isolated cation-CO complex, so the model is in vacuum.

Table 2, B3-LYP on a single naked K⁺ cation: ν(CO) of the C-bonded adduct at 2275 cm⁻¹, against 2218 cm⁻¹ computed for free CO at the same level. The naked-cation shift is far larger than the measured one because the zeolite framework is left out; embedding the cation in an Al(OH)₃H⁻ cluster cuts it to about a third. An isolated cation-CO complex, so the model is in vacuum.

Table 2, B3-LYP on a single naked Rb⁺ cation: ν(CO) of the C-bonded adduct at 2268 cm⁻¹, against 2218 cm⁻¹ computed for free CO at the same level. The naked-cation shift is far larger than the measured one because the zeolite framework is left out; embedding the cation in an Al(OH)₃H⁻ cluster cuts it to about a third. An isolated cation-CO complex, so the model is in vacuum.

Table 2, B3-LYP on a single naked Cs⁺ cation: ν(CO) of the C-bonded adduct at 2261 cm⁻¹, against 2218 cm⁻¹ computed for free CO at the same level. The naked-cation shift is far larger than the measured one because the zeolite framework is left out; embedding the cation in an Al(OH)₃H⁻ cluster cuts it to about a third. An isolated cation-CO complex, so the model is in vacuum.

Fig. 3a (KRS-5 transmission cell, −160 °C, 0.15 mbar CO, static vacuum): a Cu⁺-CO feature absent from the unpromoted Cu/SiO₂ and appearing only once Ga is loaded. Its deconvoluted area gives the Cu⁺/(Cu⁰+Cu⁺) ratio, which rises linearly with Ga content (Fig. S4a) and correlates with TOF(MeOH) at every temperature with R² above 0.95 (Fig. 3b). Assigned to Cu⁺ at the Cu-Ga₂O₃ interface, the proposed methanol active site.

Figs. S3a and S3b (DRIFTS, 5% CO/He flowing at 20 mL min⁻¹, 1 bar): the same Cu⁺ carbonyl at high coverage under flowing CO, 22 cm⁻¹ above the value the transmission experiment gives at −160 °C under vacuum. The paper attributes the whole difference to coverage and to static against dynamic conditions rather than to a different site, noting that the Cu⁰ to Cu⁺ separation holds near 27 cm⁻¹ in both. Well defined at 220 °C only on CuGa(0.15) and CuGa(0.20); desorption is followed in Figs. S5 and S6.

Figs. S3c, S4b and S10 (DRIFTS, 10% CO₂/Ar at 20 mL min⁻¹, 3 bar, 220 °C): no CO is fed here. The band grows when CO₂ alone is dosed, and the authors read it as Cu⁺(O)-CO, the carbonyl left on a Cu⁺ that has just split CO₂ into CO* and O*. It is absent on the unpromoted catalyst and its area scales with Ga loading (Fig. S4b), which is their evidence that the interfacial Cu⁺ dissociates CO₂ without hydrogen. Switching to H₂/Ar moves it to 2165 cm⁻¹ (Fig. S10), read as the oxygen being taken off the site.

Table S5 and Fig. S10 (operando DRIFTS, 220 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 6 bar, 25 mL min⁻¹): Cu⁺-CO under working conditions, and the band the 2196 cm⁻¹ Cu⁺(O)-CO turns into once H₂ reaches the surface. This is the carbonyl the paper's RWGS plus CO-hydrogenation route runs through, so its presence under reaction rather than under a CO probe is the point of the measurement. Literature values quoted alongside it are 2166 to 2173 cm⁻¹.

Table S5: assigned to Cu²⁺-CO, against a literature value of 2199 cm⁻¹. The table lists its feed condition as CO₂+H₂, but the only figures showing the band are the formic acid and methanol adsorption experiments over Cu/SiO₂ (Figs. S15a and S16a), so the table and the figures do not agree on which experiment it came from and the sample is recorded as the one those figures name. A Cu²⁺ carbonyl on a catalyst reduced at 300 °C is a minority claim, and the paper neither argues it further nor uses it.

Table 1 and Sect. 3.1.3 (Cu-ZSM-5, Si/Al 25 and 1.01 wt% Cu, ion-exchanged from copper acetate, calcined at 673 K, reduced in 5 kPa CO at 473 K and evacuated; self-supporting pellet, transmission, 2 cm⁻¹; CO at 100 K, and low coverage at ambient temperature, SI Fig. S2 not read here): Cu⁺–CO resolved into three families of dry Cu⁺. 2158 cm⁻¹ on the principal cationic sites (type II); a shoulder at 2166 on a minor, more electrophilic family that water covers first (type I), backed by a second νₛ dicarbonyl component at 2182; and 2141 at higher coverage on Cu⁺ not in cationic positions, more highly coordinated, from an oxide-like phase (type III). Dosed at 100 K the principal band appears at 2157. The water-coordinated sites are a claim of their own.

Sect. 3.2.1 and Table 1, type IV (same Cu-ZSM-5 with water: added to a CO-precovered sample, or adsorbed and evacuated at ambient temperature before CO at 100 K; SI Figs. S4 and S5 not read here): mixed aqua-carbonyls. Water moves the 2158 cm⁻¹ band to 2132, Cu⁺(H₂O)₂CO; lowering the water pressure gives 2139, Cu⁺(H₂O)(CO), and long evacuation returns 2158. The paper reads the lower frequency as a weaker σ and electrostatic bond, the π back-bond barely changed since the integrated intensity hardly moves. 2139 nearly coincides with CO on oxide-like Cu⁺ at 2141.

Fig. 5A, p. 63 (Au, Au-Ag and Ag embedded in silicalite-1, operando DRIFTS at 100 °C under 2.8 % CO + 8 % O₂ in He): Ag⁺-CO at 2189 and 2172 cm⁻¹ on the plain silver sample moves to about 2160 on the alloy, and the Au⁺-CO signal at 2134 falls by half with the gold loading and particle size unchanged. The two together are the review's evidence for a genuinely alloyed phase. Silver has the lower surface tension of the pair, 1086 against 1333 mJ m⁻², so it takes the corner and edge sites and displaces the gold that would otherwise sit there.

Section 2.3.2, pp. 95–96 and Table 2.11, p. 99 (a monograph; the sampling geometry behind the number is not stated). One band at 2190 cm⁻¹ after CO adsorption on ZnO at 293 K, with photoelectron work on the same system showing the bond is made through the carbon and the 5σ orbital. On a coordinatively unsaturated cation the bond is essentially σ only, so ν(CO) sits above the 2143 cm⁻¹ of the free molecule, and the shift upward grows with the cation's ratio of charge to radius. Such complexes are relatively unstable and are usually removed by degassing at room temperature, which is one way to tell them from the far more stable M⁺ and M⁰ carbonyls (p. 274). Measured under CO: the complex is removed by degassing at room temperature.

bands.description: CO on a metal cation carrying ¹³C, the same σ-dominated stretch about 50 cm⁻¹ below its ¹²CO position. Its use is the isotope check and the mixed-isotope test for geminal species, where ¹²CO and ¹³CO are put on the same cations at once.

references.note: Sect. 3.3.1, Fig. 4A spectrum a (Cu-ZSM-5 precovered with equal amounts of ¹²CO and ¹³CO, evacuated at ambient temperature to remove the dicarbonyls, cooled to 100 K, before any NO): Cu⁺–¹³CO at 2108 cm⁻¹ beside Cu⁺–¹²CO at 2158.

bands.description: CO coordinated through its oxygen rather than its carbon, the reverse orientation of every other CO band here. On an electrostatic cation site with no backdonation the field polarises the bond the other way, so O-bonding puts ν(CO) below the free-gas value while C-bonding on the same site puts it above. The two orientations coexist as close-lying isomers, with the C-bonded one preferred and far stronger.

references.note: Table 1, the measured LF band on LiZSM-5 (Si/Al = 14), from self-supporting wafers activated at 723 K in vacuo and dosed with about 1 Torr of CO at liquid-nitrogen temperature. Below the 2143 cm⁻¹ of free CO, and it rises as the cation grows while the HF band falls; its intensity relative to the HF band grows steadily from Li to Cs, which with the calculations is the paper's evidence that this is CO bound through its oxygen.

Section 2.3.2, p. 95 of a monograph, with no single measurement behind it, so no position is recorded here. A low-frequency band between 2100 and 2130 cm⁻¹ has been assigned by several authors to Mⁿ⁺···OC adducts, CO bound through the oxygen lone pair rather than the carbon, which shifts the stretch down where the ordinary orientation shifts it up. The book records an isomerisation equilibrium between the two orientations on NaZSM-5, Z-Na···CO against Z-Na⁺···OC, with an enthalpy of 3.8 kJ mol⁻¹, so on an alkali cation the two coexist rather than one of them winning. A summary rather than one measurement; the experiments it draws on adsorb CO on samples held under the probe gas, so gas is this collection’s reading.

bands.description: Asymmetric ν(CO) component of a geminal dicarbonyl species: two linear CO ligands bound to a single isolated cationic metal center, stretching out of phase (one lengthens as the other shortens). The symmetric/asymmetric pair appearing together, rather than a single linear-CO band, is itself diagnostic of an atomically dispersed cationic site — a single metal atom isolated enough to bind two CO molecules at once. The symmetric component lies above the antisymmetric one, and the splitting depends on the cation: 29 cm⁻¹ for Cu⁺(CO)₂ in ZSM-5, about 70 for Rh⁺(CO)₂. The firm test of a geminal pair is a ¹²CO/¹³CO mixture: two ligands coupled on one cation give mixed-isotope bands that two neighbouring monocarbonyls cannot.

references.note: Sect. 3.1.3 (Cu-ZSM-5, Si/Al 25 and 1.01 wt% Cu, ion-exchanged from copper acetate, calcined at 673 K, reduced in 5 kPa CO at 473 K and evacuated; self-supporting pellet, transmission, 2 cm⁻¹): CO dosed at 100 K in increasing amounts first gives Cu⁺–CO at 2157 cm⁻¹, then the Cu⁺(CO)₂ dicarbonyl, νₐₛ at 2151 with νₛ at 2180. Under gas-phase CO much of it goes on to the tricarbonyl (2191, 2167 cm⁻¹); evacuation at 100 K removes the tricarbonyl and leaves the dicarbonyl. The geminal structure rests on Sect. 3.3.1: the same pair forms when NO is dosed onto a sample precovered with equal ¹²CO and ¹³CO, and the mixed-isotope bands match a force-field calculation; those positions are their own bands. Corrected: this note once described that test as adsorbing the isotopic mixture alone.

bands.description: The lower band of a geminal dicarbonyl carrying ¹³C: the antisymmetric stretch shifted down when both ligands are labelled, and mostly the ¹³CO ligand when only one is.

references.note: Sect. 3.3.1, Fig. 4A (Cu-ZSM-5 precovered with equal ¹²CO and ¹³CO, evacuated at ambient temperature, then NO dosed at 100 K, which turns monocarbonyls into dicarbonyls and dinitrosyls, 2Cu⁺–CO + 2NO → Cu⁺(CO)₂ + Cu⁺(NO)₂): the lower band of Cu⁺(¹³CO)₂ at 2103 cm⁻¹, as calculated, and of the mixed Cu⁺(¹²CO)(¹³CO) at 2112, against 2113 calculated. Filing the mixed species' lower band with the antisymmetric mode is this collection's reading.

bands.description: Symmetric ν(CO) component of geminal dicarbonyl species with two linear CO ligands bound to a single isolated cationic metal center. Appears together with the asymmetric band and is characteristic of isolated cationic adsorption sites.

references.note: Sect. 3.1.3 (Cu-ZSM-5, Si/Al 25 and 1.01 wt% Cu, ion-exchanged from copper acetate, calcined at 673 K, reduced in 5 kPa CO at 473 K and evacuated; self-supporting pellet, transmission, 2 cm⁻¹; CO at 100 K): νₛ of Cu⁺(CO)₂ at 2180 cm⁻¹, 29 cm⁻¹ above νₐₛ at 2151. At low coverage a second component near 2182 cm⁻¹ belongs to the dicarbonyls of a minor, more electrophilic Cu⁺ family (monocarbonyl 2166 cm⁻¹), absent on a water-precovered sample (Sect. 3.2.1). The paper's own tricarbonyl bands are at 2191 and 2167 cm⁻¹. Corrected: this note once gave 2190, 2164 and 2140 cm⁻¹, Zecchina's 1994 values that the paper only quotes in its introduction.

bands.description: The upper band of a geminal dicarbonyl carrying ¹³C. With both ligands labelled it is the symmetric stretch shifted down; with one of each, the two ligands no longer vibrate as a symmetric pair and the upper band is mostly the ¹²CO one. Seeing that mixed band at all is what proves two CO share one cation.

references.note: Sect. 3.3.1, Fig. 4A (Cu-ZSM-5 precovered with equal ¹²CO and ¹³CO, evacuated at ambient temperature, then NO dosed at 100 K, which turns monocarbonyls into dicarbonyls and dinitrosyls, 2Cu⁺–CO + 2NO → Cu⁺(CO)₂ + Cu⁺(NO)₂): the upper band of Cu⁺(¹³CO)₂ at 2131 cm⁻¹ and of the mixed Cu⁺(¹²CO)(¹³CO) at 2169, both where a force-field calculation from the ¹²C dicarbonyl puts them. The paper takes the agreement as unambiguous proof of dicarbonyls rather than mixed carbonyl-nitrosyls. Filing the mixed species' upper band with the symmetric mode is this collection's reading.

bands.description: Upper band of a tricarbonyl, three CO on one cation: the totally symmetric stretch. Cu⁺ in zeolites, with three free coordination sites, takes a third CO only at low temperature and under CO pressure, and gives it up on evacuation, back to the dicarbonyl. With the back-donation shared three ways, both tricarbonyl bands sit high, the upper one above every Cu⁺ mono- and dicarbonyl band.

references.note: Sect. 3.1.3 (Cu-ZSM-5, Si/Al 25 and 1.01 wt% Cu, reduced in 5 kPa CO at 473 K and evacuated; self-supporting pellet, transmission, CO dosed at 100 K and kept in the gas phase): under gas-phase CO a large part of the Cu⁺(CO)₂ dicarbonyls converts into Cu⁺(CO)₃ tricarbonyls, with bands at 2191 and 2167 cm⁻¹; evacuation at 100 K destroys them and leaves the dicarbonyls. The paper gives the two positions without naming the modes; filing 2191 cm⁻¹ as the symmetric mode is this collection's reading, the totally symmetric stretch of a C₃ᵥ tricarbonyl lying above the degenerate one.

bands.description: Lower band of a tricarbonyl, three CO on one cation: the degenerate antisymmetric stretch. It falls among the Cu⁺ monocarbonyl and dicarbonyl bands, so it is identified by appearing together with its upper partner under CO pressure at low temperature and leaving with it on evacuation.

references.note: Sect. 3.1.3 (Cu-ZSM-5, Si/Al 25 and 1.01 wt% Cu, reduced in 5 kPa CO at 473 K and evacuated; self-supporting pellet, transmission, CO dosed at 100 K and kept in the gas phase): under gas-phase CO a large part of the Cu⁺(CO)₂ dicarbonyls converts into Cu⁺(CO)₃ tricarbonyls, with bands at 2191 and 2167 cm⁻¹; evacuation at 100 K destroys them and leaves the dicarbonyls. The paper gives the two positions without naming the modes; filing 2167 cm⁻¹ as the antisymmetric mode is this collection's reading, the totally symmetric stretch of a C₃ᵥ tricarbonyl lying above the degenerate one.

bands.description: Surface formyl C=O stretch (HCO*); mechanistic intermediate from CO + H. Often observed transiently. Distinguishes the CO-H pathway from formate-mediated routes.

references.note: Table 3 and Fig. 3B, 30 bar. CZ, a coprecipitated Cu/ZnO with Cu:Zn 2.1:1, diluted to 8 wt% in KBr and activated in H₂ at 513 K; 3H₂/CO₂ at 20 NmL min⁻¹, 513 K, 4 cm⁻¹, 64 scans. ν(C=O) at 1759 cm⁻¹, assigned either to formyl *HCO or to *HCOOH held by a weak hydrogen bond, the small red shift from gaseous HC(=O)OH at 1776 cm⁻¹ being the argument for the latter. One of four bands (1759, 1691, 1457 and 1398 cm⁻¹) whose intensity rises with the GHSV and with the methanol in the outlet gas, which is this paper’s criterion for a true intermediate rather than a spectator. Absent under a 2H₂/CO feed, where no adsorbate could be identified between 2400 and 2000 cm⁻¹ at all.

Fig. S31: Cu film electrode in CO₂-saturated 0.1 M CsHCO₃, one spectrum every 50 mV from −0.2 to −1.1 V vs. RHE, against open circuit in Ar-saturated CsHCO₃. The figure labels a broad *CHO band across 1700 to 1800 cm⁻¹ beside a separate bridged CO at 1800; the main text calls the feature "likely CO(B) or *CHO". Under pulsed electrolysis (Fig. 4) it shows only at −1.1 V and alternates with linear CO under −0.8 V pulses, and on that behaviour they assign it to the C=O stretch of *CHO, the next intermediate after *CO. No single position is given, so none is recorded.

bands.description: Formyl C-H stretch (HCO*); lower than formate ν(CH) at ~2870-2900 and weaker. Diagnostic when paired with C=O at ~1750.
Adsorbed formaldehyde C=O stretch (H₂CO*); reduction product of formyl. Key methanol precursor in some mechanisms.
Adsorbed formaldehyde CH₂ asymmetric stretch (H₂CO*).
Adsorbed formaldehyde CH₂ symmetric stretch (H₂CO*).
Adsorbed formaldehyde CH₂ scissoring (H₂CO*); overlaps monodentate carbonate νₐₛ.
Generic surface acyl/aldehyde C=O stretch (R-C=O*); broad attribution used when species cannot be specifically identified. Distinguishes from formate by absence of ν(CH) at ~2870.

C=O stretch of formic acid adsorbed without losing its proton. It is the one band that tells molecular HCOOH* from the formate it becomes: formate has no localised carbonyl, its two C-O bonds being equivalent, so nothing of its own absorbs here. An absorption in this window after dosing formic acid therefore means the acid did not fully dissociate, and its disappearance on warming tracks the deprotonation. It sits among the surface carbonyl and carbonate bands, which is the standing ambiguity where the acid was not deliberately dosed.

references.note: Table 1 and Fig. 6b, 6f (IRRAS, UHV, room temperature): a band absent from the group's earlier unpolarized work, strong in s-polarized light and much weaker in p, which puts the C=O bond tilted rather than flat. DFT for a monodentate molecular species gives 1721 cm⁻¹. It is the paper's evidence that formic acid adsorbs monodentate and undissociated alongside the formate on this facet. Nothing equivalent appears on Fe₃O₄(001) at room temperature, where a 1700 cm⁻¹ band was seen only at 190 K in earlier work.

bands.description: Hydroxymethyl O-H stretch (H₂COH*); late methanol precursor. Often masked by surface OH.
Hydroxymethyl CH₂ stretch (H₂COH*); overlaps methoxy and methanol.
Hydroxymethyl C-O stretch (H₂COH*); overlaps methoxy ν(C-O) at ~1050-1100.

C-H stretch of methylenebisoxy (dioxymethylene), the intermediate between formate and formaldehyde with both oxygens still bound to the surface. It lands within about ten wavenumbers of formate's own ν(CH), and on catalysts where formate shows a Fermi doublet the lower arm of that doublet sits here too, so position alone cannot separate them. What identifies it is a temperature or transient profile of its own, out of step with the formate it comes from. Attributions rest on calculated frequencies rather than a reference spectrum, since the species cannot be dosed.

references.note: Figs. 5a and 5c (operando DRIFTS-MS, precipitated Ga₂O₃, CO₂/H₂ = 1:3, 30 to 450 °C; Table S2): a band the authors call new, 11 cm⁻¹ above formate's ν(CH) at 2897 cm⁻¹ and tracked apart from it because its intensity varies distinctly from the clearly assigned species. They assign it tentatively to ν(CH) of H₂COO* on the strength of the DFT path in Fig. S15, where hydrogenation of formate through H₂COO* and H₂COOH* is the lower-energy route. Its rise matches the 304 °C onset of methanol in the mass spectrometer (Fig. S16), which is their argument that it is on the path rather than beside it.

bands.description: Monodentate carbonate asymmetric stretch (m-CO₃²⁻*); small splitting (Δν ~100 cm⁻¹).

references.note: Fig. 7A, Pt(3)/MoOₓ(30)/TiO₂: in situ IR at 150 °C and ambient pressure under CO₂ (10), H₂ (30) and He (50) cm³ min⁻¹, on a self-supporting pellet in a quartz cell with CaF₂ windows, referenced to the sample under 30% H₂/He at the same temperature. Assigned there as νₐₛ(COO) of monodentate carbonate, alongside the formate pair at 1370 and 1555 cm⁻¹. It sits at the low edge of this band's window.
Table 3: νas(OCO⁻) at 1530 cm⁻¹; dominant CO₂ adsorption product on La-modified alumina; largely replaced by bidentate carbonate on active Ni-Ce-Fe/La-Al₂O₃.

Table 3 and Fig. 3A, 1 bar. CZ, a coprecipitated Cu/ZnO with Cu:Zn 2.1:1, diluted to 8 wt% in KBr and activated in H₂ at 513 K; 3H₂/CO₂ at 20 NmL min⁻¹, 513 K, 4 cm⁻¹, 64 scans. νₐₛ(OCO) of what the paper calls unidentate carbonate at 1464 cm⁻¹, paired with νₛ at 1400 cm⁻¹, a splitting of 64 cm⁻¹. Literature values cited alongside it: 1469, 1466 and 1467 cm⁻¹.

CO₂ dosed on precipitated Ga₂O₃ at 300 °C, then purged with Ar and with H₂ (Fig. S12; Table S2 gives the mode as νₐₛ(OCO) of CO₃): assigned to carbonate together with the band at 1423 cm⁻¹, and left behind when Ar purging removes the bicarbonate. The paper writes only CO₃ and does not distinguish monodentate from bidentate; the pair is recorded on the monodentate bands because of the roughly 70 cm⁻¹ splitting.

Fig. 3b, Gaussian fit of the spectrum after 120 min evacuation of hydroxylated nanoparticulate Fe₂O₃ dosed with 274 mTorr CO₂ at 296 K. The fit resolves three species: monodentate carbonate at 1446 and 1383 cm⁻¹, bidentate carbonate at 1553 and 1316 cm⁻¹, and the residual bicarbonate. The carbonates are what survives evacuation, while the bicarbonate bands are almost gone after 120 min.

Fig. 1A and Table 1 (operando DRIFTS, 6 wt% Cu/ZrO₂, 220 °C, 3 bar, 20 % CO₂ + 60 % H₂ in He): carbonate on the zirconia at 1468 cm⁻¹, and an ill-defined negative feature at 1465 in the difference spectrum of Fig. 3b where carbonate is being lost 9 s after CO₂ removal. The paper writes only carbonates on ZrO₂ and gives no dentation, so the monodentate placement is the author's reading of the position. Integrating the formate with the carbonate (region 4) and without it (region 3) gives the same decay, which is the paper's evidence that the carbonate contributes little. It reads these as the carbonates far from the copper, reduced slowly because hydrogen spillover does not reach them.

bands.description: Monodentate carbonate symmetric stretch (m-CO₃²⁻*).

references.note: Table 3: νₛ(-C-O) at 1340 cm⁻¹.

Table 3 and Fig. 3. CZ, a coprecipitated Cu/ZnO with Cu:Zn 2.1:1, diluted to 8 wt% in KBr and activated in H₂ at 513 K; 3H₂/CO₂ at 20 NmL min⁻¹, 513 K, 4 cm⁻¹, 64 scans. νₛ(OCO) of unidentate carbonate at 1400 cm⁻¹ at 1 bar and 1398 cm⁻¹ at 30 bar, the partner of νₐₛ at 1464 cm⁻¹. The 30 bar band is one of the four (1759, 1691, 1457, 1398 cm⁻¹) whose intensity follows the GHSV and the methanol in the outlet gas, so the paper reads it as an intermediate, unlike the far stronger formate beside it. Literature values cited: 1376, 1415, 1383 and 1404 cm⁻¹.

CO₂ dosed on precipitated Ga₂O₃ at 300 °C (Fig. S12; Table S2 gives the mode as νₛ(OCO) of CO₃): the lower of the two carbonate bands, the companion of the 1496 cm⁻¹ one. Both survive Ar purging and are consumed once H₂ is introduced, giving formate at 1581 cm⁻¹, which is the reaction the surface Ga-H hydride is proposed to carry out.

Fig. 3b, the symmetric partner of the 1446 cm⁻¹ band in the same Gaussian fit, on nanoparticulate Fe₂O₃ after evacuation. The 63 cm⁻¹ splitting is at the low end of what is usually quoted for monodentate carbonate.

bands.description: Bidentate carbonate asymmetric stretch (b-CO₃²⁻*); large splitting (Δν ~200–350 cm⁻¹). Position shifts with the base strength of the support: ~1510–1550 cm⁻¹ on less basic oxides (ZnO, CuO), ~1600–1670 cm⁻¹ on strongly basic ones (La₂O₃, CeO₂).

references.note: Fig. 3a and Section 3.2 (5%Ru-6.1% "Na₂O"/Al₂O₃ dual function material, 320 °C, 15% CO₂/N₂): bidentate carbonate formed by nucleophilic attack of the Al-O⁻-Na⁺ surface species on CO₂, paired with 1370 cm⁻¹. It dominates the spectrum and covers the bicarbonate bands underneath, and it disappears under H₂ as formate and CH₄ appear.
Table 3: νas(-C=O) 1670 + νas(OCO⁻) 1560 + νₛ(OCO⁻) 1500 cm⁻¹; dominant CO₂ activation product on active catalyst under DRM at 600°C; stabilised by surface oxygen vacancies.

Fig. 4c (3 wt% Pt/CeO₂ reduced in 10% H₂ at 300 °C; 200 °C, 1 bar, H₂/CO₂ = 4 in He; internal background, the last spectrum of the ¹³CO₂ cycle, so ¹²C species point up and ¹³C species down): a positive band at 1605 cm⁻¹, which the paper, after López et al., ascribes to carbonate on ceria, and its MCR analysis (Fig. S6, not read here) to bidentate carbonate on the support. Carbonates exchange faster than CO(g) at every bed position (Fig. 5), which the paper reads as their direct part in making CO, by decomposition at or near the Pt.

Table 3 and Fig. 3. CZ, a coprecipitated Cu/ZnO with Cu:Zn 2.1:1, diluted to 8 wt% in KBr and activated in H₂ at 513 K; 3H₂/CO₂ at 20 NmL min⁻¹, 513 K, 4 cm⁻¹, 64 scans. νₐₛ(OCO) of bidentate carbonate at 1543 cm⁻¹ at 1 bar and 1511 cm⁻¹ at 30 bar. The splitting against νₛ at 1319 cm⁻¹ is 224 cm⁻¹, wide, which for a carbonate is the bidentate signature. Both values sit at the low end of the bidentate range, as is usual on ZnO and CuO rather than on a more basic oxide. Literature values cited: 1530, 1512, 1510 and 1515 cm⁻¹.

Fig. 3b, Gaussian fit after 120 min evacuation of nanoparticulate Fe₂O₃ dosed with CO₂ at 296 K. With gas-phase CO₂ still present the same band sits a few wavenumbers higher, at 1557 cm⁻¹, and a further band at 1590 cm⁻¹ is assigned to a less stable form of bidentate carbonate that evacuation removes entirely.

Figs. 6a, S56d and S56e (operando DRIFTS, 320 °C, 20 bar, 20 vol% CO₂ in N₂ for 1 h, background N₂ at 320 °C): bidentate carbonate at 1532 cm⁻¹ on 30ZnHfOₓ, 1523 cm⁻¹ on 20ZnHfOₓ and 1525 cm⁻¹ on 90ZnHfOₓ. The last is mostly segregated ZnO decorated with HfOₓ clusters, yet matches the solid solutions within a few wavenumbers, which the paper uses to argue that CO₂ is activated at the same kind of site on both. The band vanishes the moment H₂ replaces CO₂ and formate appears. No adsorption site is named for the carbonate.

Fig. S56f and the accompanying SI text (ZnO reference, 20 vol% CO₂ in N₂, 320 °C, 20 bar): the only bidentate carbonate on ZnO. The other bands of the same spectrum are assigned differently, polydentate carbonate at 1511 and 1324 cm⁻¹ and linearly adsorbed CO₂ at 1370 cm⁻¹. The ZnO spectrum as a whole is weaker and unlike the ZnHfOₓ ones, the paper's point that Hf changes how CO₂ binds.
Fig. S56 (operando DRIFTS, 320 °C, 20 bar, the protocol of Fig. 6a): bidentate carbonate νₐₛ(OCO) at 1523 cm⁻¹ on 20ZnHfOₓ, against 1532 cm⁻¹ on 30ZnHfOₓ (claim 125), which carries the full account.

Fig. S56 (operando DRIFTS, 320 °C, 20 bar, the protocol of Fig. 6a): bidentate carbonate νₐₛ(OCO) at 1525 cm⁻¹ on 90ZnHfOₓ, against 1532 cm⁻¹ on 30ZnHfOₓ (claim 125), which carries the full account. 90ZnHfOₓ is mostly segregated ZnO with HfOₓ clusters, so a value this close to the solid solutions is the paper’s evidence for the same site on both.

bands.description: Bidentate carbonate symmetric stretch (b-CO₃²⁻*).

references.note: Fig. 3a and Section 3.2 (5%Ru-6.1% "Na₂O"/Al₂O₃ DFM, 320 °C, 15% CO₂/N₂): the symmetric partner of the 1600 cm⁻¹ bidentate carbonate band. The pair is absent on Ru/Al₂O₃, so the paper attributes it specifically to the alkali sites the sorbent phase adds.
Table 3: νₛ(-C-O) at 1310 cm⁻¹; paired with the asymmetric modes at 1670/1560/1500 cm⁻¹.

Fig. 4c (3 wt% Pt/CeO₂ reduced in 10% H₂ at 300 °C; 200 °C, 1 bar, H₂/CO₂ = 4 in He; internal background, the last spectrum of the ¹³CO₂ cycle, so ¹³C species point down): a negative band at 1251 cm⁻¹ beside the positive 1605, both ascribed to carbonate on ceria after López et al. and, through MCR, to bidentate carbonate. By the paper's own construction the 1251 band belongs to a ¹³C species, so it is not recorded as this ¹²C mode's position, and the paper gives none for it. This collection once paired 1251 with 1605 as νₛ and νₐₛ of one carbonate; the paper does not.

Table 3 and Fig. 3A, 1 bar. CZ, a coprecipitated Cu/ZnO with Cu:Zn 2.1:1, diluted to 8 wt% in KBr and activated in H₂ at 513 K; 3H₂/CO₂ at 20 NmL min⁻¹, 513 K, 4 cm⁻¹, 64 scans. νₛ(OCO) of bidentate carbonate at 1319 cm⁻¹, the partner of νₐₛ at 1543 cm⁻¹ and the narrow half of a 224 cm⁻¹ splitting. Literature values cited: 1332, 1323 and 1325 cm⁻¹.

Fig. 3b, the symmetric partner of the 1553 cm⁻¹ band on nanoparticulate Fe₂O₃ after evacuation; 1324 cm⁻¹ with gas-phase CO₂ present. The 237 cm⁻¹ splitting is what separates this bidentate population from the monodentate one at 1446 and 1383 cm⁻¹.

Figs. 6a, S56d and S56e (operando DRIFTS, 320 °C, 20 bar, 20 vol% CO₂ in N₂ for 1 h, background N₂ at 320 °C): the symmetric partner, 1358 cm⁻¹ on 30ZnHfOₓ, 1373 cm⁻¹ on 20ZnHfOₓ and 1380 cm⁻¹ on 90ZnHfOₓ. Its splitting from νₐₛ, 145 to 174 cm⁻¹, is small for bidentate carbonate and sits between the values usually quoted for the two geometries; the paper assigns it bidentate throughout, and the window is widened to 1380 cm⁻¹ to hold the 90ZnHfOₓ value.
Fig. S56 (operando DRIFTS, 320 °C, 20 bar, the protocol of Fig. 6a): bidentate carbonate νₛ(OCO) at 1373 cm⁻¹ on 20ZnHfOₓ, against 1358 cm⁻¹ on 30ZnHfOₓ (claim 132), which carries the full account.

Fig. S56 (operando DRIFTS, 320 °C, 20 bar, the protocol of Fig. 6a): bidentate carbonate νₛ(OCO) at 1380 cm⁻¹ on 90ZnHfOₓ, against 1358 cm⁻¹ on 30ZnHfOₓ (claim 132), which carries the full account. 90ZnHfOₓ is mostly segregated ZnO with HfOₓ clusters, so a value this close to the solid solutions is the paper’s evidence for the same site on both.

bands.description: Asymmetric OCO stretch of polydentate carbonate: a carbonate bound through more than two oxygens, or bridging several cations, typically built into the top layer of a basic oxide rather than sitting on it. It overlaps the monodentate νₐₛ band and the bottom of the bidentate one, and its splitting from the symmetric partner falls between theirs, so position and spacing alone rarely identify it. What does is stability: polydentate carbonate outlasts the other two on heating and under hydrogen. No binding-geometry field is set, because the carbonate vibration-modes page has only monodentate and bidentate forms so far.

references.note: Fig. S56f and the accompanying SI text (ZnO reference, 20 vol% CO₂ in N₂, 320 °C, 20 bar): polydentate carbonate, p-CO₃*, paired with 1324 cm⁻¹ for a splitting of 187 cm⁻¹. It sits 84 cm⁻¹ below the bidentate carbonate of the same spectrum and has no counterpart on any ZnHfOₓ catalyst.

bands.description: Symmetric OCO stretch of polydentate carbonate, the partner of νₐₛ(OCO) p-CO₃²⁻. It lands in the same window as the bidentate symmetric stretch and on top of formate's, so it is the less useful of the pair: the two carbonates are told apart by their asymmetric partners and by how long they survive heating, not here.

references.note: Fig. S56f and the accompanying SI text (ZnO reference, 20 vol% CO₂ in N₂, 320 °C, 20 bar): the symmetric partner of polydentate carbonate at 1511 cm⁻¹, seen only on the Hf-free oxide.

bands.description: Doubly degenerate asymmetric stretch of the free carbonate ion in solution. In the free D₃ₕ ion it is one band; binding to a surface lowers the symmetry and splits it into the two OCO stretches the adsorbed carbonate bands carry, so a single band here is the sign that the ion is not bound. At an electrode its intensity follows the local pH, rising as hydroxide from the reduction converts bicarbonate to carbonate.

references.note: Supplementary Note 4, Figs. S24 and S25, Table S4: SnO₂ nanoparticles cast on the Au/Si prism, CO₂-saturated 0.1 M CsHCO₃, static at −1.1 V or pulsed with E(c) = −1.1 V and E(a) = −0.35 or −0.2 V vs. RHE; the reference is the single-beam spectrum at 0.65 V before electrolysis, and the deconvolutions are the 10th cycle (t(c) = 188.3 s, t(a) = 198.3 s). The strong peak near 1397 cm⁻¹ is assigned to dissolved carbonate. It vanishes during the anodic pulses, which the authors read as the local carbonate falling with the interfacial pH. No surface is recorded.

bands.description: Bidentate carbonate ν₂ in-phase symmetric stretch of the two surface-bound C-O bonds (b-CO₃²⁻*): both surface-bonded oxygens expand and contract in unison while the free terminal oxygen counter-moves slightly. Lower-frequency member of the split degenerate pair (the out-of-phase counterpart is νₐₛ(OCO) at ~1500–1670 cm⁻¹). Rarely reported separately from the higher-frequency modes because it falls in a region also occupied by methoxy ν(CO) and formaldehyde bands.

references.note: Fig. 2 (nanoparticulate Fe₂O₃, 274 mTorr CO₂ at 296 K): the symmetric C-O stretch of the bidentate carbonate, with the monodentate counterpart 20 cm⁻¹ higher. Weak beside the OCO stretches, and this pair is the lowest position reported for the mode.

Fig. 6a (operando DRIFTS, 320 °C, 20 bar, 20 vol% CO₂ in N₂ for 1 h, background N₂ at 320 °C, 30ZnHfOₓ): the third bidentate carbonate band, gone as soon as H₂ is introduced like the other two. Only the 30ZnHfOₓ spectra reach this far; Fig. S56 stops at 1200 cm⁻¹.

bands.description: Symmetric C-O stretch of monodentate carbonate: infrared-inactive in the free ion and weakly allowed once coordination to the surface lowers its symmetry. Weak and rarely resolved, and it shares its window with methoxy ν(C-O) and with the bidentate counterpart a few tens of cm⁻¹ below.

references.note: Fig. 2 (hydroxylated nanoparticulate Fe₂O₃, 274 mTorr CO₂ at 296 K): reported together with the bidentate carbonate stretch 20 cm⁻¹ lower, as the pair of symmetric C-O stretches of the two carbonate geometries.

Table 3 and Fig. 3A, 1 bar. CZ, a coprecipitated Cu/ZnO with Cu:Zn 2.1:1, diluted to 8 wt% in KBr and activated in H₂ at 513 K; 3H₂/CO₂ at 20 NmL min⁻¹, 513 K, 4 cm⁻¹, 64 scans. Two weak bands at 1081 and 1052 cm⁻¹, tabulated as methoxy or carbonate and sketched as unidentate carbonate, against cited literature values of 1100 and 1080 cm⁻¹ for methoxy. The authors prefer carbonate on a kinetic argument rather than a spectroscopic one: the GC saw no methanol at all at 1 bar, so a methoxy population has nothing to come from. Reported only at 1 bar: at 30 bar everything below 1100 cm⁻¹ is buried under the combination bands and overtones of pressurised gaseous CO₂, which is why Fig. 3B is cut there.

bands.description: Out-of-plane deformation of the carbonate ion, the carbon moving through the plane of its three oxygens. The free ion has it at 879 cm⁻¹, and coordination to a surface moves it by only a few tens of wavenumbers, so unlike the OCO stretches it says almost nothing about the binding geometry. It is weak, and it sits at the edge of the window an oxide leaves open, since below roughly 800 cm⁻¹ the lattice absorbs everything. Where it is seen it confirms that carbonate is present at all; a bulk carbonate phase tends to put it near 835 cm⁻¹.

references.note: Table 3 and Fig. 3A, 1 bar. CZ, a coprecipitated Cu/ZnO with Cu:Zn 2.1:1, diluted to 8 wt% in KBr and activated in H₂ at 513 K; 3H₂/CO₂ at 20 NmL min⁻¹, 513 K, 4 cm⁻¹, 64 scans. π(CO₂) out of plane at 834 cm⁻¹, assigned to carbonate the authors take to sit in the bulk rather than on the surface, against a cited literature value of 837 cm⁻¹. Reported only at 1 bar: at 30 bar everything below 1100 cm⁻¹ is buried under the combination bands and overtones of pressurised gaseous CO₂, which is why Fig. 3B is cut there.

bands.description: Carbonate in-plane OCO bend / scissoring (CO₃²⁻*); O-C-O angle deformation within the molecular plane. Position is general/approximate — not yet tied to a specific reference.

Bicarbonate asymmetric OCO stretch, the strongest band of the species together with its symmetric partner. Its splitting from that partner, around 210 to 220 cm⁻¹, is the geometry diagnostic: adsorbed bicarbonate bridges two neighbouring metal sites through both of its non-protonated oxygens rather than binding through one, and the splitting comes out the same on oxides as different as iron and aluminium. Distinguishing it from carbonate rests on the COH bend near 1220 cm⁻¹ and on its disappearance under deuteration, since carbonate has no proton to lose.

references.note: Fig. 1a and Section 3.1 (5%Ru/Al₂O₃, 320 °C, 15% CO₂/N₂, Harrick cell with ZnSe windows, background the same material under N₂ at 320 °C): the O-C-O stretch of bicarbonate, paired with 1440 cm⁻¹.
