The same pair appears on bare γ-Al₂O₃ (Fig. 1b), which is the paper's argument that the alumina hydroxyls alone make bicarbonate from CO₂ without any Ru.
Table 3: δ(–OH) at 1650 cm⁻¹; formed by CO₂ interaction with surface OH groups; suppressed by La modification and Ni-Ce-Fe loading.

Table 2, ν₂(OCO)ₐ. Nanoparticulate amorphous Fe₂O₃, 229 m² g⁻¹, hydroxylated, 274 mTorr CO₂ at 296 K and RH below 1%. One of the three strongest bicarbonate bands, with the symmetric partner at 1410 and the COH bend at 1220 cm⁻¹. It sits 27 cm⁻¹ below the same mode on the aluminas, the largest difference between the oxides in this study. Substituting D and ¹⁸O and comparing all five isotopologues against five DFT cluster models is what identifies the structure as bridged rather than monodentate. Table 3 gives the ¹⁸O positions of this mode: 1599 cm⁻¹ for HC¹⁸O₃⁻ and 1613 and 1609 cm⁻¹ for the two mixed isotopologues.

Table 2, ν₂(OCO)ₐ of bicarbonate on hydroxylated α-Al₂O₃ (Alfa Aesar, 12.4 m² g⁻¹), 274 mTorr CO₂ at 296 K: 1650 cm⁻¹, against 1648 on γ-Al₂O₃ in the same table. The paper averages the two aluminas for its comparison with Fe₂O₃, finding they differ by a few wavenumbers at most.

CO₂ dosed on precipitated Ga₂O₃ at 300 °C (Fig. S12): of the three bands formed, this one is assigned to bicarbonate and the other two to carbonate. It is the least stable of them: Ar purging removes the bicarbonate while the carbonates stay, which is the paper's evidence that the carbonate, not the bicarbonate, is what the surface hydride goes on to reduce. Table S2 names the mode δ(OH) of CO₃H at 1634 cm⁻¹ rather than the OCO stretch this band records, the same label Rajput et al. use at 1650 cm⁻¹; the species is not in dispute, only which motion carries the band.

Figs. 6a, S56d and S56e (operando DRIFTS, 320 °C, 20 bar, 20 vol% CO₂ in N₂ for 1 h, background N₂ at 320 °C): bidentate bicarbonate, b-CO₃H*, at 1622 cm⁻¹ on 30ZnHfOₓ, 1603 cm⁻¹ on 20ZnHfOₓ and 1604 cm⁻¹ on 90ZnHfOₓ. The paper labels the species and not the mode; this band is where the position falls. It disappears instantly under H₂ together with the carbonate. The carbonate-to-bicarbonate intensity ratio is similar on 20 and 90ZnHfOₓ, the SI's evidence that CO₂ activation does not change when the bulk becomes ZnO. The window is widened to 1600 cm⁻¹ for the two lower values.

Table 2, ν₂(OCO)ₐ of bicarbonate on hydroxylated γ-Al₂O₃ (Degussa, 101 m² g⁻¹), 274 mTorr CO₂ at 296 K: 1648 cm⁻¹, against 1650 on α-Al₂O₃. With C¹⁸O₂ on the unlabelled ¹⁶OH surface (HC¹⁶O¹⁸O₂⁻, Table 3) it moves to 1634, recorded on the ¹⁸O band.
Fig. S56 (operando DRIFTS, 320 °C, 20 bar, the protocol of Fig. 6a): bidentate bicarbonate at 1603 cm⁻¹ on 20ZnHfOₓ, against 1622 cm⁻¹ on 30ZnHfOₓ (claim 145), which carries the full account.

Fig. S56 (operando DRIFTS, 320 °C, 20 bar, the protocol of Fig. 6a): bidentate bicarbonate at 1604 cm⁻¹ on 90ZnHfOₓ, against 1622 cm⁻¹ on 30ZnHfOₓ (claim 145), which carries the full account. 90ZnHfOₓ is mostly segregated ZnO with HfOₓ clusters, so a value this close to the solid solutions is the paper’s evidence for the same site on both.

bands.description: Bicarbonate symmetric OCO stretch (HCO₃⁻*). Shifts together with νₐₛ(OCO) above; the gap between the two (Δν) is itself diagnostic of binding geometry, with this bridged/bidentate structure giving a smaller split than a monodentate one would.

references.note: Fig. 1a and Section 3.1 (5%Ru/Al₂O₃, 320 °C, 15% CO₂/N₂): the lower O-C-O stretch of bicarbonate, the partner of 1650 cm⁻¹. On the DFM it is buried under the much larger bidentate carbonate bands at 1600 and 1370 cm⁻¹, so it can only be read on the Ru/Al₂O₃ and bare alumina spectra.
Table 3: νₛ(-C-O) at 1434 cm⁻¹; intense band confirming bicarbonate as the dominant CO₂ species on Al₂O₃.

Table 2, ν₃(OCO)ₛ on hydroxylated nanoparticulate Fe₂O₃, 274 mTorr CO₂ at 296 K. The strongest of the bicarbonate bands here. Its splitting from the asymmetric partner is 212 cm⁻¹, against 217 and 210 cm⁻¹ on the two aluminas: the same splitting on every surface tested is the paper's argument that the structure is the same on all of them. Table 3: ¹⁸O labelling moves it to 1388, 1401 and 1389 cm⁻¹ for the three labelled species, and deuteration does not move it at all.

Table 2, ν₃(OCO)ₛ of bicarbonate on hydroxylated α-Al₂O₃ (Alfa Aesar, 12.4 m² g⁻¹), 274 mTorr CO₂ at 296 K: 1433 cm⁻¹, against 1438 on γ-Al₂O₃ in the same table. The paper averages the two aluminas for its comparison with Fe₂O₃, finding they differ by a few wavenumbers at most.

Table 2, ν₃(OCO)ₛ of bicarbonate on hydroxylated γ-Al₂O₃ (Degussa, 101 m² g⁻¹), 274 mTorr CO₂ at 296 K: 1438 cm⁻¹, against 1433 on α-Al₂O₃. With C¹⁸O₂ on the unlabelled ¹⁶OH surface (HC¹⁶O¹⁸O₂⁻, Table 3) it moves to 1416, recorded on the ¹⁸O band.

bands.description: Bicarbonate COH bending (HCO₃⁻*); distinguishing feature vs. carbonate, which has no O-H and therefore no analogous band at all.

references.note: Table 3: δ(O-C-O) at 1200–1220 cm⁻¹.

Table 2, δ₄(COH) on hydroxylated nanoparticulate Fe₂O₃, 274 mTorr CO₂ at 296 K; the reported literature range is 1220 to 1269 cm⁻¹. Exchanging the surface hydroxyls with D₂O moves it to 969 cm⁻¹, by far the largest shift of any bicarbonate mode, which is what confirms the attribution. A residual band at 1220 cm⁻¹ survives that exchange, from CO₂ reacting with the ¹⁶OH groups left on the surface. ¹⁸O labelling moves it far less, to 1205, 1216 and 1209 cm⁻¹.

Table 2, δ₄(COH) of bicarbonate on hydroxylated α-Al₂O₃ (Alfa Aesar, 12.4 m² g⁻¹), 274 mTorr CO₂ at 296 K: 1230 cm⁻¹, against 1231 on γ-Al₂O₃ in the same table. The paper averages the two aluminas for its comparison with Fe₂O₃, finding they differ by a few wavenumbers at most.

Table 2, δ₄(COH) of bicarbonate on hydroxylated γ-Al₂O₃ (Degussa, 101 m² g⁻¹), 274 mTorr CO₂ at 296 K: 1231 cm⁻¹, against 1230 on α-Al₂O₃. With C¹⁸O₂ on the unlabelled ¹⁶OH surface (HC¹⁶O¹⁸O₂⁻, Table 3) it moves to 1215, recorded on the ¹⁸O band.

bands.description: The O-H stretch of adsorbed bicarbonate, and the one band that shows the species still carries its proton. It sits well below the free surface hydroxyls it forms from, and far above the roughly 2550 cm⁻¹ of the hydrogen-bonded dimer in the bulk salt, so its position also says the adsorbed species is not dimerised. Weak beside the OCO stretches, and it falls inside the hydroxyl envelope of the support, so it is read against the clean surface rather than in an absolute spectrum.

references.note: Fig. 1a and Section 3.1 (5%Ru/Al₂O₃, 320 °C, 15% CO₂/N₂): the O-H stretch of bicarbonate, with a second component at 3740 cm⁻¹. The paper is explicit that this region is contested: it reads 3740 and 3640 cm⁻¹ as bicarbonate O-H and 3700 and 3600 cm⁻¹ as CO₂ overtones, where other authors assign the whole set one way or the other. Both components fall as the bicarbonate is consumed under H₂.

Table 2, ν₁(OH) on hydroxylated nanoparticulate Fe₂O₃, 274 mTorr CO₂ at 296 K. Exchanging the surface hydroxyls with D₂O moves it to 2671 cm⁻¹, a shift of 948 cm⁻¹, and ¹⁸O labelling moves it by 10 cm⁻¹. Table 3: 3609, 3610 and 3609 cm⁻¹ for the three ¹⁸O-labelled species, which is why they are recorded as shifts here rather than as bands of their own.

Table 2, ν₁(OH) of bicarbonate on hydroxylated γ-Al₂O₃ (Degussa, 101 m² g⁻¹), 274 mTorr CO₂ at 296 K: 3623 cm⁻¹. Not observed on the low-area α-Al₂O₃ (12.4 against 101 m² g⁻¹). With C¹⁸O₂ on the ¹⁶OH surface (HC¹⁶O¹⁸O₂⁻, Table 3) it moves to 3614.

bands.description: The single-bond C-OH stretch of adsorbed bicarbonate, the mode carbonate cannot have at all, since it has no such bond. Weak, and it lands where carbonate symmetric stretches and methoxy ν(C-O) also absorb, so it is reported only where the lattice of the oxide leaves the region open.

references.note: Table 2, ν₅(C-OH) on hydroxylated nanoparticulate Fe₂O₃, 274 mTorr CO₂ at 296 K. Not observed on either alumina, and outside the 1100 to 2100 cm⁻¹ window of the isotope experiments, so no labelled position is reported for it either.

bands.description: Out-of-plane deformation of the bicarbonate CO₂ fragment, the carbon moving through the plane of its two oxygens. It sits at the edge of the window an oxide leaves open: below roughly 800 cm⁻¹ the lattice absorbs everything, which is why this mode and the three bicarbonate modes below it are so rarely observed.

references.note: Table 2, δ₈(CO₂)oop on hydroxylated nanoparticulate Fe₂O₃, 274 mTorr CO₂ at 296 K. Not observed on either alumina. The remaining three bicarbonate modes, δ₆(OCO), ν₉(H torsion) and ν₇(OC-OH), all fall below 800 cm⁻¹ and are buried under the iron oxide lattice absorption. No labelled position is reported for this mode: the isotope spectra of Fig. 5 cover 1100 to 2100 cm⁻¹ and Table 3 lists only the two OCO stretches, the COH bend and the O-H stretch.

bands.description: The bicarbonate O-H stretch after the surface hydroxyls have been exchanged with D₂O. It moves by nearly 950 cm⁻¹, out of the hydroxyl region altogether and into the quiet window between the C-H stretches and the carbonyls, which makes it the cleanest evidence that the adsorbed species carries a proton at all.

references.note: Table 3 (nanoparticulate Fe₂O₃ with its surface hydroxyls exchanged by D₂O at 295 K, then dosed with 274 mTorr C¹⁶O₂ at 296 K): ν₁(OD) of DC¹⁶O₃⁻, shifted 948 cm⁻¹ from the 3619 cm⁻¹ of the protonated species.

bands.description: The bicarbonate COH bend after exchange with D₂O. It drops by about 250 cm⁻¹, far more than the OCO stretches move, because it is the mode that actually swings the hydrogen. That large and predictable shift is the standard confirmation that a band near 1220 cm⁻¹ is bicarbonate rather than a carbonate, which has no such mode to lose.

references.note: Table 3 (D₂O-exchanged nanoparticulate Fe₂O₃, 274 mTorr C¹⁶O₂ at 296 K): δ₄(COD) of DC¹⁶O₃⁻, 251 cm⁻¹ below the protonated bend. The OCO stretches of the same species barely move by comparison, 16 cm⁻¹ for the asymmetric one and not at all for the symmetric one, so they are recorded as shifts on the ordinary bands rather than as bands of their own.

bands.description: Bicarbonate O-H stretch with ¹⁸O on the oxide. It moves by only about 10 cm⁻¹, since the hydrogen carries almost all of the motion and the oxygen mass barely enters it, and it moves by that much whether or not the labelled oxygen is the protonated one. That is the first sign that the oxygen the proton ends up on is not the one it started on.

references.note: Table 3, ν₁(OH) of bicarbonate on hydroxylated nanoparticulate Fe₂O₃ at 296 K under 274 mTorr CO₂, in the order HC¹⁸O₃⁻, HC¹⁸O¹⁶O₂⁻, HC¹⁶O¹⁸O₂⁻: all three oxygens heavy (3609 cm⁻¹, C¹⁸O₂ on ¹⁸OH, Fig. 5e), only the hydroxyl oxygen heavy (3610, C¹⁶O₂ on ¹⁸OH, Fig. 5c), and only the two from CO₂ heavy (3609, C¹⁸O₂ on ¹⁶OH, Fig. 5d). The unlabelled band sits at 3619 cm⁻¹.

Table 3, ν₁(OH) on γ-Al₂O₃ (Degussa, 101 m² g⁻¹) at 296 K under 274 mTorr C¹⁸O₂ on the unlabelled ¹⁶OH surface, so HC¹⁶O¹⁸O₂⁻ with the two oxygens from CO₂ heavy and the hydroxyl oxygen light: 3614 cm⁻¹ against 3623 unlabelled. The other labellings were run on Fe₂O₃ only.

bands.description: Bicarbonate asymmetric OCO stretch with ¹⁸O on the oxide. Labelling all three oxygens moves it about 23 cm⁻¹, the two that came from CO₂ about 13, and the hydroxyl oxygen alone about 9. The shift is smaller than the distance the unlabelled band moves between one oxide and another, so a labelling experiment is only readable against an unlabelled spectrum of the same sample.

references.note: Table 3, ν₂(OCO)ₐ of bicarbonate on hydroxylated nanoparticulate Fe₂O₃ at 296 K under 274 mTorr CO₂, in the order HC¹⁸O₃⁻, HC¹⁸O¹⁶O₂⁻, HC¹⁶O¹⁸O₂⁻: all three oxygens heavy (1599 cm⁻¹, C¹⁸O₂ on ¹⁸OH, Fig. 5e), only the hydroxyl oxygen heavy (1613, C¹⁶O₂ on ¹⁸OH, Fig. 5c), and only the two from CO₂ heavy (1609, C¹⁸O₂ on ¹⁶OH, Fig. 5d). The unlabelled band sits at 1622 cm⁻¹.

Table 3, ν₂(OCO)ₐ on γ-Al₂O₃ (Degussa, 101 m² g⁻¹) at 296 K under 274 mTorr C¹⁸O₂ on the unlabelled ¹⁶OH surface, so HC¹⁶O¹⁸O₂⁻ with the two oxygens from CO₂ heavy and the hydroxyl oxygen light: 1634 cm⁻¹ against 1648 unlabelled. The other labellings were run on Fe₂O₃ only.

bands.description: Bicarbonate symmetric OCO stretch with ¹⁸O on the oxide. Labelling the two oxygens that came from CO₂ moves it about 21 cm⁻¹, nearly as far as labelling all three (22); labelling only the surface hydroxyl moves it 9. Fitting such mixed-label shifts to cluster calculations is how the proton’s final position is argued: on an oxygen from CO₂ rather than the one it arrived on, a tentative reading that contradicts simple insertion of CO₂ into the M-OH bond.

references.note: Table 3, ν₃(OCO)ₛ of bicarbonate on hydroxylated nanoparticulate Fe₂O₃ at 296 K under 274 mTorr CO₂, in the order HC¹⁸O₃⁻, HC¹⁸O¹⁶O₂⁻, HC¹⁶O¹⁸O₂⁻: all three oxygens heavy (1388 cm⁻¹, C¹⁸O₂ on ¹⁸OH, Fig. 5e), only the hydroxyl oxygen heavy (1401, C¹⁶O₂ on ¹⁸OH, Fig. 5c), and only the two from CO₂ heavy (1389, C¹⁸O₂ on ¹⁶OH, Fig. 5d). The unlabelled band sits at 1410 cm⁻¹.

Table 3, ν₃(OCO)ₛ on γ-Al₂O₃ (Degussa, 101 m² g⁻¹) at 296 K under 274 mTorr C¹⁸O₂ on the unlabelled ¹⁶OH surface, so HC¹⁶O¹⁸O₂⁻ with the two oxygens from CO₂ heavy and the hydroxyl oxygen light: 1416 cm⁻¹ against 1438 unlabelled. The other labellings were run on Fe₂O₃ only.

bands.description: Bicarbonate COH bend with ¹⁸O on the oxide, moving between 4 and 15 cm⁻¹ depending on which oxygens are labelled. Deuteration moves the same mode by 250 cm⁻¹: the contrast is what shows the bend is carried by the hydrogen and only steered by the oxygens it swings between.

references.note: Table 3, δ₄(COH) of bicarbonate on hydroxylated nanoparticulate Fe₂O₃ at 296 K under 274 mTorr CO₂, in the order HC¹⁸O₃⁻, HC¹⁸O¹⁶O₂⁻, HC¹⁶O¹⁸O₂⁻: all three oxygens heavy (1205 cm⁻¹, C¹⁸O₂ on ¹⁸OH, Fig. 5e), only the hydroxyl oxygen heavy (1216, C¹⁶O₂ on ¹⁸OH, Fig. 5c), and only the two from CO₂ heavy (1209, C¹⁸O₂ on ¹⁶OH, Fig. 5d). The unlabelled band sits at 1220 cm⁻¹.

Table 3, δ₄(COH) on γ-Al₂O₃ (Degussa, 101 m² g⁻¹) at 296 K under 274 mTorr C¹⁸O₂ on the unlabelled ¹⁶OH surface, so HC¹⁶O¹⁸O₂⁻ with the two oxygens from CO₂ heavy and the hydroxyl oxygen light: 1215 cm⁻¹ against 1231 unlabelled. The other labellings were run on Fe₂O₃ only.

bands.description: Formate C-H stretch, the key HCOO* marker and strongly site-sensitive across its window: κ²-HCOO* on metallic Cu sits near 2848 to 2860 cm⁻¹ and the same mode on a cation or oxide site 20 to 40 cm⁻¹ higher, far enough to resolve two formate populations in one spectrum. Two traps at the low end: methoxy νₛ(CH₃) on silica and adsorbed methanol νₛ(CH₃) both land there, so a band near 2850 cm⁻¹ is safely formate only once its combination band near 2930 cm⁻¹ or a deuteration check backs it up.

references.note: Fig. 2 left (in situ DRIFTS, 1 wt % metal on silica, CO₂:H₂ = 1:1 at 230 °C, 1 and 40 bar). One of the three ν(C-H) region bands of κ²-formate, rising and falling together with the 1600 cm⁻¹ band under a CO₂/H₂ against Ar switch. It sits a little below the window this atlas had, which was widened to take it.

Fig. 5b, 5d and Table S5 (operando DRIFTS, 220 °C, 6 bar, 25 mL min⁻¹, switching H₂/CO₂ 3/1 → He/CO₂ 3/1), unpromoted Cu/SiO₂: ν(CH) of bidentate formate at 2890 cm⁻¹. Cutting the hydrogen stops the reaction at HCOO*, and this band grows while methoxy disappears; restoring H₂ removes it completely. Not detected at steady state, which the paper puts down to low coverage. Recorded on Cu⁰ because the paper finds the same position on CuGa(0.20) and concludes that formate sits on Cu⁰, not at the interface.

Fig. S15a and Table S5 (operando DRIFTS, 4% HCOOH/Ar at 20 mL min⁻¹, 220 °C, atmospheric pressure, then swept with Ar for 30 min): the reference experiment behind the attribution above. Formic acid dosed on Cu/SiO₂ makes bidentate formate directly, and its ν(CH) lands 6 cm⁻¹ below the band seen under CO₂ with the hydrogen cut off, close enough that the paper treats the two as the same species.

Fig. 1b (ME-DRIFTS-PSD, Cu-GaZrOₓ, 20 bar, 260 °C, CO₂ modulated at constant H₂): ν(CH) of HCOO* at 2876 cm⁻¹, responding at the modulation frequency, which is what marks it an intermediate rather than a spectator. The paper does not say where on the catalyst the formate sits. The same position on the Cu-free GaZrOₓ is a claim of its own.

Fig. 4b inset (ME-DRIFTS-PSD, Cu-free GaZrOₓ, 1 bar, CO₂ modulated at constant H₂): the formate ν(CH) at the same 2876 cm⁻¹ as on Cu-GaZrOₓ, but as a weak peak out of phase with the modulation. The authors read it as slow reduction of surface (bi)carbonates by Ga-H rather than the fast Cu-catalysed route.

Fig. S4a, reference spectrum rather than a working catalyst: formate generated on precipitated ZrO₂ by flowing CO over the surface hydroxyls (*OH + CO → HCOO*) at 260 °C and 20 bar. ν(CH) centred near 2859 cm⁻¹, and clearer once H₂ was added to the feed. This is the measurement the paper uses to attribute the catalyst's formate bands to the oxide rather than to Cu.

Fig. S4b, the same CO-dosing reference experiment on precipitated Ga₂O₃ at 260 °C and 20 bar. ν(CH) is a minor peak centred near 2887 cm⁻¹, weaker than on ZrO₂, where the asymmetric OCO region carried most of the formate intensity instead.

Fig. 4b (3 wt% Pt/CeO₂ reduced in 10% H₂ at 300 °C; 200 °C, 1 bar, H₂/CO₂ = 4 in He; external background under He): ν(CH) of formate at 2846 cm⁻¹, the lower member of the doublet the paper calls a Fermi resonance, with 2945 cm⁻¹ above it. Under ¹³CO₂ the pair moves to 2830 and 2910 cm⁻¹, which no ¹³C formate band here records yet. Formate exchanges more slowly than CO(g) at every position (Fig. 5), so the paper rules the formate route out as the main one at 200 °C, while noting it speeds up markedly at 250 °C (Fig. S7, not read here). Corrected: this row once carried 2910 cm⁻¹, the ¹³C position of the upper member, as the ¹²C ν(CH).

Figs. 4a and 4c (steady state, 10 bar), 5b (H₂/D₂ switching, 10 bar) and 7a (He+CO₂ against H₂+He, 20 bar): operando DRIFTS of CuZn/SiO₂, 230 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 10 NmL min⁻¹, after H₂ at 300 °C. Bidentate formate on Cu at 2856 cm⁻¹ in the steady-state spectra, the first and most abundant surface species, appearing together with the Zn²⁺-bound formate; 2850 in the MCR-resolved component spectra of both transients. It exchanges to κ²-DCOO* at 2167 cm⁻¹ within the 10 s time resolution, so formate formation is not rate-limiting, and in the transient it falls as CO* at 2113 cm⁻¹ rises, which the authors read as formate decomposing to CO on Cu. The 2850 is an MCR component maximum, not a raw peak.

H₂-TPSR after CO₂ adsorption on precipitated Ga₂O₃ (Fig. S13 inset and Table S2; the same band appears in Fig. 5a under CO₂/H₂ = 1:3, and at 2898 cm⁻¹ in Fig. 4c, where CO₂ is dosed onto a pre-formed Ga-H surface at 200 °C). Weak beside the 1581 cm⁻¹ OCO band of the same formate: on this oxide the C-H stretch is a minor feature, which is why it is easy to miss on Ga-containing catalysts. Fig. 4c is the cleanest of the three, since there the formate can only have come from the hydride.

Fig. 7a, 7c, 7e (IRRAS, UHV, formic acid dosed at room temperature): ν(CH) of the flatter bidentate formate on interstitial sites (bb,int), at 2848 and 2917 cm⁻¹ and seen only in s-polarized light, so its C-H dipole lies more nearly in the surface plane. The paper notes how rarely the C-H stretch of formate is reported at all by this technique, its dipole change being much smaller than that of the OCO stretches.

Fig. 7b, 7d, 7f (IRRAS, UHV, room temperature): only three C-H bands here and the 2868 cm⁻¹ one is missing. Its absence is the argument: 2868 cm⁻¹ marked the upright bidentate-bridging species, which this facet cannot host, so the C-H region independently confirms what the OCO stretches say about geometry.

Figs. 6a, S56g and S56h (operando DRIFTS, 320 °C, 20 bar; H₂ step for 30ZnHfOₓ, H₂:CO₂:N₂ = 3:1:1 for the others): formate ν(CH) at 2887 cm⁻¹ on 30ZnHfOₓ, 2892 cm⁻¹ on 20ZnHfOₓ and 2894 cm⁻¹ on 90ZnHfOₓ, labelled νₛ(C–H) in the paper. The near-identity of 20 and 90ZnHfOₓ, against 2873 cm⁻¹ on ZnO, is its argument that both kinds of catalyst hold formate at the same Zn–Vₒ–Hf motif.

Figs. 8e and S56i (operando DRIFTS, ZnO reference, 320 °C, 20 bar, H₂:CO₂:N₂ = 3:1:1): formate on the Hf-free oxide at about 2873 cm⁻¹, some 20 cm⁻¹ below the ZnHfOₓ catalysts and in line with earlier formic-acid dosing on ZnO that the paper cites. Weak: ZnO activates CO₂ poorly, and only very weak methoxy bands form alongside.

Fig. 8e and Section 2.9 (operando DRIFTS, bare monoclinic HfO₂ reference, 90 min at 320 °C, 20 bar, H₂:CO₂:N₂ = 3:1:1): formate forms on the Zn-free oxide, weaker than on 30ZnHfOₓ, although no methanol leaves the cell. The paper prints no position, only that the 30ZnHfOₓ band sits 4 to 5 cm⁻¹ lower, between HfO₂ and ZnO; that in-between position is its case for an intermediate bound at a site involving both Zn and Hf. No value is recorded: the figure is not labelled with one.

Fig. 1A and Table 1 (operando DRIFTS, 6 wt% Cu/ZrO₂, 220 °C, 3 bar, 20 % CO₂ + 60 % H₂ in He, steady state, background the reduced sample under H₂): ν(CH) of formate on the zirconia at 2873 cm⁻¹, with νₐₛ(OCO) at 1575 and a third band at 1380. Sodium-formate standards dry-impregnated on Cu-free zirconia give the same position and band shape (Fig. 1B), which is what makes the quantification possible; of the paper's two calibration bands this is the more accurate, because the C–H bond is not the part touching the surface (Fig. 1C). Two kinetically distinct zirconia formates share it, a fast one near the copper interface and a slow one away from it, and their spectra differ only in a slight shift of the maxima.

Fig. 3b and Table 1: ν(CH) of a copper-bound formate at 2840 cm⁻¹, visible only in the difference spectrum taken 9 s after CO₂ was cut from the feed and magnified 20 times, with the carboxylate stretch at 1644 and a third band at 1307. The methoxy and zirconia-formate contributions were subtracted first (Figs. S3A and S3C). The trio is assigned from formic acid adsorbed on Cu(100) rather than argued from this spectrum. It is only about 7 % of the surface formate, but it decays with k = 2.3 min⁻¹, one and three orders of magnitude faster than the two zirconia formates, at a rate matching methanol formation: the paper's case that this is the intermediate that matters.

Figs. S15 (H₂/D₂ switching, 10 bar) and S18 (He+CO₂ against H₂+He, 20 bar): MCR-resolved component spectra of the unpromoted Cu/SiO₂ made by surface organometallic chemistry (4.19 wt% Cu), 230 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 10 NmL min⁻¹, after H₂ at 300 °C. Bidentate formate on Cu at 2860 and 2852 cm⁻¹, with its combination band at 2929 and 2931. It exchanges to κ²-DCOO* at 2161 cm⁻¹ under D₂, and in the transient its decay tracks the rise of CO* at 2115 cm⁻¹. The reference catalyst: no promoter-bound formate is resolved on it.

Figs. S16 (H₂/D₂ switching, 10 bar) and S20 (He+CO₂ against H₂+He, 20 bar): MCR-resolved spectra of CuGa/SiO₂ made by surface organometallic chemistry, 230 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 10 NmL min⁻¹, after H₂ at 300 °C. Bidentate formate on Cu at 2850 and 2848 cm⁻¹, exchanging to κ²-DCOO* at 2176 cm⁻¹ under D₂. In the transient it is one of four species MCR cannot separate (with Ga³⁺ formate, Ga³⁺ methoxy and adsorbed methanol), all consumed quickly under H₂, which the authors read as fast spillover from Cu to Ga³⁺; no CO* forms on this catalyst. The 2848 comes from that mixed component.

Figs. S17 (H₂/D₂ switching, 10 bar) and S19 (He+CO₂ against H₂+He, 20 bar): MCR-resolved spectra of CuIn/SiO₂ made by surface organometallic chemistry, 230 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 10 NmL min⁻¹, after H₂ at 300 °C. Bidentate formate on Cu at 2858 and 2854 cm⁻¹; it exchanges to κ²-DCOO* at 2169 cm⁻¹ under D₂, and in the transient its decay tracks CO* at 2108 cm⁻¹.

Figs. 4a, 4c, 5b (10 bar) and 7a (He+CO₂ against H₂+He, 20 bar): operando DRIFTS of CuZn/SiO₂, 230 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 10 NmL min⁻¹, after H₂ at 300 °C. Bidentate formate on the isolated Zn²⁺ sites at 2896 cm⁻¹, the one promoter-bound formate the steady-state spectra show clearly, appearing at the same time as the Cu-bound one; 2886 in the MCR component of Fig. 7a, where the same component carries ν(C-O) at 1590. It exchanges to κ²-DCOO* at 2184 cm⁻¹ as fast as the Cu-bound formate. The authors place it there by spillover from Cu: Zn/SiO₂ without Cu converts CO₂ below the detection limit. The Zn is single cations, not a ZnO phase.

Figs. S16 (H₂/D₂ switching, 10 bar) and S20 (He+CO₂ against H₂+He, 20 bar): MCR-resolved spectra of CuGa/SiO₂, 230 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 10 NmL min⁻¹, after H₂ at 300 °C. Bidentate formate on the isolated Ga³⁺ sites, marked at 2883 and 2881 cm⁻¹. The steady-state spectra alone cannot confirm it (main text, Section 2.3); it rests on the transients, and in S20 it sits in one component with Cu-bound formate, Ga³⁺ methoxy and adsorbed methanol, so the position is a marked band inside a mixed component, not a separate species spectrum.

Fig. S19 (He+CO₂ against H₂+He, 20 bar): MCR-resolved spectra of CuIn/SiO₂, 230 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 10 NmL min⁻¹, after H₂ at 300 °C. Bidentate formate on the isolated In³⁺ sites, marked at 2877 cm⁻¹ in a component MCR cannot separate from In³⁺ methoxy. Unlike on Ga³⁺ it is not consumed under H₂ but grows to a plateau, which the authors read as formate held too strongly on In³⁺ to hydrogenate, the reason for the low methanol rate. The steady-state spectra alone cannot confirm it.
Fig. S56 (operando DRIFTS, 320 °C, 20 bar, the protocol of Fig. 6a): formate ν(CH) at 2892 cm⁻¹ on 20ZnHfOₓ, against 2887 cm⁻¹ on 30ZnHfOₓ (claim 179), which carries the full account.

Fig. S56 (operando DRIFTS, 320 °C, 20 bar, the protocol of Fig. 6a): formate ν(CH) at 2894 cm⁻¹ on 90ZnHfOₓ, against 2887 cm⁻¹ on 30ZnHfOₓ (claim 179), which carries the full account. 90ZnHfOₓ is mostly segregated ZnO with HfOₓ clusters, so a value this close to the solid solutions is the paper’s evidence for the same site on both.

Fig. 7a, 7c, 7e (IRRAS, UHV, formic acid dosed at room temperature): ν(CH) of the upright bidentate formate on octahedral Fe with tetrahedral Fe underneath (bb,tet), at 2868 cm⁻¹ and visible only in p-polarized light. It agrees with the p-only νₐₛ(OCO) at 1555 cm⁻¹ of the same species; together they are the paper’s evidence for a vertically oriented formate.

Fig. 5c, 5e and Table S5 (operando DRIFTS, 220 °C, 6 bar, 25 mL min⁻¹, switching H₂/CO₂ 3/1 → He/CO₂ 3/1), CuGa(0.20): ν(CH) of bidentate formate at 2890 cm⁻¹, the frequency the paper calls similar to the one on unpromoted Cu/SiO₂, its argument that this formate forms on Cu⁰ and not at the Cu-Ga₂O₃ interface. It grows when the hydrogen is cut and vanishes when it returns.

bands.description: Formate asymmetric OCO stretch, the marker band of HCOO* and usually the stronger of the two OCO stretches. Its position is not fixed: it moves with the adsorption geometry, so read it together with the symmetric partner and the Δν between them rather than on its own. The in-phase and antiphase C-O pair is what separates formate from carbonate and carboxylate features.

references.note: Fig. 2 right (in situ Raman, 1 wt % Cu/SiO₂ at 230 °C, 200 and 400 bar; Renishaw InVia, 532 nm Nd:YAG, 60 mW, 600 s accumulation through a micro-view-cell, SI p. S34). The second of the two Raman formate bands, with 1330 cm⁻¹. A separate row from this paper's own DRIFTS claim on this band, because it is a different measurement by a different technique, and the two positions differ by 20 cm⁻¹. The reactant mixture at 200 to 400 bar and 230 °C is above the critical point of both gases, a dense fluid (the paper speaks of fluid density), recorded as supercritical.

Fig. 2 left (in situ DRIFTS, 1 wt % metal on silica, CO₂:H₂ = 1:1 at 230 °C, 1 and 40 bar). The κ²-formate band the paper follows throughout. In the transient experiment over Ag/SiO₂ it appears and disappears in step with 2711, 2817 and 2952 cm⁻¹, which is what confirms all four belong to one species. The same set is seen on Cu and Au; formate is more pronounced on Ag, matching its lower calculated barrier of 0.61 eV against 0.71 for Cu and 0.97 for Au.

Fig. 7A, Pt(3)/MoOₓ(30)/TiO₂: in situ IR at 150 °C and ambient pressure under CO₂ (10), H₂ (30) and He (50) cm³ min⁻¹, on a self-supporting pellet in a quartz cell with CaF₂ windows, referenced to the sample under 30% H₂/He at the same temperature. The antisymmetric partner of the 1370 cm⁻¹ band, both assigned to formate, in a 1300 to 1600 cm⁻¹ region the paper describes as carrying carbonate and formate together.

Grown under UV irradiation of methoxy on TiO₂ in 10 Torr O₂, not dosed: the antisymmetric partner of the 1362 cm⁻¹ band, appearing as CH₃O* is consumed. Read there as bridging HCOO*. In the paper's ethoxy experiment the same position is overlapped by acetate, which is why it is identified by the pair rather than alone.

Table 2 and Fig. 1a (5%Ru/Al₂O₃, methanation step, 320 °C, 20% H₂/N₂ after 1 h of 15% CO₂/N₂): νₐₛ(OCO) of formate at 1520 cm⁻¹, appearing at the onset of the H₂ step. Formed by spillover of bicarbonates from the Al₂O₃ hydroxyls to Ru; a reaction intermediate en route to CH₄.

Fig. 1b (ME-DRIFTS-PSD, Cu-GaZrOₓ, 20 bar, 260 °C): νₐₛ(OCO) of HCOO* at 1600 cm⁻¹, responding at the modulation frequency of the CO₂ feed. Methanol steam reforming over the same sample at 1 bar puts the band at 1590 cm⁻¹ and shows it only while CO₂(g) is formed (Fig. 2b), which is the reverse-direction evidence for the same intermediate. On the Cu-free GaZrOₓ the peaks between 1250 and 1700 cm⁻¹ are assigned to carbonates and bicarbonates instead, so this position is not by itself proof of formate.

Fig. S4a, formate generated on precipitated ZrO₂ from CO and surface hydroxyls at 260 °C and 20 bar. The paper quotes the asymmetric OCO vibrations as lying between 1582 and 1641 cm⁻¹; only the 1582 cm⁻¹ component is recorded here, because the upper end of that range overlaps the carbonate and bicarbonate bands the same dosing experiment produces (Fig. S3) and the paper does not separate them.
Table 3: νas(OCO⁻) at 1585 cm⁻¹; dominant CH₄ adsorption product on Al₂O₃ via H-abstraction; nearly absent on La-modified and Ni-Ce-Fe/La-Al₂O₃ under DRM.

Table 3 and Fig. 3. CZ, a coprecipitated Cu/ZnO with Cu:Zn 2.1:1, diluted to 8 wt% in KBr and activated in H₂ at 513 K; 3H₂/CO₂ at 20 NmL min⁻¹, 513 K, 4 cm⁻¹, 64 scans. νₐₛ(OCO) at 1587 cm⁻¹ at 1 bar and 1603 cm⁻¹ at 30 bar, assigned to bidentate and to unidentate formate respectively. The splittings against νₛ agree with that split rather than contradict it: 227 cm⁻¹ for the 1 bar pair and 289 cm⁻¹ for the 30 bar pair, and a carboxylate bound through one oxygen splits wider than one chelating through both. The 30 bar formate is this paper’s spectator: strong, but its intensity does not follow the GHSV, it is still there on the catalytically inactive CZ-2000, and hours of H₂ flushing are needed to remove it.

Fig. 7a (He+CO₂ against H₂+He, 20 bar): MCR-resolved spectra of CuZn/SiO₂, 230 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 10 NmL min⁻¹, after H₂ at 300 °C. νₐₛ(OCO) at 1590 cm⁻¹ in the component of the Zn²⁺-bound formate (its ν(CH) at 2886 in the same component), so the C-H and C-O regions are read off one species rather than assigned separately. Fig. 6a plots the ν(C-O) of the deuterated formate per catalyst as a Sabatier volcano against the methanol rate, without number labels.

H₂-TPSR after CO₂ adsorption on precipitated Ga₂O₃ (Fig. S13, and Fig. 5b under CO₂/H₂ = 1:3 from 30 to 450 °C): introducing H₂ converts the carbonates into formate, which appears as a single dominant band at 1581 cm⁻¹ and grows from about 200 °C, the same temperature at which the Ga-H hydride becomes mobile. On this Cu-free oxide the formate is made by the hydride rather than by a metal. Fig. S12 shows the same conversion isothermally at 300 °C, where H₂ purging turns the carbonate bands into this one.

Table 1 and Fig. 6 (IRRAS, UHV, formic acid dosed at room temperature): νₐₛ(OCO) of bidentate-bridging formate on interstitial sites (νₐₛbb,int), 1548 cm⁻¹ in p- and 1538 cm⁻¹ in s-polarized light. Positive in absorbance, the opposite sign to the symmetric stretch, which places the dipole parallel to the surface.

Table 1 and Fig. 6 (IRRAS, UHV, formic acid dosed at room temperature): νₐₛ(OCO) of quasi-bidentate formate (νₐₛqbt) at 1588 cm⁻¹. With its symmetric partner at 1335 cm⁻¹ the splitting is 253 cm⁻¹, against 168 for the chelating species: the chelating geometry has the smaller O-C-O angle.

Figs. 6a to 6c (operando DRIFTS, 30ZnHfOₓ, 320 °C, 20 bar, switching 20 vol% CO₂ → 80 vol% H₂ → H₂:CO₂:N₂ = 3:1:1, all in N₂): the dominant formate band, which the paper calls ν(C=O). It appears the instant H₂ replaces CO₂ and fades as methoxy grows; re-admitting CO₂ restores it at once while methoxy falls, the formate-methoxy pathway read straight off the spectra. The site is the paper's postulate: the formate and methoxy bands on 30ZnHfOₓ sit 4 to 5 cm⁻¹ below those on HfO₂ and between the two single oxides (Fig. 8e), which it reads as stabilisation at a Zn–Vₒ–Hf motif. Fig. S49 repeats the sequence on 20ZnHfOₓ with the same result; its caption repeats Fig. 6's tracking positions word for word, so it is not recorded as a separate 20ZnHfOₓ position.

Fig. 1A and Table 1 (conditions as on the C–H stretch): νₐₛ(OCO) of formate on the zirconia at 1575 cm⁻¹, the paper's second calibration band against sodium-formate standards on Cu-free zirconia (Fig. 1D). The 1577 cm⁻¹ value is from Fig. 3b, where zirconia formate appears as a positive band 9 s after CO₂ was cut while the copper formate decays, which the paper reads as formate re-forming on the sites the lost carbonates had held. Calibrating the copper-bound formate on this band gives 0.133 wt% against 0.0945 wt% from the C–H stretch; the paper prefers the C–H value, since the carboxylate group is the part interacting with the surface.

Table 1, given as 1639 cm⁻¹ in the text (Fig. 3b, difference spectrum 9 s after CO₂ removal, magnified 20 times, zirconia-formate contribution subtracted, Figs. S3B and S3D): the carboxylate stretch of copper-bound formate, some 65 cm⁻¹ above the zirconia formate on the same sample. Integration region 1 runs 1900 to 1644 cm⁻¹ (Table S1) and was chosen because it gives the cleanest signal for this species. It is the highest νₐₛ(OCO) recorded in the atlas and it is what widened this band's window; the attribution comes from formic acid on Cu(100).

Fig. S19 (He+CO₂ against H₂+He, 20 bar): MCR-resolved spectra of CuIn/SiO₂, 230 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 10 NmL min⁻¹, after H₂ at 300 °C. νₐₛ(OCO) at 1544 cm⁻¹, tracked with the Cu-bound formate component (its C-O region drawn dashed beside the C-H one), some 46 cm⁻¹ below the Zn²⁺ formate on CuZn/SiO₂. The authors read the low ν(C-O) as formate bound too strongly, the In³⁺ end of their Sabatier volcano (Fig. 6a).

Table 1 and Fig. 6 (IRRAS, UHV, formic acid dosed at room temperature): νₐₛ(OCO) of bidentate-bridging formate on octahedral Fe with tetrahedral Fe underneath (νₐₛbb,tet), at 1555 cm⁻¹ and only in p-polarized light. The paper’s headline result: the first direct observation of this stretch for formate on that site.

Table 1 and Fig. 6 (IRRAS, UHV, formic acid dosed at room temperature): νₐₛ(OCO) of chelating formate (νₐₛchel) at 1548 cm⁻¹, very weak, in p-polarized light. Paired with νₛ at 1380 cm⁻¹ it gives the 168 cm⁻¹ splitting of a chelate, smaller than the 253 cm⁻¹ of the quasi-bidentate species.

Fig. 3a (5%Ru-6.1%"Na₂O"/Al₂O₃ dual function material, methanation step, 320 °C, 20% H₂/N₂ after 1 h of 15% CO₂/N₂): νₐₛ(OCO) of formate at 1520 cm⁻¹, the same position as on Ru/Al₂O₃ although it forms by another route, after bidentate carbonates on Al-O⁻-Na⁺ sites spill over to the Ru-support interface.

bands.description: Asymmetric OCO stretch of formate bound through one oxygen. With the other oxygen free the mode is close to a C=O stretch, and papers often name it that. It lies above the 1515 to 1650 cm⁻¹ of bridging and chelating formate because the two C-O bonds no longer share the bond order equally, and that gap is what identifies the geometry. It overlaps carbonyls, hollow-site CO and the water bend, so a lone band here needs a second argument (the symmetric partner, a calculation, isotope substitution) before it is read as formate.

references.note: Fig. 2e to g: Ag film in CO₂-saturated 0.1 M CsHCO₃, pulsed at E(c) = −1.1 V and E(a) = −0.2 V vs. RHE. A peak near 1674 cm⁻¹ appears throughout these pulses and is far stronger than under static or +0.7 V pulsed electrolysis: 1674 and 1671 in the deconvolved cathodic spectra (188.3 s, 526.7 s), about 1669 during the −0.2 V period itself (191.6 s), where it rivals bridged CO. The authors assign it to the C=O stretch of monodentate formate, *OCHO(M), from a calculation on Ag(111) and a grand canonical DFT estimate that formate is favoured over adsorbed H at −0.2 V, and tie it to the higher formate yield under −0.2 V pulses. It overlaps the hollow-CO shoulder.

Fig. 2d, with coordinates in Supplementary Data 1 (not read): spin-polarised DFT, RPBE with D3 dispersion in VASP, a three-layer 3 × 3 Ag(111) slab, frequencies by finite differences in ASE (±0.005 Å). The applied potential is left out of the frequency calculation, which the authors do for simplicity, so this is a zero-field value set against Stark-shifted measurements. Monodentate formate’s C=O stretch calculated at 1657 cm⁻¹, against 1680 to 1670 measured. The slab carries 15 Å of vacuum and the frequency calculation no solvent.

Supplementary Note 4, Figs. S24 and S25, Table S4: SnO₂ nanoparticles cast on the Au/Si prism, CO₂-saturated 0.1 M CsHCO₃, static at −1.1 V or pulsed with E(c) = −1.1 V and E(a) = −0.35 or −0.2 V vs. RHE; the reference is the single-beam spectrum at 0.65 V before electrolysis, and the deconvolutions are the 10th cycle (t(c) = 188.3 s, t(a) = 198.3 s). An extra peak near 1675 cm⁻¹ appears only when the potential steps to either anodic value, as a shoulder on the water bend, and is assigned to the C=O stretch of monodentate formate, *OCHO(M), the intermediate to formate, matching the silver result.

bands.description: Asymmetric OCO stretch of the free formate anion in solution, the product rather than the intermediate when CO₂ is reduced to formate in an aqueous electrolyte. With neither oxygen bound, the two C-O bonds are equal and the band sits inside the range of bridging formate, so position alone cannot separate dissolved from adsorbed formate; how it behaves with potential and time can. It also lies under the water bend and adsorbed carbonate, which is why it is usually read from a deconvolution.

references.note: Supplementary Note 4, Figs. S24 and S25, Table S4: SnO₂ nanoparticles cast on the Au/Si prism, CO₂-saturated 0.1 M CsHCO₃, static at −1.1 V or pulsed with E(c) = −1.1 V and E(a) = −0.35 or −0.2 V vs. RHE; the reference is the single-beam spectrum at 0.65 V before electrolysis, and the deconvolutions are the 10th cycle (t(c) = 188.3 s, t(a) = 198.3 s). Dissolved formate made at −1.1 V is identified by the peak near 1585 cm⁻¹, stronger under pulsed than under static electrolysis, in line with the higher formate Faradaic efficiency (72.9 % against 57.8 % static). No surface is recorded: the anion is in the electrolyte.

bands.description: Symmetric OCO stretch of the free formate anion in solution, the partner of the band near 1585 cm⁻¹. It coincides with the symmetric stretch of bridging formate on a surface, so on its own it does not say whether the formate is dissolved or adsorbed.

references.note: Supplementary Note 4, Figs. S24 and S25, Table S4: SnO₂ nanoparticles cast on the Au/Si prism, CO₂-saturated 0.1 M CsHCO₃, static at −1.1 V or pulsed with E(c) = −1.1 V and E(a) = −0.35 or −0.2 V vs. RHE; the reference is the single-beam spectrum at 0.65 V before electrolysis, and the deconvolutions are the 10th cycle (t(c) = 188.3 s, t(a) = 198.3 s). Table S4 assigns the peak near 1345 cm⁻¹ to "dissolved HCOO⁻ / *OCHO(B)": dissolved formate or bridging formate, without choosing. It is recorded here, on the dissolved band the table names first, and it is equally a candidate for the adsorbed symmetric stretch.

bands.description: Formate symmetric OCO stretch (HCOO*), paired with νₐₛ(OCO) above. The splitting Δν = νₐₛ − νₛ between the two paired bands is a standard diagnostic for adsorption geometry — how it compares between a more bridging-like and a more chelating-like coordination is a recurring theme in formate vibrational attributions. Where multiple coordination geometries coexist and overlap, polarization-dependent IRRAS/DRIFTS can resolve components that look like a single broad feature in an unpolarized spectrum.

references.note: Fig. 2 right (in situ Raman, 1 wt % Cu/SiO₂ at 230 °C, 200 and 400 bar; Renishaw InVia, 532 nm Nd:YAG, 60 mW, 600 s accumulation through a micro-view-cell, SI p. S34). Assigned there to surface formate, citing Wang et al. on methanol oxidation over silver. It grows strongly between 200 and 400 bar, which the paper reads as pressure driving up the formate coverage. The reactant mixture at 200 to 400 bar and 230 °C is above the critical point of both gases, a dense fluid (the paper speaks of fluid density), recorded as supercritical.

Fig. 7A, Pt(3)/MoOₓ(30)/TiO₂: in situ IR at 150 °C and ambient pressure under CO₂ (10), H₂ (30) and He (50) cm³ min⁻¹, on a self-supporting pellet in a quartz cell with CaF₂ windows, referenced to the sample under 30% H₂/He at the same temperature. Paired with 1555 cm⁻¹ and read as formate. The same bands are not prominent over MoOₓ(30)/TiO₂ without Pt, which is the paper's evidence that the metal is what makes them. Note the spectra are taken at ambient pressure while the methanol itself is made at 1 MPa CO₂ and 5 MPa H₂, so these are the species of the depressurised system.

Grown under UV irradiation of methoxy on TiO₂ in 10 Torr O₂, not dosed: formate is the photooxidation product of the methoxy this paper is following, and it appears together with the 1560 cm⁻¹ partner as CH₃O* is consumed. Read there as bridging HCOO*, and accompanied by gas-phase CO₂ at 2349 cm⁻¹.

Table 2 and Fig. 1a (5%Ru/Al₂O₃, methanation step, 320 °C, 20% H₂/N₂ after 1 h of 15% CO₂/N₂): νₛ(OCO) of formate at 1320 cm⁻¹, paired with νₐₛ at 1520, appearing at the onset of the H₂ step from bicarbonate spillover at the Ru-Al₂O₃ interface. A key CO₂ methanation intermediate.

Table 1 and Figs. 6a, 6c (IRRAS, UHV, formic acid dosed at room temperature): νₛ(OCO) of bidentate-bridging formate on octahedral Fe with tetrahedral Fe underneath (νₛbb,tet), at 1369 cm⁻¹ in p-polarized light. A negative Fano feature, which places the transition dipole perpendicular to the surface and stands the formate upright. Unpolarized light cannot separate it from the interstitial-site species at 1377 cm⁻¹.

Table 1 and Figs. 6b, 6d (IRRAS, UHV, formic acid dosed at room temperature): νₛ(OCO) of quasi-bidentate formate (νₛqbt) at 1335 cm⁻¹, fitted as its own Fano component (Fig. 8c). It appears only above 0.2 L, once hydrogen from the dissociation has covered the oxygen-terminated patches. Bidentate bridging is absent on this facet: the tetrahedral Fe atoms sit 5.9 Å apart.
Fig. 1b (ME-DRIFTS-PSD, Cu-GaZrOₓ, 20 bar, 260 °C): νₛ(OCO) marked at 1350 cm⁻¹, the companion of the 1600 cm⁻¹ asymmetric band and modulating with it.

Fig. S4a, formate generated on precipitated ZrO₂ from CO and surface hydroxyls at 260 °C and 20 bar. The paper reports symmetric OCO vibrations centred near 1290 and 1381 cm⁻¹; the 1381 cm⁻¹ component is recorded here, since 1290 cm⁻¹ sits in the carbonate region of the same spectrum and the paper does not say which species it belongs to.
Table 3: νs(OCO⁻) at 1380 cm⁻¹.

Table 3 and Fig. 3. CZ, a coprecipitated Cu/ZnO with Cu:Zn 2.1:1, diluted to 8 wt% in KBr and activated in H₂ at 513 K; 3H₂/CO₂ at 20 NmL min⁻¹, 513 K, 4 cm⁻¹, 64 scans. νₛ(OCO) at 1360 cm⁻¹ at 1 bar, bidentate, and 1314 cm⁻¹ at 30 bar, unidentate, the partners of νₐₛ at 1587 and 1603 cm⁻¹. See that entry for the spectator argument. Literature values cited: 1363, 1352, 1360 and 1363 cm⁻¹ for the first, 1352 and 1357 cm⁻¹ for the second.

H₂-TPSR after CO₂ adsorption on precipitated Ga₂O₃ (Fig. S13; also Fig. 5b under CO₂/H₂ = 1:3 from 30 to 450 °C): the lower of the two weak formate components below the dominant 1581 cm⁻¹ band. Fig. S13 marks both HCOO* without saying which is which, but Table S2 separates them, νₛ(OCO) at 1370 cm⁻¹ and δ(CH) at 1386 cm⁻¹, so the two are recorded as separate claims rather than as one pair on this band.

Fig. 6a (30ZnHfOₓ, H₂ and H₂:CO₂ steps, 320 °C, 20 bar): a band labelled HCOO* in the figure and not discussed in the text, which names no mode for it. It is recorded here because νₛ(OCO) is what this position and its 207 cm⁻¹ splitting from 1578 cm⁻¹ point to, but δ(CH) lands in the same place and the paper does not separate them. Zn–Vₒ–Hf is the paper's postulated site for all its intermediates (Section 2.9, Fig. 8e).

Fig. 1A and Table 1 (conditions as on the C–H stretch): the third of the three zirconia-formate bands, at 1380 cm⁻¹, and 1374 in the difference spectrum of Fig. 3b where it grows back as carbonate is lost. Table 1 lists the trio 2873, 1575, 1380 as formates on ZrO₂ and names no individual modes, so placing this one on νₛ(OCO) is the author's reading and not the paper's: δ(OCH) overlaps the same region. Integration region 3, 1415.5 to 1313.1 cm⁻¹ (Table S1), is the window the group's earlier kinetics were built on; regions 2 and 4 give the same decay, which is how the paper shows the carbonate contribution is minor.

Fig. 3b and Table 1: the third band of the copper-bound formate trio, at 1307 cm⁻¹, about 70 cm⁻¹ below its zirconia counterpart. The paper names no mode for it either, citing formic acid on Cu(100) for the set as a whole, so the placement on νₛ(OCO) is the author's. Seen only in the difference spectrum 9 s after CO₂ removal, magnified 20 times, with the methoxy and zirconia-formate contributions subtracted. It widened this band's window downward.

Table 1 and Figs. 6a, 6c (IRRAS, UHV, formic acid dosed at room temperature): νₛ(OCO) of bidentate-bridging formate on interstitial sites (νₛbb,int), at 1377 cm⁻¹ in p-polarized light, a negative Fano feature like its tetrahedral-site neighbour at 1369 cm⁻¹. The first time the two were told apart experimentally rather than by calculation.

Table 1 and Figs. 6b, 6d (IRRAS, UHV, formic acid dosed at room temperature): νₛ(OCO) of chelating formate (νₛchel) at 1380 cm⁻¹, fitted as its own Fano component (Fig. 8c). The chelate forms first, visible from 0.05 L.

Fig. 3a (5%Ru-6.1%"Na₂O"/Al₂O₃ dual function material, methanation step, 320 °C, 20% H₂/N₂ after 1 h of 15% CO₂/N₂): νₛ(OCO) of formate at 1320 cm⁻¹, paired with νₐₛ at 1520, here formed from bidentate carbonate spilling over to the Ru-support interface.

bands.description: Formate C-H bending (HCOO*); overlaps νₛ(OCO).

references.note: Not resolved separately: on Cu-GaZrOₓ at 20 bar and 260 °C the C-H bend falls under the νₛ(OCO) feature marked at 1350 cm⁻¹, and the paper treats the 1350 to 1400 cm⁻¹ region as one formate signal. Recorded without a wavenumber because the paper gives none for this mode alone.

Table 3 and Fig. 3B, 30 bar. CZ, a coprecipitated Cu/ZnO with Cu:Zn 2.1:1, diluted to 8 wt% in KBr and activated in H₂ at 513 K; 3H₂/CO₂ at 20 NmL min⁻¹, 513 K, 4 cm⁻¹, 64 scans. δ(CH) of unidentate formate at 1371 cm⁻¹, the middle band of the 1603/1371/1314 cm⁻¹ set that appears together and behaves as one species. Literature values cited: 1370 and 1375 cm⁻¹.

H₂-TPSR after CO₂ adsorption on precipitated Ga₂O₃ (Fig. S13; Table S2): δ(CH) of HCOO*, the upper of the two weak formate components below the dominant 1581 cm⁻¹ band and 16 cm⁻¹ above its νₛ(OCO) partner. Both are minor features on this Cu-free oxide, where formate is read almost entirely from the asymmetric OCO stretch. The same bend carries the two formate combination bands of Table S2, and 1386 + 1370 reproduces the observed 2757 cm⁻¹ exactly, which is what fixes this attribution against the νₛ(OCO) it overlaps.

Table 1 and Fig. 8a (IRRAS, UHV, room temperature): δ(CH) of bidentate-bridging formate, at 1373 cm⁻¹ in p-polarized and 1385 cm⁻¹ in s-polarized light. Its Fano line shape is inverted relative to the symmetric OCO stretch that sits almost on top of it, and that sign difference, not the position, is what separates the two. The paper reads the pair of polarizations as a C-H bond that is tilted rather than upright.
Table 1 (IRRAS, UHV, formic acid dosed at room temperature): δ(CH) of quasi-bidentate formate (δqbt) at 1385 cm⁻¹, in s-polarized light.

Table 1 (IRRAS, UHV, formic acid dosed at room temperature): δ(CH) of chelating formate (δchel) at 1280 cm⁻¹, in s-polarized light, 105 cm⁻¹ below the quasi-bidentate species: far more than this mode usually moves, and the lowest position the atlas holds for a formate C-H bend.

bands.description: Formate combination band (HCOO*): bending + asymmetric stretch; diagnostic for HCOO*. Runs low enough on cationic-promoted Cu (~2923 cm⁻¹) to sit right on top of methoxy νₐₛ(CH₃) — the two are told apart by deuteration, which moves this combination out of the C-H region altogether while methoxy's own fundamental simply shifts down to its C-D position.

references.note: Fig. 2 left (in situ DRIFTS, 1 wt % metal on silica, CO₂:H₂ = 1:1 at 230 °C, 1 and 40 bar). The highest of the three κ²-formate bands in the C-H region, synchronised with the 1600 cm⁻¹ band in the transient experiment.

Fig. 5b and Table S5 (operando DRIFTS, 220 °C, 6 bar, 25 mL min⁻¹, switching H₂/CO₂ 3/1 → He/CO₂ 3/1), unpromoted Cu/SiO₂: δ(CH)+νₐₛ(OCO) of bidentate formate at 2956 cm⁻¹, rising with ν(CH) at 2890 when the hydrogen is cut and vanishing when it returns. Dosing formic acid directly on Cu/SiO₂ puts the same combination at the same position (Fig. S15a), which is what ties the two experiments together.

Fig. 4b (3 wt% Pt/CeO₂ reduced in 10% H₂ at 300 °C; 200 °C, 1 bar, H₂/CO₂ = 4 in He): the upper member of the formate doublet at 2945 cm⁻¹, about 100 cm⁻¹ above ν(CH) at 2846, the pair the paper calls a Fermi resonance doublet for both the ¹²C and the ¹³C formate; under ¹³CO₂ it moves to 2910 cm⁻¹. Corrected: this note once paired it with 2910 cm⁻¹ and a 35 cm⁻¹ splitting, mixing the two isotopes.

Figs. 4a and 4c (steady state, 10 bar), 5b (H₂/D₂ switching, 10 bar) and 7a (He+CO₂ against H₂+He, 20 bar): CuZn/SiO₂, 230 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 10 NmL min⁻¹, after H₂ at 300 °C. Assigned as ν(C-O)+δ(C-H) of the Cu-bound bidentate formate, 2931 cm⁻¹ at steady state and in the switching experiment, 2929 in the transient, paired with ν(CH) at 2856/2850. Under D₂ it leaves the C-H region entirely, which is what shows it is a combination, and why the C-D window is the clean one for reading formate bond strengths.

H₂-TPSR after CO₂ adsorption on precipitated Ga₂O₃ (Fig. S13 inset, and Fig. 5a under CO₂/H₂ = 1:3 from 30 to 450 °C; Table S2): δ(CH)+νₐₛ(OCO) of HCOO*, the highest of the three formate features in the C-H window and well clear of ν(CH) at 2897 cm⁻¹. The fundamentals the same table reports sum to 2967 cm⁻¹, about 12 cm⁻¹ below the observed band. Its lower counterpart δ(CH)+νₛ(OCO) is also resolved here, at 2757 cm⁻¹, which is unusual: most sources report only this upper one.

Fig. 7 and Table 1 (IRRAS, UHV, room temperature): assigned as a coupling of the asymmetric OCO stretch with the C-H bend, and seen on both magnetite facets at the same position. It appears in p-polarized light on Fe₃O₄(001). Recorded here rather than as a C-H fundamental because the paper treats it as the combination, consistent with the earlier attribution of a band near 2950 cm⁻¹ on Cu(110).

Fig. 6a (30ZnHfOₓ, H₂ step, 320 °C, 20 bar): the weaker partner of the 2887 cm⁻¹ band, assigned in the paper as νₐₛ(C–H) of formate against νₛ(C–H) at 2887 cm⁻¹. Formate has a single C–H bond and so no symmetric and asymmetric pair; the atlas files this band as the δ(CH)+νₐₛ(OCO) combination its position matches, and the νₐₛ(C–H) label is the paper's.

Figs. S15 (H₂/D₂ switching, 10 bar) and S18 (He+CO₂ against H₂+He, 20 bar): MCR-resolved spectra of Cu/SiO₂, 230 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 10 NmL min⁻¹, after H₂ at 300 °C. ν(C-O)+δ(C-H) of the Cu-bound formate at 2929 and 2931 cm⁻¹, in the same component as its ν(CH).

Figs. S16 (H₂/D₂ switching, 10 bar) and S20 (He+CO₂ against H₂+He, 20 bar): MCR-resolved spectra of CuGa/SiO₂, 230 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 10 NmL min⁻¹, after H₂ at 300 °C. ν(C-O)+δ(C-H) of the Cu-bound formate at 2923 cm⁻¹ in the switching experiment, the lowest of the four catalysts, and 2929 in the transient, where it sits in a component shared with the Ga³⁺ species.

Figs. S17 (H₂/D₂ switching, 10 bar) and S19 (He+CO₂ against H₂+He, 20 bar): MCR-resolved spectra of CuIn/SiO₂, 230 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 10 NmL min⁻¹, after H₂ at 300 °C. ν(C-O)+δ(C-H) of the Cu-bound formate at 2937 and 2933 cm⁻¹, the highest of the four catalysts.

Fig. 5c and Table S5 (operando DRIFTS, 220 °C, 6 bar, 25 mL min⁻¹, switching H₂/CO₂ 3/1 → He/CO₂ 3/1), CuGa(0.20): δ(CH)+νₐₛ(OCO) of bidentate formate at 2956 cm⁻¹, unchanged from Cu/SiO₂, the paper’s argument that this formate is on Cu⁰ and not at the Cu-Ga₂O₃ interface.

bands.description: Formate combination band: the C-H bend plus the symmetric OCO stretch, and the lower partner of the δ(OCH)+νₐₛ(OCO) combination near 2950 cm⁻¹. A weak band on each side of ν(CH) is the signature the pair provides, since neither carbonate nor methoxy produces one. This is the weaker of the two and the easier to lose in a sloping baseline, so it is reported far less often than its partner. Its position is arithmetic rather than chemistry: it follows whatever the two fundamentals do, so a change in the OCO splitting between sites moves this band and its partner in opposite directions.

references.note: Fig. 2 left (in situ DRIFTS, 1 wt % metal on silica, CO₂:H₂ = 1:1 at 230 °C, 1 and 40 bar). The lowest of the three κ²-formate bands in the C-H region. It sits just below the window this atlas had, which was widened to take it.

Fig. 5a (operando DRIFTS, precipitated Ga₂O₃, CO₂/H₂ = 1:3, 30 to 450 °C; Table S2): δ(CH)+νₛ(OCO) of HCOO*, the lowest of the three formate features in the C-H window. The two fundamentals the same table gives, 1386 and 1370 cm⁻¹, sum to 2756 cm⁻¹, one wavenumber off the observed band, which is a tighter match than the upper combination manages and is what makes this the cleaner of the pair to argue from here.

Fig. S15a and Table S5 (operando DRIFTS, 4% HCOOH/Ar at 20 mL min⁻¹, 220 °C, atmospheric pressure): δ(CH)+νₛ(OCO) of bidentate formate made by dosing formic acid on Cu/SiO₂. The paper marks it as its own result with no literature value to cite, which fits how rarely this lower combination is reported next to its partner at 2956 cm⁻¹. Seen only in the formic acid experiment: it does not appear under CO₂ and H₂, where formate is below the detection limit at steady state.

bands.description: C-D stretch of κ²-DCOO*, the deuterated twin of ν(CH) HCOO* and red-shifted from it by the 0.73 mass factor. Site-sensitive in the same way: formate on metallic Cu sits 15 to 20 cm⁻¹ below formate on a cation site. Deuteration is what makes this window readable, moving the δ(OCH)+νₐₛ(OCO) combination out of the way and leaving one uncluttered fundamental. Two overlaps: gas-phase CO's R branch sits on top of it, and deuterated methoxy brackets it, with νₛ(CD₃) just below the window and νₐₛ(CD₃) at its top.

references.note: Fig. 5b (H₂/D₂ switching, 10 bar): MCR-resolved spectra of CuZn/SiO₂, 230 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 10 NmL min⁻¹, after H₂ at 300 °C, under D₂/CO₂. κ²-DCOO* on Cu at 2167 cm⁻¹, beside the Zn²⁺-bound one at 2184. Fig. 6b uses 2173 for this catalyst, the Gaussian-fitted centre of the two overlapping components rather than either species. Across the four catalysts the authors find the ν(CD) rising with the intrinsic methanol selectivity, linearly (R² > 0.99), and use it as a selectivity descriptor; the exchange with κ²-HCOO* completes in under a minute.

Fig. 5b (same MCR-resolved Cu–Zn/SiO₂ SSITKA experiment, 230 °C, 10 bar): κ²-DCOO*(Zn²⁺) at 2184 cm⁻¹, kinetically indistinguishable from κ²-DCOO*(Cu) at 2167 cm⁻¹ but spectrally separate — direct evidence that Zn²⁺ supplies a second, distinct Lewis-acid site for formate and simultaneously perturbs the formate on the adjacent Cu. Not resolved for Ga³⁺ or In³⁺ in this region (Figs. S16/S17), where the promoter-bound component overlaps κ²-DCOO*(Cu) or is too dilute at steady state.

Fig. S15 (H₂/D₂ switching, 10 bar): MCR-resolved spectra of Cu/SiO₂, 230 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 10 NmL min⁻¹, after H₂ at 300 °C, under D₂/CO₂. κ²-DCOO* on Cu at 2161 cm⁻¹, the lowest of the four catalysts and the low end of the selectivity line in Fig. 6b.

Fig. S16 (H₂/D₂ switching, 10 bar): MCR-resolved spectra of CuGa/SiO₂, 230 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 10 NmL min⁻¹, after H₂ at 300 °C, under D₂/CO₂. κ²-DCOO* on Cu at 2176 cm⁻¹, the highest of the four, matching the highest methanol selectivity. A Ga³⁺-bound formate is not resolved here and may lie under this band (main text, Section 2.5).

Fig. S17 (H₂/D₂ switching, 10 bar): MCR-resolved spectra of CuIn/SiO₂, 230 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 10 NmL min⁻¹, after H₂ at 300 °C, under D₂/CO₂. κ²-DCOO* on Cu at 2169 cm⁻¹. No In³⁺-bound formate is resolved in this region.

bands.description: Asymmetric OCO stretch of deuterated formate. The OCO frame carries almost none of the hydrogen's motion, so this band moves by ten wavenumbers or so rather than by the mass factor that drags ν(CH) down to 2160 cm⁻¹. That near-invariance is the useful part: a band in this window that stays put under D₂ while the C-H window empties is the OCO stretch and nothing else. It remains the strongest formate feature under deuterium, so a deuterated spectrum still reads as formate here.

references.note: D₂-TPSR after CO₂ adsorption on precipitated Ga₂O₃ (Fig. S14): DCOO* made by the surface Ga-D, and the dominant band of the spectrum exactly as its protiated twin is at 1581 cm⁻¹ under H₂ (Fig. S13). Deuteration moves it up by 11 cm⁻¹, which is the whole shift. The Ga-D that made it is visible at 1429 cm⁻¹ in the same spectrum, so hydride and product are seen together.

bands.description: Symmetric OCO stretch of deuterated formate, the partner of νₐₛ(OCO) DCOO*. Read the two together: the splitting between them is the same geometry diagnostic as on the protiated species, and comparing the pair against its protiated counterpart separates a real change of binding from the isotope shift. Deuteration is what clears this window, since δ(OCH) near 1380 cm⁻¹ moves away and leaves the symmetric stretch alone where the two normally sit on top of each other.

references.note: D₂-TPSR after CO₂ adsorption on precipitated Ga₂O₃ (Fig. S14): the weak lower partner of the 1592 cm⁻¹ band. It sits 29 cm⁻¹ below the 1370 cm⁻¹ νₛ(OCO) the same group reports for HCOO* under H₂, a larger move than the asymmetric partner makes. The δ(CH) at 1386 cm⁻¹ that crowds this region under H₂ is gone, which is why the deuterated spectrum shows one component here where the protiated one shows two.

bands.description: Methoxy CH₃ asymmetric stretch, one C-H bond moving out of phase with the other two. It tracks νₛ(CH₃) below, so a shift in both is a sign that the binding environment itself has changed. Coadsorbed methanol sits a little higher and is easily read as the same species. Silica is the outlier among supports: methoxy grafted as Si-O-CH₃ absorbs near 2955 to 2960 cm⁻¹, some 30 cm⁻¹ above the same mode on Cu.

references.note: Monodentate CH₃O* from CH₃OH dosing on anatase TiO₂. Measured after dosing 2 Torr of methanol and evacuating the cell (base pressure 1 × 10⁻⁷ Torr), the spectrum recorded at 35 °C.

Figs. 5a, 5c, S17b and Table S5 (operando DRIFTS, CuGa(0.20), 220 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 6 bar, 25 mL min⁻¹): νₐₛ(CH₃) of CH₃O* at steady state, 7 cm⁻¹ below the same mode on the unpromoted Cu/SiO₂. Methoxy is the most abundant surface intermediate here, and that shift is the paper's evidence that on the promoted catalyst it sits on the Cu⁺ site at the Cu-Ga₂O₃ interface rather than on Cu⁰ — an inference from the frequency, since the two catalysts are otherwise alike. Formate is not detected under these conditions.

Figs. 5a, 5b, S17a and Table S5 (operando DRIFTS, unpromoted Cu/SiO₂, 220 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 6 bar, 25 mL min⁻¹): νₐₛ(CH₃) of CH₃O* on the Ga-free reference catalyst, the counterpart of the 2919 cm⁻¹ band on CuGa(0.20). Two claims rather than one pair, because the 7 cm⁻¹ between them is the observation the paper's site argument rests on. It holds its position from 220 to 280 °C (Fig. S17a).

Fig. S16a and Table S5 (operando DRIFTS, 10% CH₃OH/Ar at 20 mL min⁻¹, 220 °C, atmospheric pressure, then swept with Ar): νₐₛ(CH₃) of the methoxy left after dosing methanol on Cu/SiO₂ and removing the physisorbed layer. This is the reference experiment that verifies the methoxy attribution under reaction. It sits 28 cm⁻¹ above the band measured under CO₂ and H₂ on the same catalyst, which the paper does not comment on; the value is close to where methoxy grafted onto silica is usually reported.

Fig. 1b (ME-DRIFTS-PSD, Cu-GaZrOₓ, 20 bar, 260 °C): the C-H stretching region of CH₃O* is marked at 2970, 2876 and 2819 cm⁻¹, with 2876 cm⁻¹ belonging to formate. The paper names no site for the methoxy on the catalyst; its own reference spectra on precipitated ZrO₂ and Ga₂O₃ (Fig. S5) are what support reading it as bound to the oxide rather than to Cu.

Figs. 4a and 4c (steady state, 10 bar), 5b (H₂/D₂ switching, 10 bar) and 7a (He+CO₂ against H₂+He, 20 bar): CuZn/SiO₂, 230 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 10 NmL min⁻¹, after H₂ at 300 °C. νₐₛ(CH₃) of methoxy on the silica at 2958 cm⁻¹, 2956 in the transient. Methoxy grafted to the silica (Si-O-CH₃), not to Cu or the promoter: it builds up slowly and exchanges over minutes to hours under D₂. Fig. S14 splits it into a reactive pool near the Cu/Zn²⁺ interface and a slow spectator pool on remote silica; hydrogenating or desorbing the reactive pool is the rate-limiting step (KIE 2.78).

Fig. 5a (operando DRIFTS-MS, precipitated Ga₂O₃, CO₂/H₂ = 1:3, 30 to 450 °C; Table S2): νₐₛ(CH₃) of CH₃O*, marked as a shoulder 39 cm⁻¹ below the formate combination band at 2979 cm⁻¹ and paired with νₛ(CH₃) at 2834 cm⁻¹. Methoxy on an oxide carrying no metal at all: it is made from formate by the surface Ga-H hydride, and gas-phase methanol follows it into the mass spectrometer from 304 °C (Fig. S16).

Figs. 6a and 6b (30ZnHfOₓ, H₂ step, 320 °C, 20 bar): νₐₛ(CH₃) of methoxy, growing as formate is hydrogenated under H₂ and falling when CO₂ returns. Zn–Vₒ–Hf is the paper's postulated site: in its DFT, CH₂O* moves to the oxygen vacancy of that motif to be hydrogenated to CH₃O* (Fig. 7).

Fig. 1A and Table 1 (conditions as on the formate C–H stretch): νₐₛ(CH₃) of methoxy at 2927 cm⁻¹. The paper distinguishes two methoxy types that share this band and the 2822 cm⁻¹ one and differ only in the C–O stretch, 1150 for type I and 1049 for type II. Most of the methoxy is read as a spectator formed by methanol re-adsorbing on the zirconia, removed by hydrolysis with water rather than by reductive elimination.

Figs. S15 (H₂/D₂ switching, 10 bar) and S18 (He+CO₂ against H₂+He, 20 bar): MCR-resolved spectra of Cu/SiO₂, 230 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 10 NmL min⁻¹, after H₂ at 300 °C. νₐₛ(CH₃) of methoxy on the silica at 2956 and 2952 cm⁻¹. Methoxy grafted to the silica (Si-O-CH₃), not to Cu or the promoter: it builds up slowly and exchanges over minutes to hours under D₂.

Figs. S16 (H₂/D₂ switching, 10 bar) and S20 (He+CO₂ against H₂+He, 20 bar): MCR-resolved spectra of CuGa/SiO₂, 230 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 10 NmL min⁻¹, after H₂ at 300 °C. νₐₛ(CH₃) of methoxy on the silica at 2958 cm⁻¹ in both. Methoxy grafted to the silica (Si-O-CH₃), not to Cu or the promoter: it builds up slowly and exchanges over minutes to hours under D₂.

Fig. S17 (H₂/D₂ switching, 10 bar): MCR-resolved spectra of CuIn/SiO₂, 230 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 10 NmL min⁻¹, after H₂ at 300 °C. νₐₛ(CH₃) of methoxy on the silica at 2956 cm⁻¹. Methoxy grafted to the silica (Si-O-CH₃), not to Cu or the promoter: it builds up slowly and exchanges over minutes to hours under D₂.

Fig. S20 (He+CO₂ against H₂+He, 20 bar): MCR-resolved spectra of CuGa/SiO₂, 230 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 10 NmL min⁻¹, after H₂ at 300 °C. Methoxy on the Ga³⁺ sites, marked at 2919 cm⁻¹ inside a component MCR cannot separate from Cu- and Ga³⁺-bound formate and adsorbed methanol, all consumed quickly under H₂. The figure names the species but not the mode; filing it as the antisymmetric CH₃ stretch is this collection’s reading of the position.

Fig. S19 (He+CO₂ against H₂+He, 20 bar): MCR-resolved spectra of CuIn/SiO₂, 230 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 10 NmL min⁻¹, after H₂ at 300 °C. Methoxy on the In³⁺ sites, marked at 2935 cm⁻¹ (with 2849) in the component shared with In³⁺-bound formate; unlike on Ga³⁺ it grows to a plateau under H₂ instead of being consumed. Filing 2935 as the antisymmetric CH₃ stretch is this collection’s reading of the position.

bands.description: Methoxy CH₃ symmetric stretch (CH₃O*), shifting in tandem with νₐₛ(CH₃) above. Often appears as a close shoulder pair with a coadsorbed methanol band sitting a little higher in frequency. Silica-grafted methoxy is the extreme case, ~2856–2859 cm⁻¹, some 40 cm⁻¹ above the same mode on Cu — high enough that it lands directly on formate's own ν(CH) on metallic Cu (the low end of ν(CH) HCOO*). On a silica-supported Cu catalyst the two are effectively coincident and cannot be separated by position alone.

references.note: Methoxy CH₃ symmetric stretch on anatase TiO₂ from methanol dosing. Measured after dosing 2 Torr of methanol and evacuating the cell (base pressure 1 × 10⁻⁷ Torr), the spectrum recorded at 35 °C.

Figs. 5a, 5c, S17b and Table S5 (operando DRIFTS, CuGa(0.20), 220 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 6 bar, 25 mL min⁻¹): νₛ(CH₃) of CH₃O* at steady state, the partner of νₐₛ(CH₃) at 2919 cm⁻¹ and shifted from the Ga-free catalyst in the same direction and by a similar amount. That the two CH₃ stretches move together is what makes the shift read as a change of adsorption site rather than as a second species.

Figs. 5a, 5b, S17a and Table S5 (operando DRIFTS, unpromoted Cu/SiO₂, 220 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 6 bar, 25 mL min⁻¹): νₛ(CH₃) of CH₃O* on the Ga-free reference catalyst, paired with νₐₛ(CH₃) at 2926 cm⁻¹. Recorded apart from the CuGa(0.20) value at 2836 cm⁻¹ for the same reason as its partner.

Fig. S16a and Table S5 (operando DRIFTS, 10% CH₃OH/Ar at 20 mL min⁻¹, 220 °C, atmospheric pressure, then swept with Ar for 30 min): νₛ(CH₃) of methoxy formed by dosing methanol on Cu/SiO₂, the experiment that verifies the attribution made under reaction. Its partner is at 2954 cm⁻¹. Both sit well above the values the same catalyst gives under CO₂ and H₂, and at this position the band is also where formate's own ν(CH) on metallic Cu is usually found.

Fig. 1b (ME-DRIFTS-PSD, Cu-GaZrOₓ, 20 bar, 260 °C): the lower of the two CH₃O* stretching peaks. The corresponding reference spectra on the single oxides (Fig. S5) put the methoxy C-H stretches between 2797 and 2935 cm⁻¹ without resolving them into symmetric and asymmetric.

Figs. 4a and 4c (steady state, 10 bar), 5b (H₂/D₂ switching, 10 bar) and 7a (He+CO₂ against H₂+He, 20 bar): CuZn/SiO₂, 230 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 10 NmL min⁻¹, after H₂ at 300 °C. νₛ(CH₃) of methoxy on the silica at 2858 cm⁻¹, 2854 in the transient, paired with νₐₛ at 2958/2956. Methoxy grafted to the silica (Si-O-CH₃), not to Cu or the promoter: it builds up slowly and exchanges over minutes to hours under D₂. Under D₂ it moves to 2080 cm⁻¹ (CD₃O*), which separates it from the formate bands it otherwise overlaps.

H₂-TPSR after CO₂ adsorption on precipitated Ga₂O₃ (Fig. S13 inset, and Fig. 5a under CO₂/H₂ = 1:3): the methoxy that formate is converted into as the temperature rises, on an oxide with no metal on it at all. It appears above roughly 250 °C and its growth follows the loss of formate (Fig. 5c). Both figures mark 2837 cm⁻¹, which is the value recorded; Table S2 lists the same band at 2834 cm⁻¹ and names the mode νₛ(CH₃). Its νₐₛ(CH₃) partner is at 2940 cm⁻¹.

Figs. 6a to 6c, S56g and S56h (operando DRIFTS, 320 °C, 20 bar): νₛ(CH₃) of methoxy, the band the paper tracks with time, at 2827 cm⁻¹ on 30ZnHfOₓ, 2832 cm⁻¹ on 20ZnHfOₓ and 2835 cm⁻¹ on 90ZnHfOₓ. After switching to H₂ it grows on every Hf-containing catalyst and markedly less on ZnO, which the paper reads as Hf stabilising methoxy at the Zn–Vₒ–Hf motif.

Figs. 8e, S56i and S56l (ZnO reference, 320 °C, 20 bar, H₂:CO₂:N₂ = 3:1:1 then H₂): methoxy on the Hf-free oxide, very weak, and growing less under H₂ than on the Hf-containing catalysts while formate decreases. Set against the ZnHfOₓ catalysts, this is the paper's evidence that Hf in the active motif is what stabilises methoxy.

Fig. 8e and Section 2.9 (operando DRIFTS, bare monoclinic HfO₂ reference, 90 min at 320 °C, 20 bar, H₂:CO₂:N₂ = 3:1:1): methoxy forms on the Zn-free oxide, weaker than on 30ZnHfOₓ, yet no methanol is detected in the off-gas. The paper suggests slow turnover, or methoxy that cannot be hydrogenated without Zn, which matches the poor H₂ activation of HfO₂ in its H₂-D₂ exchange. No position is printed; the 30ZnHfOₓ band sits 4 to 5 cm⁻¹ lower.

Fig. 1A and Table 1 (conditions as on the formate C–H stretch): νₛ(CH₃) of methoxy at 2822 cm⁻¹, shared by both methoxy types the paper distinguishes, which differ only in the C–O stretch. It sits 18 cm⁻¹ below the 2840 cm⁻¹ C–H stretch of the copper-bound formate, which is why the methoxy contribution had to be subtracted before that formate could be integrated (Figs. S3A and S3C).

Figs. S15 (H₂/D₂ switching, 10 bar) and S18 (He+CO₂ against H₂+He, 20 bar): MCR-resolved spectra of Cu/SiO₂, 230 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 10 NmL min⁻¹, after H₂ at 300 °C. νₛ(CH₃) of methoxy on the silica at 2856 and 2859 cm⁻¹. Methoxy grafted to the silica (Si-O-CH₃), not to Cu or the promoter: it builds up slowly and exchanges over minutes to hours under D₂.

Figs. S16 (H₂/D₂ switching, 10 bar) and S20 (He+CO₂ against H₂+He, 20 bar): MCR-resolved spectra of CuGa/SiO₂, 230 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 10 NmL min⁻¹, after H₂ at 300 °C. νₛ(CH₃) of methoxy on the silica at 2858 cm⁻¹ in both. Methoxy grafted to the silica (Si-O-CH₃), not to Cu or the promoter: it builds up slowly and exchanges over minutes to hours under D₂.

Fig. S17 (H₂/D₂ switching, 10 bar): MCR-resolved spectra of CuIn/SiO₂, 230 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 10 NmL min⁻¹, after H₂ at 300 °C. νₛ(CH₃) of methoxy on the silica at 2856 cm⁻¹. Methoxy grafted to the silica (Si-O-CH₃), not to Cu or the promoter: it builds up slowly and exchanges over minutes to hours under D₂.

Fig. S19 (He+CO₂ against H₂+He, 20 bar): MCR-resolved spectra of CuIn/SiO₂, 230 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 10 NmL min⁻¹, after H₂ at 300 °C. Methoxy on the In³⁺ sites, marked at 2849 cm⁻¹ (with 2935) in the component shared with In³⁺-bound formate. Filing 2849 as the symmetric CH₃ stretch is this collection’s reading of the position.
Fig. S56 (operando DRIFTS, 320 °C, 20 bar, the protocol of Fig. 6a): methoxy νₛ(CH₃) at 2832 cm⁻¹ on 20ZnHfOₓ, against 2827 cm⁻¹ on 30ZnHfOₓ (claim 249), which carries the full account.

Fig. S56 (operando DRIFTS, 320 °C, 20 bar, the protocol of Fig. 6a): methoxy νₛ(CH₃) at 2835 cm⁻¹ on 90ZnHfOₓ, against 2827 cm⁻¹ on 30ZnHfOₓ (claim 249), which carries the full account. 90ZnHfOₓ is mostly segregated ZnO with HfOₓ clusters, so a value this close to the solid solutions is the paper’s evidence for the same site on both.

bands.description: Methoxy CH₃ symmetric deformation (CH₃O*) — the methyl "umbrella" mode. Usually the only CH₃-deformation-region band resolved at all, since it's the sole totally-symmetric (A₁) one and therefore the only one with a surface-normal dipole derivative on an ideally perpendicular adsorbate; on real, less rigidly-oriented oxide-supported catalysts it can be unusually weak. Position is comparatively insensitive to binding geometry, unlike the stretches above.

references.note: Table 1, methanol dosed on TiO₂ (Degussa P25, 70% anatase and 30% rutile, ~50 m² g⁻¹) as a powder film on a tungsten mesh, measured in transmission through CaF₂ windows. Labelled δa(CH₃) there, an antisymmetric deformation, where this atlas carries the 1430–1458 cm⁻¹ region as the symmetric one; filed here on position, since the paper's own asymmetric-deformation band for methoxy would sit far lower. The disagreement is over the label, not the number. Measured after dosing 2 Torr of methanol and evacuating the cell (base pressure 1 × 10⁻⁷ Torr), the spectrum recorded at 35 °C.
Table 3: δ(–CH₃) at 1480 cm⁻¹; surface methoxy deformation from CH₄ activation via H-abstraction; observed during DRM at 600°C.

Table 3 and Fig. 3B, 30 bar. CZ, a coprecipitated Cu/ZnO with Cu:Zn 2.1:1, diluted to 8 wt% in KBr and activated in H₂ at 513 K; 3H₂/CO₂ at 20 NmL min⁻¹, 513 K, 4 cm⁻¹, 64 scans. δ(CH₃) of surface methoxy *H₃CO at 1457 cm⁻¹. Its intensity grows with the catalyst loading in the diluent, alongside the methanol in the outlet gas, and follows the GHSV; that is the paper’s argument both for reading it as methoxy and for calling it an intermediate rather than a spectator. Absent under a 2H₂/CO feed. Literature values cited: 1460, 1445 and 1470 cm⁻¹.

bands.description: Tentatively assigned methoxy CH₃ asymmetric deformation (CH₃O*). Not always separately resolved from δₛ(CH₃) above — some spectra show only the symmetric component. May overlap with formate νₛ(OCO) at ~1365 cm⁻¹, so a band here doesn't necessarily rule out formate also being present.

Monodentate methoxy C-O stretch (CH₃O* bonded via O to a single metal cation). Often resolves into several closely-spaced sub-components rather than one clean peak, reflecting a distribution of slightly different monodentate sites rather than a single uniform one. Diagnostic threshold: ν(C-O) above roughly 1100 cm⁻¹ indicates monodentate geometry, below it bidentate (see methoxy_co_stretch_bi) — the two share the same underlying vibration and just trade off in relative position with coordination number.

references.note: Sub-components at 1100/1126/1156 cm⁻¹ reflecting a distribution of monodentate sites; dominates over bidentate ~3:1 by integrated area; ~1.5× higher photoreactivity toward HCOO* than bidentate. Measured after dosing 2 Torr of methanol and evacuating the cell (base pressure 1 × 10⁻⁷ Torr), the spectrum recorded at 35 °C.

Fig. 1b (ME-DRIFTS-PSD, Cu-GaZrOₓ, 20 bar, 260 °C): the C-O stretch of CH₃O* at 1152 cm⁻¹, one of the two bands the paper follows through the modulation. It matches the 1154 cm⁻¹ peak of methoxy on precipitated ZrO₂ (Fig. S5), which is the paper's own basis for placing the methoxy on the zirconia rather than on Cu, though it never writes Zr⁴⁺ itself.

Fig. S5, reference spectrum: methanol dosed directly onto precipitated ZrO₂ at 260 °C and 1 bar, with the bubbler then switched off so that only the adsorbed species remain. The paper reports the main C-O stretching peaks at 1111 and 1154 cm⁻¹ and cites Bensitel for the attribution, but does not itself say which peak is the mono- and which the bidentate methoxy. Both are recorded on this band because both fall inside its window.

Fig. 6a (30ZnHfOₓ, H₂ step, 320 °C, 20 bar): terminal methoxy, t-H₃CO*, appearing with the bridged form at 1052 cm⁻¹ as formate is hydrogenated. The paper names the geometry and not the mode; ν(CO) is where the position falls. It tells the two geometries apart by label only and names no site for either beyond its general postulate, Zn–Vₒ–Hf for all its intermediates (Section 2.9, Fig. 8e). Fig. S49 marks both forms on 20ZnHfOₓ in the same switching sequence, without printing positions.

Fig. 1A and Table 1 (conditions as on the formate C–H stretch): the C–O stretch of the paper's methoxy type I at 1150 cm⁻¹, paired with 2927 and 2822 in the C–H region. The 1159 cm⁻¹ value is from the difference spectrum of Fig. 3b, where it appears pointing downward 9 s after CO₂ removal, meaning methoxy newly formed. The paper places that one on the zirconia rather than on the copper, because the C–O stretch of methoxy on Cu(100) is reported at 998 cm⁻¹, far below anything seen here. Type I and type II are named as such and not resolved into binding geometries, so the monodentate placement is the author's.

bands.description: Bidentate methoxy C-O stretch (CH₃O* bridging two metal centers, or bonded at a bridging-O vacancy). Diagnostic threshold: ν(C-O) below roughly 1100 cm⁻¹ indicates bidentate geometry (see methoxy_co_stretch_mono for the monodentate counterpart). Overlaps closely with molecular methanol's own ν(C-O) — distinguish via the absence of methanol's own νₛ(CH₃) marker band at higher frequency.

references.note: Similar thermal stability to monodentate (no interconversion ≤ 300 °C); ~1.5× lower photoreactivity toward HCOO* than monodentate. Measured after dosing 2 Torr of methanol and evacuating the cell (base pressure 1 × 10⁻⁷ Torr), the spectrum recorded at 35 °C.

Fig. S5, reference spectrum: methanol dosed onto precipitated Ga₂O₃ at 260 °C and 1 bar, with the bubbler switched off so only adsorbed species remain. The paper puts the C-O stretch of CH₃O* at 1071 cm⁻¹ on this oxide and gives no binding geometry. It is recorded on the bidentate band because that is where the position falls, not because the paper says so.

Fig. 6a (30ZnHfOₓ, H₂ step, 320 °C, 20 bar): bridged methoxy, b-H₃CO*, the partner of terminal methoxy at 1153 cm⁻¹. The paper names the geometry and not the mode; ν(CO) is where the position falls. Zn–Vₒ–Hf is the paper's postulated site for all its intermediates (Section 2.9, Fig. 8e).

Fig. 1A and Table 1 (conditions as on the formate C–H stretch): the C–O stretch of the paper's methoxy type II at 1049 cm⁻¹, sharing 2927 and 2822 with type I. The two types are named I and II and never resolved into binding geometries, so the bidentate placement is the author's reading of the position rather than the paper's claim.

bands.description: CD₃ symmetric stretch of deuterated methoxy, the one methoxy band that survives deuteration as a cleanly resolvable feature. In the ordinary C-H region methoxy overlaps formate's combination band and adsorbed methanol; here it sits about 80 cm⁻¹ clear of the deuterated formate bands and can be integrated on its own. The neighbourhood is crowded in a different way, since CO on reduced metals and CO₂ combination bands absorb here.

references.note: Figs. 5b and 5c (H₂/D₂ switching, 10 bar, 230 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 10 NmL min⁻¹, after H₂ at 300 °C, under D₂/CO₂), CuZn/SiO₂: CD₃O* on the silica at 2080 cm⁻¹, the νₛ(CD) of the 2858 cm⁻¹ methoxy. Its concentration profile, not the formate’s, tracks the delayed methanol, the observation that makes methoxy hydrogenation or desorption rate-limiting (KIE 2.78, Fig. S12). The νₐₛ(CD) partner, expected near 2160, is hidden under κ²-DCOO*.

Fig. S15 (H₂/D₂ switching, 10 bar, 230 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 10 NmL min⁻¹, after H₂ at 300 °C, under D₂/CO₂), Cu/SiO₂: CD₃O* on the silica at 2080 cm⁻¹, unshifted from CuZn/SiO₂: the methoxy sits on the support whatever the promoter.

Fig. S16 (H₂/D₂ switching, 10 bar, 230 °C, H₂/CO₂ = 3, 10 NmL min⁻¹, after H₂ at 300 °C, under D₂/CO₂), CuGa/SiO₂ made by surface organometallic chemistry: CD₃O* on the silica at 2080 cm⁻¹, unshifted by the promoter.
