bands.description: The highest of corundum's Raman-active lattice modes, an E(g) mode of α-Al₂O₃: doubly degenerate, Raman-active and infrared-inactive. It softens by about 28 cm⁻¹ between room temperature and 1080 °C. A weak line near 725 cm⁻¹, just below it, is not a corundum phonon: it has been seen where impurities or defects concentrate in a synthetic crystal (the defect line in this lane).

references.note: Table 1 (this work) and Fig. 3: Stokes line at 749.5 cm⁻¹, symmetry Eg as Table 1 gives it from the literature (its refs 7, 19, 21). Single-crystal sapphire rod (Micromaterials, about 2.5 cm, orientation not stated), cleaned in acetone and methanol and held at 200 °C; room temperature, ambient air, 488 nm CW argon-ion line at 1.7 W, back-scattering, Lorentzian fits, 5.33 cm⁻¹ resolution. Heated in steps to 1081 °C it softens to about 722 cm⁻¹ (read off Fig. 6b); 1σ 2 to 14 °C as a thermometer, worst at the top of the range (Table 2b). Its weak anti-Stokes line is seen too and grows on heating (Sect. 3), without a printed position. Caveat: the spectrometer was calibrated on these same room-temperature sapphire lines taken from the literature (absolute error under 3 cm⁻¹), so this position is not independent of them.

Fig. 1, 747.6 cm⁻¹, given as 748 in the text. Sample 1, the centre of a synthetic sapphire window (Czech Republic, cut from a (0001)-oriented crystal, 36 mm by 5 mm) used for two years in a cryostat at liquid-nitrogen temperature; LabRam confocal micro-Raman, 632.8 nm He-Ne at 15 mW, 100× objective, about 1 µm spot, resolution better than 1.3 cm⁻¹, calibrated on silicon at 520.7 cm⁻¹, room temperature. The paper assigns no symmetry line by line: it quotes 2A₁(g) + 5E(g) and the literature positions (378, 418, 432, 451, 578, 645, 751 cm⁻¹) in the same order as its own seven, which is the correspondence recorded here. Fig. 2, 1 cm off the centre: 748.7, there joined by a defect line at 724.6 cm⁻¹.

bands.description: A weak Raman line near 725 cm⁻¹ that a perfect corundum crystal does not have: it is none of the seven allowed lattice modes of α-Al₂O₃. It has been seen in synthetic sapphire where impurities and point defects concentrate, and attributed tentatively to a transition that iron or another 3d impurity makes allowed. Its presence beside the E(g) line at 750 cm⁻¹ therefore speaks to the purity of the crystal rather than to its phase.

references.note: Fig. 2 (Sample 1, about 1 cm off the centre of the window; instrument as for the seven lattice lines): a subtle line at 724.6 cm⁻¹, present in every spectrum taken more than 1 cm from the centre and absent at it, where all lines are also weaker. The paper reads it, with the stronger lines above 640 cm⁻¹, as iron ions or other defects concentrated off-centre, and suggests unknown impurities activate the transition, most likely d-elements of the 4th period. A second new line at 176.3 cm⁻¹ it declines to interpret, possibly a laser plasma line. At the very edge, where the window touched the cryostat, only fluorescence remained, which the paper takes as a possible partial conversion of α- to γ-Al₂O₃ after two years at liquid-nitrogen temperature.

bands.description: The lowest Raman line of cubic bixbyite In₂O₃, an In-O vibration of the InO₆ units. It softens slightly when the oxide loses oxygen, read as the lattice expanding around the vacancies.

references.note: Fig. 6 (room-temperature visible Raman, 532 nm, 7 mW, 5 s, normalized; cubic In₂O₃ from In(OH)₃ precipitated with NH₄OH, PDF 06-0416, beside Pd-P/In₂O₃ and Pd-I/In₂O₃): 130 cm⁻¹, assigned to an In-O vibration of the InO₆ units (its ref. 36). On Pd/In₂O₃ it sits slightly lower, which the paper attributes to lattice expansion and mode softening as oxygen vacancies form; no shifted position is printed.

bands.description: The bending mode of the InO₆ octahedra of cubic bixbyite In₂O₃, one of its strongest Raman lines. It changes little when the oxide is reduced, which is why it is the reference the In-O-In line near 365 cm⁻¹ is ratioed against to compare oxygen vacancies between samples.

references.note: Fig. 3c and Section 3.2 (visible Raman, 532 nm, 7 mW, 10 s, room temperature; cubic bixbyite In₂O₃ precipitated with ammonia and calcined at 723 K, PDF 06-0416), measured after H₂/N₂ (1/9) at 573 K and after 3 h of CO₂ hydrogenation at 573 K: 306 cm⁻¹, one of three bands the paper assigns to vibrations of the InO₆ octahedra (with 495 and 630). It is I₁, the reference of the I₂/I₁ ratio the paper uses to compare oxygen vacancies (Fig. 3e).

Fig. 6 (room-temperature visible Raman, 532 nm, 7 mW, 5 s, normalized; cubic In₂O₃ from In(OH)₃ precipitated with NH₄OH, PDF 06-0416, beside Pd-P/In₂O₃ and Pd-I/In₂O₃): 306 cm⁻¹, attributed to the bending mode of the InO₆ octahedra.

bands.description: The stretch of the In-O-In bridges of cubic bixbyite In₂O₃. It grows as oxygen vacancies form, by breaking one of the double oxygen bridges, so its intensity against the InO₆ bend near 306 cm⁻¹ is the usual Raman measure of how reduced the oxide is; a metal that spills hydrogen onto it, Pd or Re, raises it.

references.note: Fig. 3c and Section 3.2 (visible Raman, 532 nm, 7 mW, 10 s, room temperature; cubic bixbyite In₂O₃ precipitated with ammonia and calcined at 723 K, PDF 06-0416), measured after H₂/N₂ (1/9) at 573 K and after 3 h of CO₂ hydrogenation at 573 K: 365 cm⁻¹, the In-O-In stretch, which the paper calls sensitive to oxygen vacancies. As I₂ against I₁ at 306 cm⁻¹ it gives 0.69 for In₂O₃ after reduction and 1.15 after reaction, and 1.14 and 1.22 for 1Re/In₂O₃ and 5Re/In₂O₃ after reduction (Fig. 3e), read as more vacancies with Re and over-reduction of bare In₂O₃ under reaction.

Fig. 6 (room-temperature visible Raman, 532 nm, 7 mW, 5 s, normalized; cubic In₂O₃ from In(OH)₃ precipitated with NH₄OH, PDF 06-0416, beside Pd-P/In₂O₃ and Pd-I/In₂O₃): 364 cm⁻¹, assigned to ν(In-O-In). Its intensity grows markedly on Pd/In₂O₃, which the paper attributes in part to more oxygen vacancies, from breaking one of the double oxygen bridges In-O-In.

bands.description: A stretching vibration of the InO₆ octahedra of cubic bixbyite In₂O₃.

references.note: Fig. 3c and Section 3.2 (visible Raman, 532 nm, 7 mW, 10 s, room temperature; cubic bixbyite In₂O₃ precipitated with ammonia and calcined at 723 K, PDF 06-0416), measured after H₂/N₂ (1/9) at 573 K and after 3 h of CO₂ hydrogenation at 573 K: 495 cm⁻¹, one of three bands the paper assigns to vibrations of the InO₆ octahedra.

Fig. 6 (room-temperature visible Raman, 532 nm, 7 mW, 5 s, normalized; cubic In₂O₃ from In(OH)₃ precipitated with NH₄OH, PDF 06-0416, beside Pd-P/In₂O₃ and Pd-I/In₂O₃): 493 cm⁻¹, interpreted as the stretching vibrations of the InO₆ octahedra (its ref. 37).

bands.description: The highest Raman line of cubic bixbyite In₂O₃, attributed to vibrations of the InO₆ octahedra.

references.note: Fig. 3c and Section 3.2 (visible Raman, 532 nm, 7 mW, 10 s, room temperature; cubic bixbyite In₂O₃ precipitated with ammonia and calcined at 723 K, PDF 06-0416), measured after H₂/N₂ (1/9) at 573 K and after 3 h of CO₂ hydrogenation at 573 K: 630 cm⁻¹, the third band the paper assigns to vibrations of the InO₆ octahedra. Rui et al. 2017 name no line near it in their text on the same polymorph.

bands.description: The strongest Raman line of anatase TiO₂, the lowest of its three E(g) lattice modes. Anatase (I4₁/amd) has six Raman-active modes, A₁(g) + 2B₁(g) + 3E(g), and three infrared-active ones, A₂(u) + 2E(u); it is centrosymmetric, so none of its Raman lines absorbs in the infrared. This line is intense enough to reveal anatase at a few per cent. It nearly coincides with rutile's weak B₁(g) at 143 cm⁻¹, so in a mixture a line here is anatase. In nanocrystals it moves up by several wavenumbers and broadens.

references.note: Table II and Fig. 2 (anatase: TiO₂ from slowly evaporated tetraisopropyl titanate, heated to 450 °C in air; powder in a capillary, back-scattering, 488 nm argon-ion line, 2 cm⁻¹ slit, room temperature): 147 cm⁻¹, the strongest band of the spectrum, assigned E(g) against the single-crystal data of Ohsaka et al. (144 cm⁻¹). The paper notes it falls almost on rutile's B₁(g) at 144.

bands.description: The second E(g) lattice mode of anatase, weak, about 50 cm⁻¹ above the strongest line. Raman-active and infrared-inactive, as every anatase g mode is.

references.note: Table II and Fig. 2 (anatase: TiO₂ from slowly evaporated tetraisopropyl titanate, heated to 450 °C in air; powder in a capillary, back-scattering, 488 nm argon-ion line, 2 cm⁻¹ slit, room temperature): 198 cm⁻¹, assigned E(g) against Ohsaka et al. (197 cm⁻¹).

bands.description: The lower B₁(g) lattice mode of anatase, a medium line that with the lines near 515 and 640 cm⁻¹ identifies the phase. Its first overtone appears, weak, near 796 cm⁻¹.

references.note: Table II and Fig. 2 (anatase: TiO₂ from slowly evaporated tetraisopropyl titanate, heated to 450 °C in air; powder in a capillary, back-scattering, 488 nm argon-ion line, 2 cm⁻¹ slit, room temperature): 398 cm⁻¹, assigned B₁(g) against Ohsaka et al. (399 cm⁻¹).

Fig. 1 (anatase nanoparticles, Hombikat UV100, nominal size about 10 nm, as powder on a Si substrate; WITec α-SNOM Raman microscope, 488 nm argon-ion line, ×50 objective, about 0.3 mW): 397 cm⁻¹, labelled B₁(g). The lines serve only as markers to find TiO₂ on red blood cells in Raman maps; the paper labels them after the literature and assigns nothing itself.

bands.description: Two anatase lattice modes, A₁(g) and the upper B₁(g), only about 6 cm⁻¹ apart: at room temperature they make one line near 515 cm⁻¹, separating into 513 and 519 cm⁻¹ only on cooling to about 73 K. A source that labels this line with one symmetry is naming half of it.

references.note: Table II and Fig. 2 (anatase: TiO₂ from slowly evaporated tetraisopropyl titanate, heated to 450 °C in air; powder in a capillary, back-scattering, 488 nm argon-ion line, 2 cm⁻¹ slit, room temperature): 515 cm⁻¹, assigned to the unresolved doublet of A₁(g) and B₁(g), which Ohsaka et al. split into 513 and 519 cm⁻¹ at 73 K.

Fig. 1 (anatase nanoparticles, Hombikat UV100, nominal size about 10 nm, as powder on a Si substrate; WITec α-SNOM Raman microscope, 488 nm argon-ion line, ×50 objective, about 0.3 mW): 516 cm⁻¹, labelled A₁(g) alone; it is the A₁(g) + B₁(g) doublet, which room-temperature spectra do not resolve. The lines serve only as markers to find TiO₂ on red blood cells in Raman maps; the paper labels them after the literature and assigns nothing itself.

bands.description: The highest E(g) lattice mode of anatase, a strong line. In a mixture it sits beside rutile's A₁(g) near 612 cm⁻¹, which shows first as a shoulder on its low side.

references.note: Table II and Fig. 2 (anatase: TiO₂ from slowly evaporated tetraisopropyl titanate, heated to 450 °C in air; powder in a capillary, back-scattering, 488 nm argon-ion line, 2 cm⁻¹ slit, room temperature): 640 cm⁻¹, assigned E(g) against Ohsaka et al. (639 cm⁻¹). Scanned slowly and curve-fitted (Figs. 3 to 5), it carries a shoulder at 612 cm⁻¹, rutile's A₁(g).

Fig. 1 (anatase nanoparticles, Hombikat UV100, nominal size about 10 nm, as powder on a Si substrate; WITec α-SNOM Raman microscope, 488 nm argon-ion line, ×50 objective, about 0.3 mW): 639 cm⁻¹, labelled E(g); the paper maps the 600–650 cm⁻¹ window to find the anatase particles. The lines serve only as markers to find TiO₂ on red blood cells in Raman maps; the paper labels them after the literature and assigns nothing itself.

bands.description: The first overtone of anatase's B₁(g) lattice mode at 398 cm⁻¹, weak, at about twice its frequency.

references.note: Table II and Fig. 2 (anatase: TiO₂ from slowly evaporated tetraisopropyl titanate, heated to 450 °C in air; powder in a capillary, back-scattering, 488 nm argon-ion line, 2 cm⁻¹ slit, room temperature): a weak band at 796 cm⁻¹, assigned to the first overtone of the B₁(g) mode at 398 cm⁻¹, as Ohsaka et al. also found it.

bands.description: A weak, broad feature near 320 cm⁻¹ in anatase that is no lattice fundamental: read either as second-order, two-phonon scattering or as disorder letting otherwise silent phonons show. Rutile has a broad band of the same kind in this region.

references.note: Table II and Fig. 2 (anatase: TiO₂ from slowly evaporated tetraisopropyl titanate, heated to 450 °C in air; powder in a capillary, back-scattering, 488 nm argon-ion line, 2 cm⁻¹ slit, room temperature): a weak, broad band centred near 320 cm⁻¹, also present in rutile, which the paper attributes to second-order or disorder-induced scattering without deciding between them; earlier authors reported it too.

bands.description: The lowest Raman line of rutile TiO₂, the B₁(g) lattice mode, weak. Rutile (P4₂/mnm) has four Raman-active modes, A₁(g) + B₁(g) + B₂(g) + E(g), four infrared-active ones, A₂(u) + 3E(u), and A₂(g) + 2B₁(u) silent; every Raman line is infrared-inactive. This one lies under anatase's strongest line, so in a mixture it does not tell rutile apart.

references.note: Table I and Fig. 1 (rutile: the same sol-gel TiO₂ heated to 750 °C in air for 5 h; powder in a capillary, back-scattering, 488 nm argon-ion line, 2 cm⁻¹ slit, room temperature): 144 cm⁻¹, assigned B₁(g) from the single-crystal polarisation data of Porto et al. (143 cm⁻¹).

bands.description: The E(g) lattice mode of rutile, one of its two strong lines; with the A₁(g) near 612 cm⁻¹ it is the usual fingerprint of the phase.

references.note: Table I and Fig. 1 (rutile: the same sol-gel TiO₂ heated to 750 °C in air for 5 h; powder in a capillary, back-scattering, 488 nm argon-ion line, 2 cm⁻¹ slit, room temperature): 448 cm⁻¹, assigned E(g) after Porto et al. (447 cm⁻¹). A weak band at the same position in the anatase heated to only 400 to 450 °C is the paper's evidence that rutile forms in fine powders far below the bulk transition.

Fig. 1 (predominantly rutile nanoparticles, Sigma, nominal size up to 100 nm, as powder on a Si substrate; WITec α-SNOM Raman microscope, 488 nm argon-ion line, ×50 objective, about 0.3 mW): 445 cm⁻¹, labelled E(g). The lines serve only as markers to find TiO₂ on red blood cells in Raman maps; the paper labels them after the literature and assigns nothing itself.

bands.description: The A₁(g) lattice mode of rutile, its strongest line with the E(g) near 447 cm⁻¹. Beside anatase's E(g) at 640 cm⁻¹ it shows first as a shoulder on that line's low side.

references.note: Table I and Fig. 1 (rutile: the same sol-gel TiO₂ heated to 750 °C in air for 5 h; powder in a capillary, back-scattering, 488 nm argon-ion line, 2 cm⁻¹ slit, room temperature): 612 cm⁻¹, assigned A₁(g) after Porto et al. (612 cm⁻¹). In the anatase heated to 450 °C it is resolved only by curve fitting, as a shoulder of the 640 cm⁻¹ line (Figs. 3 to 5).

Fig. 1 (predominantly rutile nanoparticles, Sigma, nominal size up to 100 nm, as powder on a Si substrate; WITec α-SNOM Raman microscope, 488 nm argon-ion line, ×50 objective, about 0.3 mW): 610 cm⁻¹, labelled B₁(g) in Fig. 1 but A₁(g) in the text (Sect. 3.2); A₁(g) is the standard assignment of this line, rutile's B₁(g) lying near 143 cm⁻¹. The lines serve only as markers to find TiO₂ on red blood cells in Raman maps; the paper labels them after the literature and assigns nothing itself.

bands.description: The B₂(g) lattice mode of rutile, weak, the fourth of its Raman-active modes and the one most often missing from a spectrum.

references.note: Table I and Fig. 1 (rutile: the same sol-gel TiO₂ heated to 750 °C in air for 5 h; powder in a capillary, back-scattering, 488 nm argon-ion line, 2 cm⁻¹ slit, room temperature): a weak band at 827 cm⁻¹, assigned B₂(g) after Porto et al. (826 cm⁻¹); the paper notes this mode scatters weakly.

bands.description: A strong, broad band near 235 cm⁻¹ in rutile that is no lattice fundamental. Its strength had it assigned as one, but its polarisation fits none of the allowed modes and no allowed combination falls here; it is read as second-order scattering, strong in TiO₂ because its TiO₆ octahedra are very anharmonic, or as disorder-induced.

references.note: Table I and Fig. 1 (rutile: the same sol-gel TiO₂ heated to 750 °C in air for 5 h; powder in a capillary, back-scattering, 488 nm argon-ion line, 2 cm⁻¹ slit, room temperature): an anomalously strong, broad band at 235 cm⁻¹ with structure at high resolution, attributed to second-order or disorder-induced scattering. The paper weighs Narayanan's polarisation data, Porto's combination reading and Hara and Nicol's disorder reading, and leaves the choice open.

bands.description: A weak, broad band between about 320 and 360 cm⁻¹ in rutile, like the one near 235 cm⁻¹ not a fundamental: second-order or disorder-induced scattering. Anatase shows a broad feature near 320 cm⁻¹ of the same kind.

references.note: Table I and Fig. 1 (rutile: the same sol-gel TiO₂ heated to 750 °C in air for 5 h; powder in a capillary, back-scattering, 488 nm argon-ion line, 2 cm⁻¹ slit, room temperature): a weak, broad band from 320 to 360 cm⁻¹, its two maxima labelled 322 and 362 in Fig. 1; seen before by Narayanan and by Porto et al. but left out of their discussions. Second-order or disorder-induced, like the 235 cm⁻¹ band.

bands.description: The boson peak, a broad low-frequency Raman band that is a signature of tetrahedrally connected glasses and has no counterpart in the crystal. In silica glass it lies near 50-60 cm⁻¹; distorting the tetrahedra, as light network modifiers do, raises it. Its origin is still debated, the usual reading being rotation of nearly rigid tetrahedra.

references.note: Ch. 2.1 (Neuville, Cicconi, Blanc and Lancry, Raman spectroscopy of glass and glass fibre), p. 111 and Fig. 2.13: the boson peak of SiO₂ glass at 54 cm⁻¹, moving to 70 cm⁻¹ with 40 mol% Na₂O; heavy modifiers (K, Ba, Sr, Cs) leave it near 50 cm⁻¹, as in silica glass. Ascribed to rotational motion of almost rigid tetrahedra, an origin the chapter calls controversial; it puts the peak near 80 cm⁻¹ in the historical account and fits it near 60 cm⁻¹ in the fibre work.

bands.description: The strongest Raman feature of silica glass, the broad R band near 440 cm⁻¹, spread over roughly 410 to 450 cm⁻¹ by the distribution of Si-O-Si angles. It is the motion of the bridging oxygens in the larger rings (five-membered and up), read as a symmetric stretch by some sources and as a bend by others; all agree the oxygen moves. It is the usual internal standard a silica spectrum is normalised to.

references.note: Section 3.2 and Fig. 2 (in-situ Raman, 532 nm, 10 mW; dehydrated 8% V₂O₅/SiO₂ on the same fumed silica at 450 °C, during H₂¹⁸O exchange), a band the paper attributes to the silica support: the network bending mode, given as a range, 410-450 cm⁻¹, and among the bulk vibrations that do not shift during ¹⁸O exchange.

Fig. 1 and Section 2 (polarised VV Raman, double monochromator with photomultiplier; silica glasses sintered from Degussa OX50 fumed silica, about 120 nm particles, 50 m² g⁻¹; spectra normalised to the amplitude at 440 cm⁻¹): 440 cm⁻¹ is the amplitude every spectrum is normalised to, the main band of the network; the paper names no assignment for it.

Ch. 2.1 (Neuville, Cicconi, Blanc and Lancry, Raman spectroscopy of glass and glass fibre), pp. 107, 113 and 117: in SiO₂ glass, the band at about 435-440 cm⁻¹, called R in the fibre work, is the symmetric stretch of bridging oxygens, the predominant motion of oxygen in Si-O-Si bonds of five-, six- or higher-membered rings. The chapter adds that whether the motion is a stretch or a bend seems uncertain, but every study points to the oxygen of the Si-O-Si linkage.

bands.description: The D1 defect line of amorphous silica, a sharp band near 490 cm⁻¹ above the network band. It is a breathing motion of the oxygens of small rings, almost pure oxygen motion, assigned to four-membered siloxane rings in the small planar ring model and to Si=O on paracrystalline surfaces in the cluster model. Its intensity reports the ring population, which sintering, crystallisation, oxygen and water change.

references.note: Section 3.2 and Fig. 2 (in-situ Raman, 532 nm, 10 mW; dehydrated 8% V₂O₅/SiO₂ on the same fumed silica at 450 °C, during H₂¹⁸O exchange), a band the paper attributes to the silica support: D1 at 487 cm⁻¹, attributed to tetracyclosiloxane (four-membered) rings, which does not appreciably shift with ¹⁸O.

Introduction (polarised VV Raman, double monochromator with photomultiplier; silica glasses sintered from Degussa OX50 fumed silica, about 120 nm particles, 50 m² g⁻¹; spectra normalised to the amplitude at 440 cm⁻¹): D1 at 495 cm⁻¹, quoted from the literature (its ref. 2) rather than read off its own spectra; four-membered rings in the small planar ring model, double-bonded Si=O on the [100] surface of paracrystalline domains in the cluster model. Its amplitude falls with crystallisation and in water vapour and rises in oxygen and with hydrogen in the glass.

Ch. 2.1 (Neuville, Cicconi, Blanc and Lancry, Raman spectroscopy of glass and glass fibre), pp. 107 and 113: D1 near 485-490 cm⁻¹ (495 in the list of three peaks), breathing of the oxygens, perpendicular to the Si-O-Si plane, in regular but slightly puckered four-membered rings. Absent from the VH spectra of a transversely probed fibre (p. 117).

bands.description: The D2 defect line of amorphous silica, a sharp band near 605 cm⁻¹, the breathing of the oxygens of three-membered siloxane rings, decoupled from the network. Water opens such strained rings to silanols, so D2 falls when a silica is hydroxylated and grows when it is dried hot.

references.note: Fig. 1 (in-situ Raman, 325 nm, 7 mW; amorphous fumed silica, Cab-O-Sil EH-5, 332 m² g⁻¹, water-pretreated and calcined at 500 °C, dehydrated at 450 °C under flowing ¹⁶O₂): D2 of the three-membered cyclosiloxane ring at 605 cm⁻¹. After exchange with H₂¹⁸O it moves slightly, to about 600 cm⁻¹.

Introduction (polarised VV Raman, double monochromator with photomultiplier; silica glasses sintered from Degussa OX50 fumed silica, about 120 nm particles, 50 m² g⁻¹; spectra normalised to the amplitude at 440 cm⁻¹): D2 at 606 cm⁻¹, quoted from the literature (its ref. 2); three-membered rings in the small planar ring model, four-membered rings of the intercluster layer in the cluster model. It behaves like D1 under every treatment the paper tries.

Ch. 2.1 (Neuville, Cicconi, Blanc and Lancry, Raman spectroscopy of glass and glass fibre), pp. 107 and 113: D2 near 606 cm⁻¹ (600 on p. 107), breathing of the oxygens in planar three-membered rings; like D1, absent from VH spectra.

bands.description: The symmetric stretch of the Si-O-Si bridges of amorphous silica, a weak broad band near 800 cm⁻¹ that ¹⁸O exchange of the surface does not move.

references.note: Section 3.2 and Fig. 2 (in-situ Raman, 532 nm, 10 mW; dehydrated 8% V₂O₅/SiO₂ on the same fumed silica at 450 °C, during H₂¹⁸O exchange), a band the paper attributes to the silica support: the Si-O-Si symmetric stretch at about 800 cm⁻¹, among the bulk vibrations that do not shift during ¹⁸O exchange.

bands.description: The transverse-optical component of the antisymmetric Si-O-Si stretch of amorphous silica, weak and broad near 1065 cm⁻¹ in Raman. It gains intensity when a supported metal oxide perturbs the network, and the oxygen it moves exchanges with ¹⁸O.

references.note: Fig. 1 (in-situ Raman, 325 nm, 7 mW; amorphous fumed silica, Cab-O-Sil EH-5, 332 m² g⁻¹, water-pretreated and calcined at 500 °C, dehydrated at 450 °C under flowing ¹⁶O₂): the TO stretch of the network at 1065 cm⁻¹, weak and broad, shifting to about 1030 cm⁻¹ on exchange with H₂¹⁸O. It is enhanced near 1060 cm⁻¹ on Nb₂O₅/SiO₂ (Fig. 4).

Ch. 2.1 (Neuville, Cicconi, Blanc and Lancry, Raman spectroscopy of glass and glass fibre), pp. 107 and 114: pure SiO₂ glass has only two high-frequency peaks, near 1050 cm⁻¹ and a wider one near 1200 cm⁻¹, weak bands of the asymmetric Si-O stretch of the tetrahedra. The chapter does not split them into TO and LO; adding Na₂O strengthens the 1050 cm⁻¹ peak strongly.

bands.description: The longitudinal-optical partner of the antisymmetric Si-O-Si stretch of amorphous silica, a weak broad Raman band near 1200 cm⁻¹, about 135 cm⁻¹ above its TO component.

references.note: Fig. 1 (in-situ Raman, 325 nm, 7 mW; amorphous fumed silica, Cab-O-Sil EH-5, 332 m² g⁻¹, water-pretreated and calcined at 500 °C, dehydrated at 450 °C under flowing ¹⁶O₂): the LO stretch of the network at 1200 cm⁻¹, weak and broad, shifting to about 1155 cm⁻¹ on exchange with H₂¹⁸O.

Ch. 2.1 (Neuville, Cicconi, Blanc and Lancry, Raman spectroscopy of glass and glass fibre), p. 114: the wider of the two high-frequency peaks of SiO₂ glass, near 1200 cm⁻¹. Deconvolution splits it into Q⁴,II at 1100 and Q⁴,I at 1170 cm⁻¹, bridging oxygens at smaller and larger Si-O-Si angles in the Sen and Thorpe model, an assignment the chapter calls controversial.

bands.description: One of the Raman lines of β-cristobalite (120, 310, 330 cm⁻¹), the silica polymorph a glass starts to crystallise into near 1450 °C. They appear sharp on the glass background as crystallisation begins and vanish again when the sample is remelted.

references.note: Fig. 2 (polarised VV Raman, double monochromator with photomultiplier; silica glasses sintered from Degussa OX50 fumed silica, about 120 nm particles, 50 m² g⁻¹; spectra normalised to the amplitude at 440 cm⁻¹) difference spectra of sample S4, sintered in high vacuum at 1450 °C for 40 min against S1: one of the new bands at 120, 310 and 330 cm⁻¹ that the paper calls characteristic of β-cristobalite (its ref. 8), appearing where crystallisation starts and gone after remelting; a band near 320 cm⁻¹ marks the same onset again after tempering (S6).

bands.description: One of the Raman lines of β-cristobalite (120, 310, 330 cm⁻¹), the silica polymorph a glass starts to crystallise into near 1450 °C. They appear sharp on the glass background as crystallisation begins and vanish again when the sample is remelted.

references.note: Fig. 2 (polarised VV Raman, double monochromator with photomultiplier; silica glasses sintered from Degussa OX50 fumed silica, about 120 nm particles, 50 m² g⁻¹; spectra normalised to the amplitude at 440 cm⁻¹) difference spectra of sample S4, sintered in high vacuum at 1450 °C for 40 min against S1: one of the new bands at 120, 310 and 330 cm⁻¹ that the paper calls characteristic of β-cristobalite (its ref. 8), appearing where crystallisation starts and gone after remelting; a band near 320 cm⁻¹ marks the same onset again after tempering (S6).

bands.description: One of the Raman lines of β-cristobalite (120, 310, 330 cm⁻¹), the silica polymorph a glass starts to crystallise into near 1450 °C. They appear sharp on the glass background as crystallisation begins and vanish again when the sample is remelted.

bands.description: The strongest Raman line of α-quartz, near 466 cm⁻¹, its A₁ mode. A sharp line at this position on a silica sample means crystalline quartz rather than glass.

references.note: Ch. 2.1 (Neuville, Cicconi, Blanc and Lancry, Raman spectroscopy of glass and glass fibre), p. 106: α-quartz shows a very strong A₁ Raman-active mode at 466 cm⁻¹, below the 520 cm⁻¹ line of crystalline Si; its A₂ (infrared-active) and E modes split into LO and TO components.

bands.description: The Q branch of the nitrogen stretch, ΔJ = 0, and effectively the whole of what a Raman spectrum of air shows near 2330 cm⁻¹. N₂ is homonuclear, so the mode is infrared-forbidden and Raman is the only route to it. As a linear molecule in a non-degenerate vibration it takes ΔJ = 0 and ±2 only, so the band carries O, Q and S branches and no P or R. The Q lines pile up at the centre and dominate; the O and S wings hold the rest.

references.note: Sect. 3.2 and Fig. 5 (200-shot averaged, 0.1 mm slit, apparatus width 35 cm⁻¹): 2331 cm⁻¹ is the fundamental vibrational Raman frequency the paper assigns to ν₀ for its N₂ line-shape diagram, and the cross-talk discussion places the Q branch near 2330 cm⁻¹. Recorded in room-temperature air at 10 atm to fix the polarizability ratio (a₀/b₀)² = 0.25 for nitrogen, then checked against a 10 atm H₂-air flame at 1425 K. In the paper’s 30 atm spectra, which are simulated rather than measured, the pure-rotational H₂ S(10) line falls completely on top of this branch. The paper names only a pulsed Nd:YAG and never states the line; 532 nm is inferred from its own figure axes.

bands.description: The O branch of the nitrogen stretch, ΔJ = −2, falling below the Q branch. With the S branch above it this is the whole rotational structure a linear molecule in a non-degenerate vibration is allowed, ΔJ = 0 and ±2, which is why nitrogen shows no P or R branch in Raman. It is far weaker than the Q branch and usually reads as a tail rather than as resolved lines. The window is the envelope the populated levels reach, not a reported position.

references.note: Fig. 5 and Fig. 8: the O branch of vibrational N₂, marked on the figure as the blue-side tail of the Q branch and resolved in room-temperature air at 10 atm, where its intensity relative to the Q branch fixes the polarizability ratio (a₀/b₀)² = 0.25. The paper prints no position for it, so none is recorded. In the simulated 30 atm spectra it runs into the pure-rotational H₂ S(8) and S(9) lines, overlapping by 48% at an equivalence ratio of 1.5 and by 65% for S(9). Spontaneous Raman with a pulsed Nd:YAG. The paper never states the line: 532 nm is inferred from its own figure axes, where the 2331 cm⁻¹ N₂ Q branch falls at about 607 nm.

bands.description: The S branch of the nitrogen stretch, ΔJ = +2, above the Q branch and the mirror of the O branch below it. Weak, and normally an unresolved tail: nitrogen's rotational constant is about 2 cm⁻¹, so its lines sit only a few wavenumbers apart and blur together at any ordinary resolution. The window is the envelope the populated levels reach rather than a reported position.

references.note: Fig. 5 and Fig. 8: the S branch of vibrational N₂, marked on the figure as the red-side tail of the Q branch, recorded in room-temperature air at 10 atm alongside the O branch to fix the polarizability ratio (a₀/b₀)² = 0.25. The paper prints no position for it, so none is recorded. In the simulated 30 atm spectra it overlaps the pure-rotational H₂ S(11) line. Spontaneous Raman with a pulsed Nd:YAG. bands.description: The Q branch of the hydrogen stretch, ΔJ = 0, near 4160 cm⁻¹ and the highest fundamental of any common molecule. H₂ is homonuclear and infrared-forbidden, so Raman is the only route to it. Its rotational constant is very large, about 59 cm⁻¹, which throws the O and S branches hundreds of wavenumbers clear of the centre instead of leaving them as tails: hydrogen's branches are separate features rather than wings on one band.

references.note: Sect. 3.1 and Fig. 7: 4160 cm⁻¹ is the fundamental frequency the paper assigns to ν₀ for the vibrational-H₂ line-shape diagram, with an averaged line separation within the branch of 19.8 cm⁻¹, far smaller than the 180 cm⁻¹ separation of the pure-rotational spectrum. Measured in a 10 atm H₂-air flame at 1133 K, the temperature itself taken from the pure-rotational H₂ lines. The paper names only a pulsed Nd:YAG and never states the line; 532 nm is inferred from its own figure axes.

bands.description: One resolved line of the hydrogen O branch, the transition starting from J = 3. Hydrogen's rotational constant is about 59 cm⁻¹, so its rotational lines stand hundreds of wavenumbers apart and are separate features rather than the unresolved tail a heavier molecule gives: that is why this branch is carried as lines and nitrogen's as one envelope. The window is computed from the band origin at 4160 cm⁻¹ and that rotational constant, since the source names the line but prints no position.

One line of the pure rotational Raman spectrum of hydrogen, the transition from J = 2 to J = 4. Nothing vibrates: the molecule only turns faster, and Raman reaches the change directly through the polarizability. Only ΔJ = +2 arises for pure rotation, since the upper level is by definition the higher one, so this spectrum is an S branch and nothing else. Hydrogen spreads it over more than 2000 cm⁻¹, with lines about 180 cm⁻¹ apart, which is why they are carried one by one.

bands.description: Carbonic acid held on hydroxylated silica, in equilibrium with adsorbed CO₂ and water rather than existing on its own. Free H₂CO₃ is unstable, but multiple hydrogen bonds to surface silanols stabilise it enough to be seen. The band is a trap: monodentate κ¹-formate is calculated to absorb at the same position, and only its lifetime rules it out. It rises and falls with the CO₂ band near 2341 cm⁻¹, and unlike formate it has no partner in the C-H region, which is the positive evidence that no C-H bond is present.

references.note: Figs. 4 and S10 (transient DRIFTS, 1 wt % Ag/SiO₂ and bare SiO₂, CO₂:H₂ = 1:1 against Ar, 230 °C, 5 bar), resolved by multivariate curve resolution. Isotope substitution (Fig. S13) is what fixes it: the band moves to 1638 cm⁻¹ under ¹³CO₂ but only to 1684 under D₂, so it is a C-O vibration with almost no hydrogen displacement. It tracks the 2341 cm⁻¹ CO₂ band exactly. Formates, carbonates and formic acid are excluded by the absence of any matching C-H band; κ¹-formate is excluded instead by its calculated lifetime, which on Ag is of the order of a molecular vibration (Table S6).

Table S5 (PBE-D″/plane-wave, PHONON package): ν₅, the C=O stretch of H₂CO₃ adsorbed as O(top)+H(bridge) on Ag(111), calculated at 1669 cm⁻¹ against the 1688 cm⁻¹ observed. The same table puts free H₂CO₃ at 1748 cm⁻¹, so adsorption is calculated to pull the stretch down by about 80 cm⁻¹. A caveat on the comparison: the frequency is computed on the metal, while the band is assigned to carbonic acid on the silica, whose stabilisation the paper treats separately in Table S3. A periodic Ag(111) slab in vacuum.

bands.description: CO₂ held on silica through its silanol groups, rather than bound to a cation or bent into a carbonate. The position is barely shifted from the free molecule, which is the difficulty: it sits underneath the gas-phase band and is separable only by how it behaves in time, not by where it lies. The silanol stretches lose intensity reversibly as it appears, which is the evidence that the OH groups are what hold it.

references.note: Figs. S9, S10 and S12 (transient DRIFTS, 1 wt % Ag/SiO₂ and bare SiO₂, 230 °C, 5 bar). The band lies under gaseous CO₂ and is recovered only because it follows a different time course, separated by multivariate curve resolution in a plug-flow cell with minimal gas volume. Isotope substitution (Fig. S13) moves it to 2276 cm⁻¹ under ¹³CO₂ and leaves it at 2341 under D₂. It appears on bare silica as well as on Ag/SiO₂, and the silanol bands between 3500 and 3800 cm⁻¹ fall reversibly as it grows (Fig. S11), which is what ties it to the OH groups.

bands.description: Asymmetric stretch of CO₂ dissolved in a liquid. In solution the molecule no longer rotates freely, so the P and R envelopes of the gas collapse into a single band a little below the gas origin at 2349 cm⁻¹. In electrochemical difference spectra taken during CO₂ reduction it usually points down: the electrode consumes CO₂ from the thin layer of electrolyte the beam samples, so the band reports interfacial depletion, not an adsorbate. Gas-phase CO₂ in the optical path sits at nearly the same place and is told apart by its rotational envelope.

references.note: Fig. 2a to c: Ag film electrode in CO₂-saturated 0.1 M CsHCO₃, static and pulsed electrolysis alike. A downward band near 2340 cm⁻¹ marks dissolved CO₂ consumed from the electrolyte next to the electrode; the spectra are differences against a reference spectrum, so down means less. No surface is recorded because the molecule is in the electrolyte, not on the silver. The paper’s diffusion model and mass spectrometry say the same from the other side: interfacial CO₂ is replenished during the anodic pulse.

Fig. S31: Cu film electrode in CO₂-saturated 0.1 M CsHCO₃, swept from −0.2 to −1.1 V vs. RHE against open circuit in Ar-saturated CsHCO₃, so the dissolved CO₂ shows against an electrolyte that had none. The label sits at 2345 cm⁻¹. No surface is recorded: the molecule is in the electrolyte.

bands.description: The O branch of ν₃ (F₂), the pentad, ΔJ = −2, reaching below the band centre. Methane is a spherical top, and for its degenerate vibrations Raman reaches ΔJ = 0, ±1 and ±2, so this transition carries all five branches rather than the three an infrared band would show. The O branch steps by 4B against 2B for P, so it reaches roughly twice as far out.24 cm⁻¹ and the levels populated at room temperature, not a reported position. A spherical top gives fifteen branches in all once the Coriolis sublevels are counted, and they are not equal: S and R carry considerably more intensity than O and P, with S⁺, Q⁰ and O⁻ the strongest of them.

references.note: Sect. 4.2, Fig. 3 and Fig. 13: the rotational structure either side of the sharp Q branch of ν₃ (F₂), the pentad. The paper names neither the branches nor their positions, so nothing is recorded as a position here. The O branch is carried because a spherical top allows it: the wing on this side holds O lines as well as P, and the earlier reading of that wing as P alone named only the nearer half. Spontaneous Raman of ¹²CH₄ in a gas cell at about one amagat, 4 W argon-ion laser. Laser line assumed, not reported: 515 nm is the strongest green argon-ion line.

A spherical top gives fifteen branches in all once the Coriolis sublevels are counted, and they are not equal: S and R carry considerably more intensity than O and P, with S⁺, Q⁰ and O⁻ the strongest of them.

bands.description: The totally symmetric stretch of methane-d₄, the deuterated twin of ν₁ in CH₄ and the strongest single feature of its Raman spectrum. Infrared-forbidden, as in the parent. Being totally symmetric it is the one methane band restricted to ΔJ = 0, so it is a bare Q branch with no rotational wings at all, which is what makes it so sharp against the branch structure of the other two fundamentals.

references.note: Gaseous CD₄ at 1 atm, photographed on a grating spectrograph at 10.5 cm⁻¹ per mm with about 1 cm⁻¹ resolution, excited by the mercury arc (Hg 4047 and Hg 4078). A Q branch at 2107.8 cm⁻¹, called the strongest single feature of the spectrum and assigned here to ν₁, correcting MacWood and Urey, who had read this shift as 2ν₂ and placed ν₁ at 2084.7 cm⁻¹. The line is somewhat broadened, probably by a superimposed band tentatively assigned to the E component of 2ν₂ in Coriolis interaction with ν₃.

bands.description: The O branch of the doubly degenerate deformation of methane-d₄, the deuterated twin of ν₂ in CH₄. This is the band that settles what a spherical top shows in Raman: Placzek and Teller give ΔJ = 0, ±1, ±2 for a degenerate band of a spherical top, and all five branches are resolved and assigned here line by line. The window is the span of the assigned lines themselves, not an envelope computed from a rotational constant.

references.note: Table I (gaseous CD₄ at 1 atm, Hg 4358, 10.5 cm⁻¹ per mm, about 1 cm⁻¹ resolution). O(2) at 1075.1 cm⁻¹ down to O(14) at 964.2, assigned line by line. With P below it this is the direct evidence that a spherical top reaches both ΔJ = −2 and −1 in one Raman band.

references.note: Table I (gaseous CD₄ at 1 atm, Hg 4358, 10.5 cm⁻¹ per mm, about 1 cm⁻¹ resolution). A single Q maximum at 1092.2 cm⁻¹. The Q transitions involve the alpha sublevels, as in CH₄, which the 0.7 cm⁻¹ observed shift establishes.

references.note: Table I (gaseous CD₄ at 1 atm, Hg 4358, 10.5 cm⁻¹ per mm, about 1 cm⁻¹ resolution). R(3) at 1113.3 cm⁻¹ upward, running to R(39) at the top of the table near 1342.7. The R lines fade out at J = 21 and reappear from J = 29 to 39, an intensity pattern the paper attributes to perturbation by ν₄.

bands.description: The S branch of the doubly degenerate deformation of methane-d₄, the deuterated twin of ν₂ in CH₄. references.note: Table I (gaseous CD₄ at 1 atm, Hg 4358, 10.5 cm⁻¹ per mm, about 1 cm⁻¹ resolution). S(0) at 1107.4 cm⁻¹ upward to S(19) near the top of the table. Fitting the O and S branches together gave B₀ = 2.631 cm⁻¹, the paper’s headline result.

bands.description: The triply degenerate stretch of methane-d₄, the deuterated twin of ν₃ in CH₄. Coriolis interaction splits the degenerate components into three sets of sublevels, so the band carries fifteen branches in all rather than five, and shows three Q branches instead of one. The number here is the band origin recovered from the rotational analysis; the three observed Q maxima straddle it.

references.note: Gaseous CD₄ at 1 atm, photographed on a grating spectrograph at 10.5 cm⁻¹ per mm with about 1 cm⁻¹ resolution, excited by the mercury arc (Hg 4047). Fitting the O⁰ and S⁰ branches gave a band origin of 2258.6 cm⁻¹, and the P⁰ and R⁰ branches fall on the same straight line, unlike CH₄ where they do not. Three Q branches are observed at 2250.9, 2257.5 and 2266.9 cm⁻¹ against 2250.0, 2256.8 and 2265.9 calculated. Coriolis splitting gives fifteen branches in all, the predominant intensity being in S⁺, Q⁰ and O⁻.
